Love with nowhere to go

📅 27 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3866 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Aeon

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, I have been grieving my mother for years, even though she is still alive.
  • Recent findings suggest that and yet what I felt for them, what I still feel, has the unmistakable gravity of mourning.
  • It has been revealed that over the past few years I have accumulated many such losses.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, I have been grieving my mother for years, even though she is still alive. Sometimes before falling asleep – in that liminal space between waking and sleeping where the self becomes porous – I’d see the image of the sweet and caring woman who would come to say goodnight, her cheeks covered in thick layers of night cream. Then, out of nowhere, the image would flip into the raging woman who was so entangled in her own suffering that she turned her frustration on us. Over the years, that second woman slowly swallowed the first, as she got pulled into my brother’s addiction. It’s hard to say where her own unhappiness ended and my brother’s suffering began, but together they drifted into a parallel reality, cut off from the world beyond their heads. There was no funeral for this. No condolence cards. No flowers. No phone calls. No leave of absence. What was I supposed to mourn?

Recent findings suggest that and yet what I felt for them, what I still feel, has the unmistakable gravity of mourning. Can there be grief without death? I have come to think that we grieve much more often than we realise, and that death is grief’s most visible occasion rather than its essence. If that doesn’t match your experience, it may be because we rarely call these other losses by their name. Most of our losses arrive without a funeral. That is the human predicament: we are creatures built to attach, living in a world where nothing stays. Sooner or later, we lose the things we care about. And since we are complex beings with a body, a mind, a community and an environment – beings who love many different things – there is a great deal we can lose, from our physical health to our sense of who we are, from relationships to homelands to the natural world we share with other species. For creatures like us, there is no way around heartbreak: to live is to lose. Grief is what love does when its object is gone. It is love with nowhere to go.

It has been revealed that over the past few years I have accumulated many such losses. There is the psychological loss of my father as I knew and loved him: a brutal stroke rendered him incapable of walking and cycling, and cycling was the only thing that could ‘make his thoughts liquid’, as he used to say. There is the loss of old friendships. First you are no longer part of each other’s lives – you just update one another about your life – and then, one day, it becomes awkward to reach out at all. There is the gradual softening of an academic identity I’d spent the most vital years of my life constructing. It was a genuine vocation, a life of the mind that taught me to think slowly and carefully. But it was also, as I came to realise, a way of living safely at one remove from where actual life takes place. What is slipping away is a future in which being an academic philosopher would be the whole answer to the question of who I am.

Recent findings suggest that there was the woman whose calmness, clarity and silence embodied the qualities I have come to like so much about the Nordics since moving to Norway. Like a magical stranger, she entered my life unexpectedly, but at the same time her arrival felt so natural, her presence so obvious, that it was as if she had always been there. After our first meeting, which lasted almost 24 hours, I wrote in my journal: Ze is gekomen om te blijven. ‘She had come to stay.’ And she did, for nine intense months. She tried to teach me to ski. We listened to the music of Nils Frahm, which reminded her of melting snow. And she made me see that the deepest form of intimacy happens in the space between the words.

According to recent reports, but despite the depth of our bond, she left, abruptly, as if she had never been there. She had fallen in love with another man. I was left behind, dazed and disoriented, and although my heart was broken, this kind of loss did not have a name that matched how shattered I felt. It was ‘just a breakup’, and it didn’t even deserve that name: we had been dating, but it never technically became a relationship. It was also a romantic connection that ran alongside another one, a long partnership that was open by mutual agreement and conscious design. Much about it wasn’t legible to most people around me. I faced the grief largely by myself. No scripts, no rituals, no recognised form, no legitimacy, no shared language, no way to make sense of what had happened to me.

Part of what made the experience so disorienting was a narrow idea of what grief is. In psychology, in philosophy and in our Western culture at large, grief has been treated almost exclusively as a response to the death of someone we love. It’s a neat, tidy understanding. The most celebrated grief memoirs – think of The Year of Magical Thinking (2005) by Joan Didion and A Grief Observed (1961) by C S Lewis – are concerned with the loss of a life partner. And Michael Cholbi’s Grief: A Philosophical Guide (2021) – one of the most extensive philosophical treatments of the emotion – focuses mostly on the grief we experience at the death of someone we love or who otherwise matters to us.

Restricting grief to bereavement is like restricting pain to cluster headaches.

Sources indicate that death is visible and final: it has a body, a date, a medical certificate. The other losses are blurrier: they have no physical object, no clear beginning or end, no tangible proof they happened. We also have an infrastructure for death: funerals, condolence cards, flowers, casseroles, bereavement leave – a whole social script. Perhaps the infrastructure defines what counts: if there is no social and cultural scaffolding to digest the experience, it must not be real grief.

The prime reason for the single-minded focus on death loss, however, must be that bereavement is simply the most striking instance of a broader emotional phenomenon that comes in degrees. But restricting grief to bereavement is like restricting pain to cluster headaches, anxiety to panic attacks, sadness to depression, or pleasure to ecstasy – it is taking the most extreme instantiation of something and making it the essence of that thing.

If grief isn’t just about death, what is it about? What do all these cases of grief share? A good way to answer this question starts from the observation that every emotion has a characteristic thing it is about. Fear is about danger or threat; anger is about offence or injustice; happiness and joy are about flourishing or harmony between self and world. What is grief about? If you say ‘death’, you are doing something weird: you are defining the emotion by the particular thing that sets it off, rather than by what that thing means to us. In technical philosophical jargon, you are making the mistake of conflating an emotion’s material object with its formal object. Fear of sharks, fear of public speaking and fear of heights aren’t three different emotions – shark-fear, public-speaking-fear and heights-fear. All three count as fear because they are about danger: their aim is to tell you something is threatening.

Grief clearly has something to do with loss. Although this gets us somewhere, it doesn’t get us far enough. Mere loss is necessary but not sufficient. If I lose a pen or an old sweater, I am not experiencing any grief. If I have any emotional reaction at all, it will be a slight ripple of annoyance. Perhaps we should add that for there to be grief we must lose something we care about or love, but, again, this is necessary but not sufficient. If I lose a book I really like or don’t get a dream job I applied for, what I experience is frustration or disappointment, sadness perhaps, but not grief.

What sets grief apart is how deeply the loss reaches into the fabric of your life: grief begins where your identity is disrupted. What is lost in the case of grief is not just some concrete, historical object, but a cluster of (future) possibilities that are tightly woven into your sense of identity, life structure or experiential world. When they go, you don’t just lose something: you lose a version of yourself, your life is turned upside down, and you come to inhabit, in a real sense, a different world. This is why death is grief’s most extreme instance, rather than its only one. When someone we love dies, every possibility – not only our own possibilities with them, but their possibilities too – is wiped out. As Matthew Ratcliffe and Louise Richardson, academic philosophers at the University of York, put it in their paper ‘Grief Over Non-Death Losses: A Phenomenological Perspective’ (2023):.

This reorganisation is not merely cognitive. It lives in many other places: in the body (the hand that still reaches for the phone to text someone who no longer answers your messages), in how you experience your surroundings (the café you used to visit together that now feels alien or even hostile), or in your autobiographical memories (the shared joke that simply doesn’t land with other people).

‘I am grieving the future children I imagined and believed I would have but am unable to’.

My mother is still alive. No one has died: there is no concrete, historical object that has been pulled beyond my grasp. But a whole set of possibilities that had been woven into the structure of my life and world, all bound up with having a mother who was present, responsive, good enough – those are gone. It has become impossible to call her and poke that mind of hers, so unusually free and unusually deep.

The same goes for my father. Sure, he survived the stroke. But the man whose restless mind needed to cycle to make his thoughts liquid – the future I had with that man, the shared cycling trips in the south of France, the conversations that needed repetitive, cyclical movement to come alive – that future was negated. The same structure holds for the woman whose disappearance collapsed an experiential world that felt like a home I had only just found, and for the academic identity I had built over almost two decades. As other vocations began to call more insistently, a single, all-consuming way of being in the world – the thinker, the life of the mind, the person whose future would be organised around reading and writing – loosened its hold.

It has been revealed that the case that makes this way of thinking about grief most compelling, though, is one where there is no concrete object of loss at all. Ratcliffe and Richardson’s central example is involuntary childlessness – grief for a child who never was, a future that was imagined, anticipated and deeply woven into one’s sense of self, but that never materialised. Here, no one died and no one left. There is nothing tangible to point to: no grave, no anniversary, no recorded name, no memorial service, no shared practices to give words or meaning to the loss. And yet, as one respondent in their study put it: ‘No one can understand what it’s like to carry this loss. In their minds, no baby meant no loss.’ Another respondent simply called their grief by its name: ‘I am grieving the future children I imagined and believed I would have but am unable to.’ And a third spoke, chillingly, of ‘the death of a future life’.

They lack the interpretative resources to understand and share significant aspects of their experience.

Sources indicate that ‘No baby meant no loss.’ Many forms of non-death loss are what the family therapist Pauline Boss calls ‘ambiguous loss’. These are losses without clear boundaries, without a definite beginning or end – cases where someone is physically present but psychologically gone, or physically gone but psychologically still there. Think of an Alzheimer’s patient whose self has been erased by the disease or of a soldier missing in action. Because many non-death losses are ambiguous, the grief that follows them is not openly acknowledged, socially validated or publicly mourned – what the grief scholar Kenneth Doka has called ‘disenfranchised grief’.

In a recent development, those whose grief is disenfranchised because their losses are ambiguous don’t just lack scripts or rituals or traditions. They lack the interpretative resources to understand and share significant aspects of their experience. When we lack the concepts to name what it is like to be us, what it is we are going through, we suffer what the philosopher Miranda Fricker calls a ‘hermeneutical injustice’ – an inability to make our own experience intelligible to ourselves and to others. This is not because we are confused, but because the shared language or conceptual apparatus – the frameworks we use to make sense of ourselves – hasn’t caught up. As two of Ratcliffe and Richardson’s respondents put it: ‘It took me a while to understand that what I was feeling was grief’; ‘I never realised this was grief until I found others in a similar situation.’.

The same happened to me: when the magical stranger disappeared, my loss was ambiguous – she still existed, we were never officially together, I had another partner – and my grief went into hiding. In a culture where the end of a relationship is ‘just a breakup’ and monogamy is the unspoken rule, I lacked the rituals to digest the grief and the hermeneutical resources to conceptualise and communicate what had happened to me. For ‘self-interpreting animals’ like us, in the words of the philosopher Charles Taylor, the result is that we end up in the dark, as strangers to ourselves.

The narrowing of grief to bereavement is more than a conceptual mistake. It does real damage. What the writer and grief counsellor Stephen Levine called ‘unattended sorrow’ doesn’t dissolve but goes underground, hiding in the shadows, later resurfacing as unexpected symptoms. I have been there. A mechanical tightness in the chest and a hard belly, like wearing a harness to brace against life. Harrowing dreams. Attempts to numb what is too painful to feel alone. And, worst of all, cynicism and a slow erosion of trust. Not just in other people, but in your own feelings, your own intuitions about the depth, sustainability and future of any new connection. When no one around you recognises your grief, you begin to wonder whether you were wrong to feel it at all.

Industry observers note that sigmund Freud understood this, though he read it as pathology. In the essay ‘Mourning and Melancholia’ (1917), he contended that grief is healthy and normal, but only if it is intelligible and bounded. The job of mourning, he argued, is to detach you from the lost object and reinvest your emotional energy elsewhere. If you can’t complete that job, if the loss is unclear or unnamed or ambiguous, you are no longer mourning. Instead, you are suffering from an illness called melancholia. For Freud, grief that cannot do its work calcifies into something darker, something more elusive.

If you deny someone the right to grieve, you deny them access to themselves.

But the damage runs deeper than that. When we cannot grieve a loss, we lose something else along with it: the chance to register what mattered to us. Grief is how we come to know what we loved in the presence of its absence. Or as the psychotherapist and grief worker Francis Weller puts it in The Wild Edge of Sorrow (2015):.

Your grief tells you that you had the courage to love, that you allowed someone or something else to enter ‘the core of [your] being and find a home in [your] heart’. If you deny someone the right to grieve, you deny them access to what they loved and valued, which is to say that you deny them access to themselves. You don’t just rob them, then, of their love; you also rob them of self-knowledge.

Sources indicate that the tradition I spent most of my life in – the lineage of Western thinkers who asked how a human being should live – was the first place I looked to understand what was happening to me. These thinkers had a lot to say about grief, but most of it was suspicious and sceptical. Plato believed a good man is the most self-sufficient of all, and least shaken by loss. In the Phaedo, Socrates’ wife Xanthippe is led away wailing before the philosophy can begin, and towards the end of the dialogue, Socrates rebukes his weeping friends for behaving like women. A similar sentiment can be found among the Stoics. Epictetus, in the Enchiridion, compares the loss of a wife or child to a jug breaking. And Marcus Aurelius, who lost many of his own children, reminds himself in his Meditations not to pray that he might keep his child, but to pray that he might not fear losing him.

Sources indicate that behind this way of thinking lies an expensive belief: that attachment is a liability, and that a wise person – someone who has figured out how to live the best possible life – does not need anything that can be taken away from him. If grief is love with nowhere to go, a tradition that treated such love as an error was never going to know what to do with it.

Industry observers note that christianity kept the verdict the ancients had arrived at. In his Confessions (397-400 CE), Saint Augustine looks back on his devastation after a friend’s death, and diagnoses it as a spiritual mistake: ‘Why had that grief penetrated me so easily and so deeply, if not because I had poured out my soul onto the sand, loving someone who would die as if he never would?’ Baruch Spinoza – not religious in any conventional sense of the word – reached the same conclusion. Sadness, he writes in his Ethics (1677), is the mind’s move to a lesser perfection, a loss of its power to act. This means it can never be a good in itself, and its typical source is too much love for things that are impermanent. The cure for grief – and this puts him squarely back into the ancient intellectualist tradition – is understanding: the moment it dawns on us that what we lost could never have been kept, our grief will relax.

The sense that part of oneself has been lost now appears in psychiatry’s most crucial manual as a mark of disorder.

In a recent development, arthur Schopenhauer, unlike many before him, did not despise grief. In The World as Will and Representation (1818), he values sorrow for one reason only: great personal suffering breaks the will and leads to self-renunciation (Selbstverneinung). Grief is worth having, then, because it has the power to cure us of wanting the world at all, which means that, in the end, he is not so far from the thinkers who came before him. A good life, for all of them, is a matter of loosening our attachments to what is impermanent and fragile.

What began as a doctrine of philosophers leaked into the wider culture. In his landmark study Death, Grief, and Mourning in Contemporary Britain (1965), the anthropologist Geoffrey Gorer found that mourning was increasingly seen as ‘a weakness, a self-indulgence, a reprehensible bad habit instead of as a psychological necessity’. In the 1970s, the historian Philippe Ariès traced the same shift across the industrial West: death, once familiar, had become shameful, something to be hidden. Meanwhile, medicine had entered the debate. In 1961, the psychiatrist George Engel asked, half provocatively, whether grief was a disease. In 2000, the philosopher Stephen Wilkinson answered: yes. In one of academic philosophy’s leading journals, he argued that even normal, healthy grief qualifies as a mental disorder because it meets the standard definition of one. Like all mental disorders, it involves significant distress and interrupts normal functioning. In 2013, the fifth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders removed the clause that had excluded the recently bereaved from receiving a diagnosis of major depressive disorder. Then, in 2022, the revised edition added prolonged grief disorder, whose possible symptoms include identity disruption, such as the feeling that part of oneself has died. The sense that part of oneself has been lost now appears in psychiatry’s most important manual as a mark of disorder – though, tellingly, only when someone has actually died.

Sources indicate that but the Western tradition had it backwards. Suppressing, eradicating, denying or pathologising grief doesn’t protect the good life; it sabotages human flourishing by cutting us off from the things we love. More than that, it cuts us off from each other. Grief named and disclosed is grief that can be met, grief that can be placed between you and another person, where the two of you can look at it and hold it together. That shared vulnerability lets one person recognise another in their common humanity. Grief, as Weller reminds us, was never meant to be carried alone; it was meant to be held and processed by a whole village. Strip it of its name and you strip people of the possibility of being seen in their loss, of discovering that the wound they thought was theirs alone is in fact shared by those around them.

Recently, while in the Netherlands, I visited the Kröller-Müller Museum with my father, the same father whose future was negated by a stroke. I looked at him from a distance, the man who once built his life around cycling – to France, to Rome, to Spain’s Santiago de Compostela – now hunched behind his rollator. We stood together in front of Vincent van Gogh’s painting At Eternity’s Gate (1890): an old man, face buried in his fists, clearly hurting. A sorrowful man, looking at a sorrowful man, looking at a sorrowful man painted by a sorrowful man. Years before he painted it, when he first drew the same figure for a lithograph, Van Gogh wrote that there can be an ‘unutterably moving’ quality, ‘something precious, something noble’, in the expression of an old man like that.

In a recent development, at Eternity’s Gate (1890) by Vincent van Gogh. Courtesy the Kröller-Müller Museum, Netherlands.

I didn’t know my father loved Van Gogh as much as I do. We stood there for a long time – somehow in contact with the magic of grief – and something opened up between us that had no name but felt important, exquisitely alive. We didn’t talk about my mother, or how our family had unravelled, or what the stroke had taken from him. We didn’t have to. The painting stated what neither of us could.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For thousands of years, ancient Egyptian was spoken along the Nile, and plenty of its words got out. Greek traders and Roman writers picked some of them up; Arabic and Spanish passed others along; and a handful made it all the way into English, where most people use them without a second thought. Here are nine words that are believed to have started out in Egypt. Some of these trails are well marked, and some run cold partway back, so etymologists hedge a few of them.

The word paper reached English in the mid-14th century, by way of Old French papier, from the Latin papyrus, the reed that gave the Ancient Egyptians a cheap, convenient writing surface. The Greeks called the plant papyros, and the Online Etymology Dictionary calls that a loanword of unknown origin that is âoften said to be Egyptian.â So the trail runs from the Nile to your printer tray, with one smudged signpost in the middle.

Egyptian had a word, hbnj, for a dark, hard wood prized for carving, and itâs probably where the Greeks got ebenos. From there the Romans made it ebenus, and English took ebony in the 1590s. Writers were using it to mean a vary dark black color by the 1620s, which is why a word for lumber now reveals up in poetry, piano lessons, and paint-chip names.

Before English borrowed ivory from French in the 13th century, Old English speakers called the stuff elpendban, or âelephant bone.â The newer word traces back to the Latin ebur, which the Online Etymology Dictionary claims likely came from an African source by way of Phoenician, and it points to the Egyptian ab, âelephant,â and the Coptic ebu, âivory.â By 1782, ivories was slang for teeth, and by 1818 it meant piano keys.

The sun-dried brick of the American Southwest has an Egyptian name. English got adobe from Spanish in 1739, and the 19th-century Dutch Arabist Reinhart Dozy traced the Spanish word to the Arabic al-tob, âthe brick.â Before that it was the Coptic tobe, from an ancient Egyptian word for brick, á¸bt, that turns up in hieroglyphics.

A competing theory ties adobe to the Spanish verb adobar, âto plaster,â but if Dozy was right, a mud brick in New Mexico still answers to roughly the name it had on the Nile.

English got oasis through Latin from the Greek Oasis, and behind the Greek is the Egyptian wá¸¥ê£t, which, according to Raymond Faulknerâs dictionary of Middle Egyptian, could mean both âoasisâ and âcauldron.â The word passed through a later stage of Egyptian on its way to the Greeks, and its cousins survive in Coptic as ouahe and in Arabic as wÄá¸¥a.

The sticky stuff that seeps out of trees went from the Egyptian qmyt, a word for resin, to the Greek kommi, to the Latin gummi, and on into Middle English. Chewing gum came much later and simply inherited the name. The gums in your mouth are a different word entirely, from the Old English gÅma, âpalate,â so only half of the gum you have right now is Egyptian.

Sources indicate that greek had a word, baris, for a specifically Egyptian kind of boat, borrowed from Egyptian (Coptic bari, âsmall boatâ). The Online Etymology Dictionary calls the next step uncertain, but a likely route runs through Latin and Old French to give English barge in the early 14th century. Its relatives bark and barque may share the same Nile ancestor. The sense of barging into a room, from the rough way barges got handled, dates only to 1898.

Recent findings suggest that hereâs one for the cleaning cabinet. The ancient Greeks and Romans worshipped the Egyptian god Amun as Ammon, whose name is stated to mean âhidden,â and he had an oracle at a desert shrine in what they called Libya. Mineral salts gathered near it came to be called sal ammoniac, Ammonâs salt, and in 1782 the Swedish chemist Torbern Bergman coined ammonia for the gas made from it.

The etymologist Joseph Shipley wrote that the salts traditionally came âfrom the sands where the camels waited while their masters prayed for good omens.â.

This is the most debated word on the list. Chemistry was used to mean alchemy around 1600, and alchemy goes back through Arabic al-kimiya to a Greek word that turns up around 300 CE in a decree by the Roman emperor Diocletian against âthe old writings of the Egyptians.â One theory traces it to Khemia, an old name for Egypt that means âland of black earth.â The other links it to a Greek word for pouring.

The Online Etymology Dictionaryâs verdict is that the word âseems to have elements of both origins,â so Egypt gets at least partial credit.

The Amarna letters

📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (140 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Aeon

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Industry observers note that first discovered in Egypt in the late 19th century, the collection of clay tablets known as the Amarna letters is one of our richest windows into the ancient world. The letters are extraordinary not only for their contents – diplomatic communications exchanged between Egyptian pharaohs and other nearby rulers in the 14th century BCE – but also for their script: they were written not in Egyptian hieroglyphs but largely in cuneiform, a writing system most often associated with ancient Mesopotamia. In this video from the British Museum, the always entertaining Assyriologist Irving Finkel details how the letters came to be and how they were discovered, and delves into the fascinating correspondence itself, which includes petty disputes over perceived slights, leaders lobbying for military support and more than a few requests for gold.

Quite literally in motion since I arrived, Baraghani finishes his point on stagnancy: He fears a life in which he is not learning, moving, or evolving “as a writer, a cook, and a good gay,” he says.

In the decade or so since he became a household name for a certain set of a certain era (food-obsessed aesthetes who love an acidic drizzle and a hard, salty cheese), as a video star for a certain magazine—okay, this one—his fandom has only continued to explode.

Industry observers note that when Baraghani confirmed he would be opening a restaurant this fall near Union Square with restaurateur Michael Silber, publications began tripping over themselves to cover the news. It has been revealed that baraghani takes a seat on one of the iron stools beside the prep table and there is a rare, brief silence, which is broken almost immediately by the tinny opening notes of a techno song emanating from the crew performing a renovation on the lower floor. Recent findings suggest that baraghani grins. “I feel calm,” he insists. “If something goes wrong, I can fix it, because I feel pretty clear on what I want to achieve.”.

It has been revealed that his background too. Years ago, he penned an essay for this magazine about growing up Iranian in a post-9/11 America; he started to go by Andy instead of Andisheh and bought an “Italian Stallion” T-shirt. He wrote about learning to accept his sexuality in restaurant kitchens, where he rarely encountered other gay men, and in his family life. He grew up in the Bay Area, the son of parents who had emigrated from Iran to Berkeley in 1977. Moore jumps up in disbelief to flee the restaurant as Patrick Swayze, the boyfriend, scrambles to find a way to prove to her that he’s right there. “Tell her ‘ditto,’” he urges Goldberg, who screams “ditto” after Moore as she bolts. “Ditto!” It’s their code word for “I love you too.”.

Moore stops in her tracks and turns, her gaze connecting with a man she misses, who she isn’t totally sure is there.

In a recent development, and for the first time in a while, she is no longer in motion. She is still.

According to recent reports, during the late 18th and early 19th centuries, Edinburgh was one of the leading hubs for anatomical study. But although surgeons were making great strides in the field, they were running out of cadavers to dissect. Grave robbers were only too happy to profit from that gap and began digging up recently buried bodies to sell to anatomists (who didnât tend to ask questions about where the corpses came from). Body snatching was a risky business, though, with some graveyards having armed guards to catch resurrectionists in the act. But two men turned to a different method of sourcing bodies: murder.

According to recent reports, between 1927 and 1828, Irish-born William Burke and William Hare murdered 16 people and sold their bodies to Dr. Robert Knox, who dissected them in his anatomy lectures. Their scheme was discovered and stopped in early November of that year, and has gone down as one of the most notorious murder cases in Scottish history.

Beyond those basic and fairly well-known details, here are seven fascinating facts about the Burke and Hare murders that you might not know.

At the end of 1827, Hare ran a lodging house in Edinburghâs West Port district. On November 29, his lodger, a man called Donald (his surname isnât known), died of dropsy while still owing rent. With the help of his friend Burke, Hare decided to sell Donaldâs body to an anatomist to make up the money.

In a recent development, they filled Donaldâs coffin with bark (so that the weight wouldnât arouse suspicion when it was carted off), hid his body under a bed, and then waited until nightfall to seek out an anatomist. They ended up finding Dr. Robert Knox, who paid them Â£7 and 10 shillings (about Â£700 or $940 in todayâs money) for the corpse. As they were leaving, one of Knoxâs assistants noted he âwould be glad to see them again when they had another to dispose of.â.

Just a few weeks later, Burke and Hare were back at Knoxâs door, having committed their first murder to get the body (although the exact date of their first kill isnât known).

In a recent development, burke and Hare knew that Knox would struggle to turn a blind eye to corpses that had obviously been murdered, so they killed their victims via suffocation because it didnât leave any signs of violence. âWe made the persons drunk, and then suffocated them by holding the nostrils and mouth, and getting on the body,â Burke later testified. They varied which one of them would use their hands (or sometimes a pillow) to block the personâs airways and which one of them would sit on their chest.

This method of murder led to the coining of a newly introduced wordânamed after Burke himselfâonce their crimes were revealed: burking, which means to âmurder by smothering.â Nowadays the word isnât necessarily linked to murder and can simply mean âto suppress quietly or indirectly.â.

Although itâs often only Burke and Hareâs names that are pinned to the murders, itâs thought that their wivesâHelen McDougal was Burkeâs common-law wife and Margaret Laird was Hareâs wifeâwere also involved in the criminal scheme. The prevailing theory has it that the women helped to lure victims to the lodging house, but the extent of their involvement isnât known for certain. âThere was little actual evidence of the crimes, so there was very, very little chance of unraveling the extent of the murders or of achieving a conviction without a confession,â explains Dr. Tacye Phillipson from the National Museum of Scotland.

Burke and Hareâs final victim was Margaret Docherty, who was killed on October 31, 1828. They stuffed her body into a pile of straw at the bottom of a bed until they could transport it to Knox, but two other lodgers, Ann and James Gray, discovered her remains the next day and reported the murder to the police.

It has been revealed that burke, Hare, McDougal, and Laird were all taken into police custody, and although they were suspected of committing multiple murders, there was little physical evidence that could be used against them. In an attempt to secure a conviction, Hare was offered immunity (and spousal privilege meant that Laird would go free too) if he testified against Burke and McDougal. Only Burkeâs testimony has survived, but he paints Hare in a negative lightâno doubt due to having been turned on by his friend.

Industry observers note that on Christmas Day, 1828, the jury found Burke guilty of murder, while McDougal went free. Knox was also exonerated thanks to Burke stating that the doctor had no knowledge of the cadavers being murder victims, but his career still suffered.

Burkeâs execution was a huge spectacle, with between 25,000 and 35,000 people gathering to see him hang on January 28, 1829âwhich is thought to be the largest crowd for a hanging in Edinburghâs history. Due to being a convicted criminal, he was denied a proper burial and his body was instead donated to an anatomist for dissectionâmeaning he suffered the same fate as his 16 victims.

It has been revealed that knoxâs rival, Dr. Alexander Monro, performed the public dissection, during which he penned a brief note written in blood âtaken from [Burkeâs] head.â A few other gruesome mementos were also kept from Burkeâs body: a death mask was made, his skeleton was stripped of flesh and displayed, and a small pocketbook was even bound in his skin.

Recent findings suggest that hareâs fate is a little more mysterious than his murderous counterpart. Although he wasnât formally convicted, people knew that he was just as guilty as Burke, and he had to be smuggled out of Edinburgh in disguise. Police were transporting him south to Dumfries when he was recognized and disorder broke out. He was taken to jail (because it was the safest place) and a mob attacked the building. Once things had calmed down during the night, he was then taken to the townâs border on foot and set loose, after which his trail goes cold. Some people think he went to Londonâwhere he was thrown into a lime pit, went blind, and then lived as a beggarâwhile others believe he returned to Ireland.

Industry observers note that in 1836, a group of boys were exploring a cave on Arthurâs Seatâa prominent hill in Edinburghâwhen they found 17 tiny coffins that contained strange dolls. Who carved the little figures and why remains a mystery to this day, but some theorize that theyâre linked to Burke and Hare. Itâs been suggested that either Burke or Hare felt guilty about the murders and made the dolls to give their victims (including Donald, who they didnât kill but whose body they sold) a symbolic burial.Â.

According to recent reports, other possible explanations for the dolls include that they were objects used for witchcraft or that they were made as lucky charms for sailors. No one really knows for sure, but the eight dolls that have survived can be viewed at the National Museum of Scotland.Â Â.

The physics of getting fired

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3644 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Aeon

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The senior partner didn’t waste any time.
  • It has been revealed that it was the summer of 2001.
  • Industry observers note that but then I got a phone call, telling me that one of the senior American partners wanted to meet me.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The senior partner didn’t waste any time. ‘I’m sorry, Zahaan,’ he noted, ‘your services are no longer required at the firm.’ We sometimes called him the Burger King behind his back, because he ate a Whopper Meal at his desk every day. I’d never spoken to him before, and now I never would again.

It has been revealed that it was the summer of 2001. I was fresh out of university and nine months into my first job as a management consultant in London. My parents had allowed me to move back into my old room, where I routinely collapsed after getting home from the office well after midnight. Professional life was punishing, but I gave it my all. For a brief time, I felt like I was flying: at my first performance review, I was told I had ‘partner potential’.

Industry observers note that but then I got a phone call, telling me that one of the senior American partners wanted to meet me. That was unusual; but then again, I’d been working so hard and getting such good feedback, I figured it couldn’t be anything too bad. I was directed to an office on the first floor, several levels below where I usually sat.

In a recent development, after he fired me, my ears buzzed and my chest tightened; I don’t remember much else, except being told that I shouldn’t even return to my desk. It became apparent that the location of the meeting had been chosen because it would allow me to take a single flight of stairs down to the ground floor. No one would need to see me, and I wouldn’t need to speak to anyone.

Recent findings suggest that the decision felt cruel and unfair. But more than anything, it seemed to violate the laws that for many years had been my way of making sense of the world: the laws of physics. Cause and effect, action and reaction. What followed was an unlikely journey – one in which the equations I thought I’d left behind at university became, unexpectedly, a companion through the messiest parts of life.

Industry observers note that before work, before university, I attended a competitive and prestigious all-boys school in London. While I’ll be forever grateful for the opportunities my education afforded me, life still felt tough for me as a lonely and anxious teenager. The school’s social currency was confidence, quick comebacks, and an effortless cool I never quite mastered. I often felt like I was watching from the edges, trying to decode the rules of a game that everyone else grasped intuitively.

The only thing that got me through was physics. The most fundamental of the sciences, physics represented a world that was perfectly ordered. It offered structure, rules and predictability. There was no social speculation; I could just work hard and try to figure things out. Problems and solutions, equations and outcomes. It didn’t matter how popular I was – what mattered was whether I understood the system. Slowly, the chaos of the world developed a sense of form and structure.

In a recent development, that clarity stayed with me, through school and into university. I read physics at Oxford, convinced for a long time that I wanted to become a scientist. It wasn’t always easy; there were late nights, bitter struggles with problem sets, moments I wondered if I’d ever get it. But when it clicked, it was wonderful: entropy, quantum mechanics, cosmology, all those deep, strange laws that govern the Universe. Physics seemed like it had a purpose, and I thought we’d go the distance.

Sources indicate that but at some point in my final year at university, things started to change. Physics still fascinated me, but I found myself drawn to other subjects too – politics, economics, business. I wanted to understand not just how the Universe worked, but how people did. So after graduating, I decided to leave physics behind and see where those other interests would take me.

For the first time in years, physics seems to be at the heart of the cultural zeitgeist.

As it turns out, when I stepped away from physics, many others did too. In the years after I left university at the turn of the millennium, physics began to fade from view in the English classroom. In 2006, physics A-level entries (post-16 qualifications in the UK) were down 37 per cent from where they were in 1991. The absolute numbers have since rebounded – but not for everyone. Today, the gender gap remains stark: only 23 per cent of A-level physics entries in 2026 came from girls, a figure that hasn’t budged much in decades. And more than half of GCSE physics classes in England (taken by 14- to 16-year-olds) are taught by a non-specialist, with a shortage of some 3,500 physics teachers nationally.

Research looking at why students choose or reject physics has found that it’s seen as abstract, difficult, and disconnected from real life – a perception that’s remained steady, even as enrolment has recovered. Meanwhile, newer fields – computer science, behavioural economics, even data journalism – have felt more immediate, more applicable. They speak the language of now.

What’s strange is that this perception problem has happened at the same historical moment in which physics has begun popping up in other surprising places.

Sources indicate that dominic Cummings, the strategist behind Brexit and later Boris Johnson’s chief adviser, gave physics a fair share of the credit for the success of his campaigns. In one of his highly popular newsletters, he paraphrased the theoretical physicist Richard Feynman: ‘The most notable thing is not to fool yourself and you are the easiest person to fool.’ Then there’s Elon Musk, who credits the success of his many business ventures to physics and ‘first-principles thinking’: discard convention, start from fundamental truths. And for decades, the legendary investor Charlie Munger made the same case in finance, saying that the ‘logic and power’ of physics had helped him enormously.

Recent findings suggest that for the first time in years, physics seems to be at the heart of the cultural zeitgeist, praised by public figures whose decisions affect millions of lives. But look closer, and the picture is more complicated.

In the first instance, billionaires and political operatives make for awkward ambassadors; Cummings, Musk and Munger might be brilliant, but they’re also extremely divisive. But more than who they are, what interests me is how they’re putting physics to work – whether they’re truly thinking with the discipline, or just brandishing it for rhetorical effect. Is ‘physics’ simply a shorthand for cutting through complexity, for stripping down problems to their most basic parts? Or does it genuinely offer something distinctive that other sciences and ways of thinking cannot?

Sources indicate that philosophers call the first approach ‘reductionism’: the idea that if you break any system into small enough components and trace them far enough, you eventually arrive at physics. That view can be powerful, and explains why so many people find it attractive.

Industry observers note that it’s also been spectacularly successful. When 19th-century physicists showed that heat was simply the motion of atoms – that temperature, seemingly its own phenomenon, was actually just particles bouncing faster – an entire science collapsed into physics. Years later, that same approach helped particle physicists break matter into smaller and smaller pieces until arriving at something apparently irreducible. From the reductionist instinct came quarks, leptons and the Higgs boson. Their catalogue blueprint, the Standard Model, remains one of the greatest intellectual achievements in human history.

But reductionism has its limits. Take politics: a radical reductionist might say that this too comes down to physics, because politics is about the behaviour of groups of people; groups are made of individual people; people are made of atoms; atoms are governed by physics. But does this mean that we could predict the outcome of, say, a national election by studying the behaviour of individual atoms inside the brains of every registered voter? Unlikely. Putting aside problems of practicality, what would be the point? Economists already have economics. Psychologists already have psychology. Politicians have political theory. Physics has value only if it’s additive and illuminating.

Sources indicate that for me, the real value of physics had never been as a cudgel for smashing things up into their smallest bits, but as a framework for navigating systems – for recognising patterns, probing assumptions, and testing whether the models we rely on actually work as they’re meant to. We see this way of thinking throughout the history of science. When cholera swept through Soho in 1854, the physician John Snow didn’t know its cause. But he mapped the cases, identified the pattern, and traced the outbreak to a single water pump on Broad Street. The founder of what we now know as epidemiology, Snow worked by constructing and interrogating mental models of the world, probing their assumptions, and following the data wherever they led.

Map from Report on the Cholera Outbreak in the Parish of St James, Westminster, During the Autumn of 1854 by John Snow. Cholera cases are represented by black rectangles, with clusters of cases indicated by stacked rectangles. The contaminated water pump is marked in green, while surrounding water pumps are marked in red. Courtesy the Wellcome Collection, London/colour annotations by Aeon.

It has been revealed that the question, then, is not simply whether physics can be borrowed as rhetoric, but whether it really helps us to see the world more clearly, in ways that complement and benefit other disciplines. That, at least, was what stayed with me after I stopped studying it formally. Not equations or textbooks, but a way of thinking that I found myself reaching for when my world was falling apart.

According to recent reports, getting fired was one of those moments. I had worked so hard, yet somehow I’d still failed. Everything I understood about cause and effect told me this shouldn’t have happened. But here I was, after months of working flat out, with nothing to show for it.

An infinitesimally small shift in starting positions for the three objects can throw the whole system off balance.

Industry observers note that while some might have turned to therapy or career counselling, I turned back to physics to try to move on. The immediate cause was clear enough. The dot-com bubble had burst, sending ripples across the global economy that eventually reached my desk. Belts tightened, and the harsh rule in such circumstances tends to be last in, first out.

In a recent development, the dot-com bust was not the first nor last time something like this would happen. In 2008 came the subprime mortgage crisis; in 2011, the eurozone crashed; in 2013, the rupee tanked; in 2015, there was turbulence on the Chinese stock market; and in 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic. All these crises had two things in common. First, almost no one saw them coming – at least not precisely when or where or how. Second, they weren’t triggered by some enormous dramatic collapse, but by small, seemingly innocuous failures that cascaded into something far larger. For example, it just took a few small incidents that might otherwise have passed unnoticed – like the failure of a local mortgage lender in Southern California – to precipitate the subprime mortgage crisis.

Sources indicate that all these events are examples of what physicists might call chaotic systems – deterministic in theory, but in practice so sensitive to initial conditions that tiny variations can spiral into radically different outcomes. A well-known example is the ‘three-body problem’, popularised by Liu Cixin’s 2008 novel of the same name and a 2024 Netflix adaptation. If you have two planets orbiting each other, you can write down neat equations to predict their paths forever. But add a third planet, and suddenly the maths explodes into unpredictability. The three bodies are still governed by clear laws, but an infinitesimally small shift in starting positions for the three objects can throw the whole system off balance.

The mathematician Edward Lorenz discovered something similar in 1961 when running weather simulations. His first attempt entered starting values rounded to six decimal places. His second try was rounded only to three. Yet the results diverged so dramatically that he initially suspected it was a computer fault. In fact, tiny differences in initial conditions had cascaded into entirely different weather systems. The atmosphere, like the economy, like a career, was deterministic in principle and unpredictable in practice.

It has been revealed that as a young graduate, I had been living without surge capacity. In truth, most of us do.

Understanding the crash was one thing, but physics also helped me think about what came next. I had believed that inputs led to proportional outcomes; logically, in that world, the way to get ahead was to work as hard as possible. But physics teaches that chaotic systems play by different rules. They call instead for surge capacity, an extra buffer that allows them to absorb shocks. Without it, even small failures can lead to total collapse.

It has been revealed that think of a power grid. Most of the time it hums along without problem. But during an unexpected surge, such as a heatwave when millions of air conditioners are switched on at once, the system can overload and shut down. To prevent this, engineers design grids with slack in the system and extra capacity to handle unexpected spikes. Without it, a minor disruption can cascade into a blackout.

That was my mistake. As a young graduate, I had been living without surge capacity. In truth, most of us do. We optimise everything from our schedules to our to-do lists – convinced that if we just push a bit harder, we’ll be fine. But the more we operate at our limits, the more fragile we become.

Physics provides a different lesson. Rather than relentlessly maximising, resilience is about building the capacity to withstand outlier events when they come. That might mean time slack, leaving space in our lives to recover rather than scheduling every minute. It might mean career slack, developing new skills, side projects and networks, rather than relying on a single path. Surge capacity might not prevent a crisis, but it sure helps survive one.

After my brief and bruising spell in consulting, I joined the civil service and spent most of the rest of my 20s working in government. I loved the sense of purpose, the colleagues and the privilege of shaping policy. Yet, if I’m honest, I still carried a small canker of resentment and jealousy towards my former consulting colleagues.

Compared with the UK national average, I know I was paid well as a civil servant. But with friends on six-figure salaries, it felt like I was failing at something. They could afford nicer clothes, cars and apartments. And then there was the magic trick of turning money into more money by buying assets, further widening the gap between their bank balances and mine. What stung wasn’t the inequality itself, but the perceived unfairness of the circumstances. I felt like I’d worked just as hard and still fallen behind. That distinction between inequality and unfairness became notable to me.

According to recent reports, psychologists have shown that we’re wired to make this distinction from a very young age. In one Yale study, children were asked to split 10 coins between two people based on their performance on a task. When the two people performed equally, the children split the coins five-five – equal and fair. When one person did better, the children split the coins six-four – unequal but still fair. The interesting result happened when the children were told that both people had performed equally, but they now had to split 11 coins. With no way to maintain fairness, what could the children do? They decided to simply throw away one coin. Time and again, the children prioritised fairness.

People will accept a world where some have more, so long as they believe the game isn’t rigged.

This distinction is also evident in physics. Inequality, in the literal sense of unevenness, is built into the fabric of the Universe. In the very beginning, the cosmos was smooth and equal, a uniform fog. Only when tiny imperfections appeared – quantum fluctuations that allowed matter to clump in some places more than others – did galaxies, stars and planets emerge. Without that inequality, there would have been no structure, no possibility of life. In that sense, inequality is not always a flaw. Sometimes it is the condition for growth and diversity.

We see the same principle in natural systems. Rivers branch into unequal tributaries. Lungs and blood vessels evolve into networks with a few large arteries feeding many smaller ones. That inequality of size isn’t corruption or greed, but a kind of efficiency. It allows flow. Yet when the flow is blocked, like when a river silts up or a vessel clogs, the system fails. The problem, in other words, is not inequality itself, but unfairness: the obstruction of flow, the stacking of rules, the blocking of opportunity.

I think this is true in human systems, too. A society where some are richer than others may be tolerable, even healthy, so long as opportunities and resources can still move freely. But a society where opportunity is blocked, where the rules are stacked, where unfairness rules – people reject that instinctively. Just as I did when I looked at my friends’ consulting careers and wondered why I’d been cast out. Physics, then, suggests that a lack of justice is the real problem, rather than inequality per se. People will accept a world where some have more, so long as they believe the game isn’t rigged.

It has been revealed that suddenly I saw this dynamic about fairness everywhere I looked. The financial crisis of 2007-08 wasn’t just about banks making risky bets, but about the perception that ordinary people paid the price while bankers walked away with bonuses intact. The eurozone crisis wasn’t just about debt, but about southern European countries being squeezed by rules they hadn’t set. The Occupy protests, the Arab Spring, Brexit, Donald Trump – all, in their different ways, were rebellions against unfairness.

In a recent development, looking at the world through a physicist’s lens, these moments resemble phase transitions. You can heat water gradually and nothing seems to change – until you reach a critical threshold, a boiling point, and suddenly the whole system transforms from liquid to gas. Human societies, too, can bear strain for a while. But once unfairness feels systemic, the pressure builds until the system flips.

Small wonder, then, that in an age of tumult and transition, physics has found upcoming admirers – especially among those who want to catalyse radical change, for better or worse. Musk speaks of first principles, Cummings of complexity. Their examples show how the tools of physics can shape thinking far beyond the laboratory. But in their hands, physics can feel more like a weapon than a framework, a way of bulldozing nuance in the name of clarity. For the rest of us, the challenge is not simply to borrow the garb and glamour of physics, but to carry forward its mindset – one that values humility as much as boldness, and curiosity as much as certainty.

That, I think, is where physics can still make its greatest contribution. Not by giving us ready-made answers or comforting illusions of inevitability, but by training us to question ourselves and live with the resulting uncertainty. Public discourse is saturated with physics, yet we need a deeper grounding in what it really teaches us about how to ask better questions, to test our own blind spots, and to admit what we don’t know. That need feels more urgent as new technologies only increase the temptation to reach for shortcuts.

We need artists who understand systems, scientists who can tell stories, leaders who can hold both.

So what would it take to embed this shift? My journey with physics began when I was a teenager, and that’s where I believe we need to start now. Too often, we present physics to young people as dry and technical. We teach them equations but not frameworks, facts without wonder. We rarely tell them that physics can help with the messiest parts of life, bound up as they are with uncertainty, resilience, decision-making.

In a recent development, in the UK, we make things worse by forcing students to choose just three or four subjects to study for the final two years of school. In practice, this often forces a split between being on the ‘science’ track or the ‘arts’ track. That false binary deprives us of exactly the kind of multidisciplinary thinkers we need: artists who understand systems, scientists who can tell stories, leaders who can hold both.

When I visit schools now, I try to show physics as a kind of superpower. I want young people to feel that physics is something they can use, not something that excludes them. More than anything, I want them to feel it’s theirs.

I started this essay as a young man being shown the door by a superior. I ended it somewhere else entirely, with physics as a way of making sense of the messiest parts of life. But, really, what I’ve been edging up to is a story about how certain hardwon habits of mind can help us find meaning in the messiness and unpredictability of reality. For those of us who are not professional scientists, maybe the real task isn’t to love physics uncritically, or wield it carelessly, but to use it wisely. Physics shouldn’t be a shortcut to rock-solid certainty, so much as a way to live more humanely without it.

#98. Tech Report: Where to See the World’s Creepiest Dolls and Toys

Tech Report: Where to See the World’s Creepiest Dolls and Toys

📅 23 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1970 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Atlasobscura

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that humans have played with dolls for thousands of years, but it was not until the 18th century, when improved manufacturing rendered them more lifelike, that they started to be seen as sinister.
  • At these places around the world, dolls and other eerie toys are the main attraction.
  • This tiny shop just outside Paris specializes in vintage objects from French factories, the odder the better.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that humans have played with dolls for thousands of years, but it was not until the 18th century, when improved manufacturing rendered them more lifelike, that they started to be seen as sinister. Doll makers pivoted to porcelain skin, glass eyes, and wigs made of human hair, creating children and babies whose uncanniness to real people made them more unnerving than lovable. Later, in the Victorian Era, “mourning dolls” became a common way to remember deceased children, wearing their clothes and even sitting atop their coffins. Throw in Chucky, Annabelle, Slappy the Dummy, and numerous other evil dolls from pop culture, and boom: Dolls = creepy.

At these places around the world, dolls and other eerie toys are the main attraction. Some spots are happy-go-lucky art projects that, despite their creator’s intentions, still have the power to unsettle visitors. Others were always shrouded in darkness, created to showcase murders and mysteries. All of them are excellent examples of the creativity — and lore — that a single toy can embody, as well as our enduring fascination with the uncanny and ever-so-slightly “off.”.

This tiny shop just outside Paris specializes in vintage objects from French factories, the odder the better. The name of the store (which translates to “goods that have fallen off the back of a truck”) is perhaps the first sign that this isn’t your average antique store; inside, you’ll find ephemera ranging from glass dolls’ eyes to coffin handles to bicycle-shaped sunglasses, with items sorted into small wooden boxes or attached to the ceiling.

The owner, sculptor and interior designer Charles Mas, wanted to give visitors the chance to find all the toys, tools, and trinkets they enjoyed as children. “I focus on objects that have no market value, but an emotional and nostalgic value,” he says. “Many things that, without imagination, are worthless.”.

Sources indicate that for close to 90 years, the Squatriti family has pieced broken dolls back together from this small shop in Rome’s Centro Storico. Inside, benches and shelves are cluttered with various body parts, while the work tables are filled with paintbrushes, twine, and plaster. Each year, the Squatritis save upwards of 1,000 period pieces: not only dolls, but also vases, statuettes, plates, and more. The shop’s owner, Federico Squatriti, indicates that the “hospital” has changed very little since his relatives first opened it. At that time, the Squatritis lived above the shop, and as a boy, Federico would drop in to say hello to his father, uncle, and grandmother while they worked. Locals have referred to the space as a “shop of terror,” but to the entire Squatriti family, it is a second home.

Sources indicate that back in the mid 20th century, when forensic science was still in its infancy, Chicago socialite Frances Glessner Lee created 20 dioramas of real-life crime scenes on a 1-inch-to-1-foot scale. To ensure accuracy, Lee attended autopsies for all the cases and re-created their settings with astonishing detail. (One even contains a hanging wall calendar for the year of the crime.) She called her project the Nutshell Studies because of the purported purpose of a forensic investigation: to “convict the guilty, clear the innocent, and find the truth in a nutshell.”.

Industry observers note that at Harvard’s Magrath Library of Legal Medicine, Lee led seminars in which she guided students through the dioramas, helping them draw conclusions about the crime based on the information displayed. After she passed away in 1962, the Nutshell collection was obtained by the Maryland Office of the Chief Medical Examiner and fully restored. Today, the models are still used for educational purposes by investigators.

The lavishly designed home of textile designer and art director Stephen Wright also serves as a museum of his work, with Wright residing in his upstairs flat even while guests wander the halls below. The entire ground floor of the home (including its garden and exterior) exists as one exquisite sculpture of mosaics, collages, dolls, and handwritten “memory boards,” showcasing all of Wright’s loves and losses. He started transforming the home in 1992 as a side project, but after the death of his partner and his parents in quick succession, it became an outlet for his grief. Even today, the space is evolving, with Wright adding bits and pieces donated by visitors or discovered at flea markets.

According to artist Mary Paulsen, God commissioned her to give her collection of 6,000 dolls a proper home, complete with painted windows, tin cans, glass shards, and whatever other scraps and goods neighbors have donated. Mary will gladly transform anything she’s given into “gonna-make-you-smile art” for the village, which consists of a little red schoolhouse, soda pop shoppe, library, and chapel (where she herself got married). She also sells some of her pieces, with all proceeds going to Feed the Children, a nonprofit fighting childhood food insecurity.

While the village may be a bit unsettling at first, most visitors quickly warm up to the cheerful whimsy of Mary’s vision. In fact, Mary is often around to greet visitors and will drop whatever she’s working on to give a tour and introduce you to the dolls. “Mary is a delight to talk with and her place is incredibly creative,” one visitor reflected. “A lot of junk…lovingly presented!”.

Opened in 1830, this is one of the world’s oldest doll repair shops, and it has the collection to prove it. Over its nearly two centuries of operation, any doll that’s gone unclaimed has been kept by the shop proprietors in their “museum,” which also holds a slew of different body parts sorted in drawers, miniature furniture pieces, and costumes hung on a clothesline. The shop designs many of these doll clothes itself and also makes toy cars, planes, and carousels.

This underground cable railway has connected Liljeholmen and the Nybohov hill since 1964, but no one knows exactly when dozens of toys started turning up there. Still, locals have grown quite fond of these colorful additions to the dark tunnel, so much so that when authorities tried to remove them in 2012, Stockholm residents protested, demanding the plushies be left in peace. Their efforts paid off: The nearly 30 toys still adorn the metal rails and concrete walls of the funicular, waving hello to any children who pass.

In a recent development, in Atlanta’s Constitution Lakes nature preserve, a strange pathway winds through the wetlands and forest. Doll arms rise from the ground holding toy cars, with a nearby brick reading “Giving daddy a hand.” Clothed dolls lean against tree trunks, their heads replaced by rusty tools. One baby’s face sits atop a board that indicates “fashion” in neon paint, while another is positioned among mossy bricks and pinecones.

According to recent reports, this collection of oddities was created by Joel Slaton, a local carpenter who wanted to repurpose discarded materials he found in the area. Soon, others started contributing their own art pieces, with one caveat: Every work must be made of things from inside the park itself. Bringing things with you is strongly discouraged, with a sign at the trailhead explaining that “litter makes the angels cry.”.

In the early 20th century, young Gene Otto received this straw-filled doll and, naming it Robert, started bringing it with him everywhere he went. It wasn’t long before Gene’s family heard him having full conversations alone in his room and screaming in the middle of the night. Later, when furniture was mysteriously upturned, Gene blamed it on Robert. Some visitors to the Otto family home even heard high-pitched giggling and spotted a doll-like figure in the window.

Gene has long since passed away, but Robert is still around, living happily at the Fort East Martello Museum in Key West, Florida. You can visit him here, but beware: He’s known to curse those who take his photo without asking permission first.

Nearly a decade after “Anatomy Murderers” William Burke and William Hare terrorized Edinburgh, these 17 dolls were found in a city park, each one nested in a miniature coffin. Rumors arose that the figures were effigies of the duo’s victims, though other folks theorized they depicted local sailors who had never received a proper burial. Regardless of who they were meant to represent, the dolls were most likely crafted by a cobbler, as they’re made from the profession’s special hinges and nails.

Recent findings suggest that hundreds of straw dolls go about their regular lives in this large garden: cutting down trees, cooking meals, riding bikes, and sawing wood. They were all crafted by the garden’s owner, Daina Kučere, whose answer to why she made the village is more or less “Why not?” Residents wear all kinds of attire, from police uniforms to wedding dresses to baggy sweats (really just whatever Kučere digs up). Anyone can pass through the garden at their leisure and show their support by dropping a few coins in the central donation box.

Japan’s first public museum dedicated to yokai (the supernatural spirits and monsters of Japanese folklore) contains over 5,000 artifacts, including many dolls and action figures depicting the quirky creatures. There’s even an interactive room full of yokai-related activity stations, where guests can use light projections to make images move and change, or color their own yokai, which then appear as animations on a screen. The “yokai camera” is another fun element to try out, letting visitors take selfies inside a historic yokai picture scroll and transform into yokai themselves.

In a recent development, shortly after World War II, artist and toy collector Claudia Kelsey moved to Juneau with her family of dolls and figurines. By the time she passed away 60 years later, her collection had grown to number in the hundreds, and her close friend decided to open it up to the public as a gallery.

While Claudia was especially focused on finding handmade Alaskan Indigenous dolls, her collection included items from all over the world. Since the gallery opened in 2010, it has received donations from doll enthusiasts in Greenland, Scandinavia, Russia, and more, showcasing many different methods and materials used by doll makers. In fact, the gallery’s director and curator, Mary Ellen Frank, is a maker herself, crafting figurines of Alaska Native leaders and elders using traditional carving techniques.

On a small isle in the middle of Lake Michigan lives this colorful (and slightly creepy) toy collection, with items ranging from doll heads in jars to midcentury action figures to a massive jar of tacks. The space is small, so items are arranged creatively, with old bicycles hanging from the rafters and toy cars and planes glued to the walls. The toys also flow into the yard: an endearing hodgepodge of overgrown potted plants, colorful deck chairs, and stone animal sculptures. In the back shed, local artists’ work is exhibited, including a photo series of Bigfoot lounging about the toy museum and island.

Even in her 80s, the museum’s founder, Mary Rose, can be found greeting visitors most days and still maintains her expert eye for toy curation. Start chatting with her and she may just show you some of her son’s artwork, or steer you toward the perfect toy to take home.

Sources indicate that since 2014, owner Sherry Groom has shared her love of Scandinavia’s ugly, mountain-dwelling folk creatures at this elaborate museum, which features a grotto, waterfalls, and naturally, a 10-foot troll mountain. In 2012, Sherry took home the Guinness record for World’s Largest Troll Collection, and it’s pretty easy to see why: Everywhere you look are rows and rows of trolls, from the smiley, wild-haired dolls created in the 1950s to rare ninja trolls and a vintage Trollmobile. The Troll Hole also features a coffee shop, The Grumpy Troll Cafe, and hosts meet-and-greets with the “Trolls” movie character, Queen Poppy, every Sunday.

Recent findings suggest that “I don’t have time” should never be an excuse to skip breakfast. Take this overnight oat–chia pudding hybrid, which comes together in barely 10 minutes. (I’m betting that’s less time than it takes to stand in line at the grocery store to buy a container of worse-tasting, more expensive oatmeal!) Grab a can of pumpkin and some baking staples, mix it up, then pop the bowl in the fridge. The next morning you’ll be rewarded with a lightly sweet, mousse-like treat that’s actually good for you—don’t forget to finish each bowl with a dollop of yogurt for a pumpkin-pie-with-whipped-cream vibe. Self-care rarely tastes this good.

Using an unsweetened soy or nut milk will keep the pudding more pumpkin-forward than dairy milk (and keeps the recipe vegan, of course), but any milk you have on hand will work here.

Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares nourishing, craveable recipes that you can pull off in 10 ingredients or fewer.

20 minutes (plus 8 hours for chilling).

According to recent reports, whisk one 15-oz. can pure pumpkin purée, 1½ cups unsweetened milk of choice, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, ¼ cup pure maple syrup, and ½ tsp. ground cinnamon or cardamom in a large bowl until smooth. Add 3 Tbsp. chia seeds and whisk to combine. Let sit 10 minutes. (Doing this gives the seeds a head start on hydrating and prevents them from sticking together. But if you can’t spare the time, just give the mixture a good stir before serving.).

Stir chia mixture again, then add 1¼ cups old-fashioned oats and mix well to combine. Cover oat mixture and chill at least 8 hours.

Spoon oat mixture into bowls and top with plain whole-milk yogurt, unsalted roasted pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or granola, maple syrup, and cinnamon as desired.

It has been revealed that do Ahead: Oat mixture (without toppings) can be made 4 days ahead. Keep chilled.

Anchorage: A City Within the Wild
