📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in Anchorage, exploring nature isn’t only for a rare free day or a well-planned vacation; it’s a part of daily life, as integral to the city as its infrastructure and cultural offerings. A day here may start with a morning walk on any of the hundreds of miles of trails, continue with freshly caught salmon for lunch at a restaurant with coastal views, and end with a sunset picnic on a rocky outcropping, where the only sounds are crashing waves and the fleeting glimpses of beluga whales.

Located on a coastal plain that shifts into alpine slopes farther east, Anchorage is unique in how its different ecosystems overlap, creating rich diversity in wildlife, botany, and geology. You can experience the best of nature while still enjoying all the creature comforts of urban life and stumble across breathtaking sights without even looking for them. In this guide, we’ve given you some starting points for exploring the wild from Alaska’s biggest city, with wonders ranging from undisturbed wooded trails to marshes that all kinds of animals call home. Ready to take a walk on the wild side?

In a recent development, this 25-mile-long river flows from the Chugach Mountains down into the Port of Alaska on Anchorage’s northern side, where it’s become a popular spot for sport fishing and bird watching. Thanks to its mud and sedge flats, and ocean-fed waters, this area is home to a massive annual run of coho and Chinook salmon. In fact, it’s the only urban Chinook fishery in the world.

The 5.8-mile Ship Creek Trail is a perfect way to spend time in nature without leaving the city limits, providing views of salmon spawning and swimming upstream during the summer. Stops along the way, like Ship Creek Overlook Park and the pedestrian bridge just off King’s Landing, provide especially great panoramas of the river and the surrounding mountains. It’s not uncommon to see anglers trying their luck for 20- to 30-pound salmon, and you can even visit the statue of Dena’ina matriarch Grandma Olga, fish filets in her hands and a bronze drying rack behind her.

Recent findings suggest that for a longer walk, try this 11-mile path that stretches from downtown Anchorage all the way to the Kincaid Park Chalet. However, if you’re looking for a shorter trek, have no fear: The trail is accessible from multiple points in the city, meaning you can hop on or off. You don’t have to explore on foot either, as the trail can be traversed easily by bike and, in the winter, cross-country skis. No matter how you travel the trail, you’re guaranteed some incredible views of downtown Anchorage, Mount McKinley (Denali), Mount Susitna, and Fire Island, especially as you reach the hills near Point Woronzof.

Recent findings suggest that the trail offers a rare chance to pass through a number of different biomes, as it winds through marsh, muskeg (acidic, waterlogged peatland), and thick spruce forest. There’s also plenty of wildlife nearby, with moose, in particular, enjoying long walks on the path during the winter. Other animals often spotted include sandhill cranes, ermine, bald eagles, and even beluga whales in Cook Inlet, so don’t forget your camera.

For even more great hiking, visit Kincaid Park, a 1,400-acre green space that was once a Cold War missile base. There’s plenty to do in Kincaid: walk down the 40 miles of cleared trails, practice archery on a designated range, paddle through Little Campbell Lake, or play disc golf on an 18-hole course. There are also seven different soccer fields, a motocross course, and a giant sand dune with stunning views of Cook Inlet and the Kenai Peninsula. In the winter, the park becomes a premier destination for sledding and cross-country skiing, with trails for every skill level.

Just 15 minutes south of downtown, this part of the Anchorage Coastal Wildlife Refuge is one of the best wildlife viewing spots in all of Alaska, offering sweeping vistas of the Turnagain Arm tidal waterway and half a mile of boardwalk across the channels and sedges. This wetland ecosystem is full of creatures substantial and small, from muskrats paddling through the water to the occasional moose taking a dip. And birders, rejoice: The marsh is home to more than 130 bird species, including Arctic tern, Canada geese, trumpeter swans, red-necked grebes, and northern pintails.

Pro tip: Visit in April for the greatest variety of migrating birds, or in midsummer to see three different species of salmon schooling under the boardwalk. Information panels and telescopes along the path make it easy to enjoy a self-guided tour and take in the sights and sounds of the marsh at your own pace. You can also see the marsh from aboard the Alaska Railroad or while driving down the Seward Highway.

In a recent development, also along the Seward Highway sits Beluga Point, a rocky promontory named for the population of beluga whales that can be spotted each July and August when they come to catch salmon in the inlet. However, no matter what time of year you visit, 180-degree views of the Chugach Mountains make this a worthwhile place to stop and take in your surroundings.

Sources indicate that nearly every day, the Turnagain Arm bore tide — a dramatic wave caused by incoming tides — sweeps through the inlet. At a height of 6 to 10 feet, it’s one of the largest bore tides in the world, and because it’s relatively slow moving, surfers from all over the globe come to tackle it.

The most-climbed mountain in Alaska is just east of Anchorage in Chugach State Park, accessible from the Glen Alps Trailhead (reachable by a shuttle that leaves from downtown Anchorage). It’s a 1.5-mile hike from the trail parking lot to the top of the plateau, with an elevation gain of 1,500 feet and incredible views of the Anchorage skyline, as well as Denali, Mount Foraker and Mount Spurr on clear days. For an even greater challenge, visitors can make their way up an additional trail to the peak, though this is a steep journey best suited for experienced outdoor adventurers.

Aside from hiking, Flattop is a popular destination for berry picking in the summer and fall, with its trails (especially the Powerline Pass) taking you past wild blueberries, crowberries, and lowbush cranberries. The summit of Flattop is also a hub for paragliders, with its level surface and multidirectional open areas allowing for many possible setups (and plenty of photo ops).

With all this and more to explore, what are you waiting for? Embark on your Anchorage adventure today!

💡 Key Takeaways

  • But much of that comes from his upbringing in Manhattan, where chronic asthma kept him indoors watching movies while the surrounding neighborhood exposed him to street violence and the complicated world of Italian-American identity.Â.
  • His career has moved from the raw New York stories of the 1970s to the crime epics of the '90s, and he has also made increasingly ambitious historical and spiritual explorations in the decades since.Â.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that some casual filmgoers might say that Martin Scorsese's filmography primarily contains gangster movies, but that overlooks just how varied his 50-plus-year career actually has been. Sure, his films often return to familiar themes of guilt, faith, masculinity, and people destroying themselves in pursuit of something they believe will make them whole.Â.

But much of that comes from his upbringing in Manhattan, where chronic asthma kept him indoors watching movies while the surrounding neighborhood exposed him to street violence and the complicated world of Italian-American identity.Â.

His career has moved from the raw New York stories of the 1970s to the crime epics of the '90s, and he has also made increasingly ambitious historical and spiritual explorations in the decades since.Â.

For a filmmaker so associated with restless energy, his later work has often been focused on looking backward, and along those lines, confronting mortality and questioning the people and things he once found fascinating.

Scorsese has dozens of acclaimed movies, and these are his ten highest-rated ones on Rotten Tomatoes. This list focuses on his narrative features, so you won't find documentaries like Rolling Thunder Revue and The Last Waltz on here.Â.

The King of Comedy has aged pretty well for the current times. In the movie, Robert De Niro plays Rupert Pupkin, an aspiring comedian whose delusions of grandeur lead him to believe that fame is pretty much owed to him.Â.

His obsession with a talk-show host gradually crosses beyond every type of acceptable fan behavior, and this makes the film a great examination of celebrity culture and parasocial relationships that is as relevant now as ever.Â.

Pupkin doesn't really see himself as someone doing anything wrong, and considers his increasingly outrageous behavior to be simply what it takes to get his big break.Â The film also takes some sharp swings at the entertainment industry's obsession with fame and the people willing to exploit it.

After Hours starts off as a perfectly ordinary night out, but then turns into an increasingly elaborate nightmare for the main character, Paul (played by Griffin Dunne) as his attempt to meet a woman in Manhattan sends him from one bizarre encounter to another.Â.

In a recent development, every attempt to fix his latest problem creates three more, and the story keeps making things worse until the entire city seems to be conspiring against him. Although the movie is technically a comedy, it creates some genuine dread and suspense throughout Paul's increasingly desperate attempts to achieve a task as simple as getting home.Â.

In a recent development, its strange characters and surreal atmosphere make it feel like a fever dream. After the cancellation of The Last Temptation of Christ, Scorsese was left looking for another project, and this relatively inexpensive film gave him an opportunity to rediscover the experimental side of his earlier work.Â.

In a recent development, scorsese finally won his long-overdue Best Director Oscar for The Departed, which is a crime thriller built around an elaborate game of double identities. Leonardo DiCaprio plays an undercover police officer who infiltrates a Boston crime syndicate, while Matt Damon is part of that same crime syndicate and works his way through the police. Both are trying to identify the other, which creates a narratively tense cat-and-mouse story.

The movie leverages its multiple opportunities to play with paranoia and the psychological toll of living a double life, especially through DiCaprioâs character.Â.

Its sharp dialogue and relentless momentum make it one of Scorsese's most accessible thrillers. It's also a remake of the Hong Kong film Infernal Affairs, though Scorsese transforms this adaptation into something of his own that is arguably even better.Â.

Recent findings suggest that one of the best examples of why Scorsese shouldn't be pigeonholed into a specific genre is Alice Doesn't Live Here Anymore. The movie is a character-driven story about a recently widowed woman trying to rebuild her life. Ellen Burstyn stars as the titular Alice, who leaves her home and heads toward California in pursuit of her dream of becoming a singer.

Itâs a great change of pace from the male-dominated stories that would become associated with Scorsese's early career. Burstyn's performance is amazing, and it won her the Academy Award for Best Actress. The movie also does a great job of finding drama in everyday interactions rather than relying on violence or spectacle.Â.

Mean Streets may occasionally feel like a slow burn, especially for viewers expecting the pacing found in other Scorsese crime flicks, but the movie is a very rewarding experience.Â.

Set in New York's Little Italy, the film follows Charlie (played by Harvey Keitel), a small-time criminal trying to balance his life. His biggest problem is Johnny Boy (Robert De Niro), a friend whose inability to control himself repeatedly brings trouble to everyone around him.

Unlike the polished and almost grand crime worlds of his later gangster classics, Mean Streets demonstrates organized crime at its lowest level, focusing on cramped apartments, fights over petty debts, and people who aren't half as powerful as they imagine themselves to be.Â.

The movie also dedicates a pretty good portion of the film's soundtrack to classic rock, pop, and soul music, using songs by The Rolling Stones and The Ronettes to express the characters' psychology and the energy of their surroundings.

Raging Bull is one of Scorsese's most technically impressive films, and Thelma Schoonmaker's editing gets the substantial credit for making its boxing sequences so visceral.Â.

Rather than just presenting the fights as straightforward sporting spectacles, the film uses subjective camera movements and very different visual perspectives to place viewers inside the main characterâs increasingly distorted experience.Â.

Robert De Niro's performance as the troubled boxer is great, but the character is hardly someone the audience is expected to admire. He is paranoid, jealous, controlling, and abusive, and thankfully, the movie doesnât soften those elements at all, nor does it turn his self-destruction into a heroic tragedy.Â.

Hugo is probably the most unexpected entry in Scorsese's filmography. Itâs a whimsical adventure about an orphan living inside a Paris train station, and the film at first appears to be a straightforward family movie.Â.

But as Hugo's attempts to repair an automaton lead him to a mysterious toy-shop owner, the story transforms into something more personalâa heartfelt tribute to the history of cinema and the people who helped invent its visual language.

The use of 3D is a major part of the experience, and this film is frequently mentioned alongside the original Avatar as one of the medium's most impressive applications of its time. The story also introduces audiences to filmmaker and magician Georges MÃ©liÃ¨s, whose pioneering technical work helped establish the possibilities of cinematic fantasy.Â.

For a director who has spent decades championing film preservation, Hugo is easily one of his most affectionate projects.

Scorsese's most recent movie is also one of his most poignant (and acclaimed). Based on the true story of the murders of members of the Osage Nation in the 1920s, Killers of the Flower Moon showcases these events with a level of patience and moral complexity that makes it difficult to watch at times.Â.

Sources indicate that lily Gladstoneâs performance is exceptional and conveys enormous emotional depth while relying on silence and subtle expressions. The cinematography also gives the Oklahoma landscape a striking presence and captures its beauty, while never allowing viewers to forget the violence taking place within it. The film's final stretch is particularly compelling, as it finds an unusual way to confront the responsibility of telling someone else's history.Â.

In a recent development, few movies have shaped the modern crime genre as much as Goodfellas. While following Henry Hill's (Ray Liotta) rise through the ranks of the Mafia, the movie indicates a version of organized crime that slowly reveals the falsity beneath its surface.Â.

According to recent reports, unlike The Godfather, which portrayed the Mafia through the lens of family legacy and Shakespearean ambition, Goodfellas treats it more like a cutthroat corporate workplace. Everyone is chasing money, status, and/or power, and loyalty tends to last only as long as it's profitable or useful.Â.

Sources indicate that the film's violence is often sudden and brutal, and its relatively few on-screen deaths make a lasting impression just because of how casually they take place. And did you know that the movie shares 27 cast members with The Sopranos? Its influence on the genre canât be overstated.Â.

The Irishman is a perfectly fitting choice for being the highest-rated film in Scorsese's filmography, especially considering how thoroughly it reexamines the gangster stories that made him so beloved.Â.

The movie has Robert De Niro playing a truck driver who becomes involved with organized crime and eventually develops a close relationship with labor union leader Jimmy Hoffa (Al Pacino). Joe Pesci, meanwhile, gives us one of the most understated performances of his career as Russell Bufalino. Unlike the explosive and volatile criminals he played in Goodfellas and Casino that viewers came to love and enjoy watching, Pesci's character here is frightening in far more subtle ways.Â.

It has been revealed that thereâs not a scene wasted in its three-and-a-half-hour-long runtime. Guilt and mortality, which are recurring themes throughout Scorsese's work, become especially prominent as De Niroâs character approaches the end of his life with very little left to show for it. It's a perfect reflection on the director's own filmography.Â.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares feel-good recipes for any day of the week.

I’m not going to tell you that breakfast is the most important meal of the day. Humans have been on the planet for hundreds of thousands of years and our ability to thrive simply isn’t rooted in whether we eat first thing in the morning. In fact, the cliché is barely a century old, stemming not from nutritional science but good old-fashioned advertising.

Throughout the 19th and 20th centuries, advocates for breakfast cereal used religious rhetoric and maternal guilt to fuel their marketing efforts, while public relations executives at a pork organization convinced doctors to recommend a heartier breakfast of bacon and eggs for sustained energy, aimed at working families.

According to recent reports, yet today breakfast is one of the most commonly skipped meals. So instead of wagging my finger at you about missing something so “important,” I think it’s worth asking: Why did you miss it in the first place?

In a recent development, on a jam-packed holiday like Thanksgiving, there are plenty of reasons. You have a turkey to roast. The table has to be set. Someone needs to pick up the wine. And oh, there’s still the pie dough to roll out! Maybe you even want to “save room” for the glorious feast you’re putting so much effort into.

But skipping this meal does come at a cost. Even if you aren’t ravenous, it’s metabolically valuable to eat in the morning. Breakfast stabilizes energy, and studies have shown that forgoing it leads to a reduced consumption of important nutrients like fiber, potassium, iron, and calcium, often found in morning staples like fruit, whole grains, and dairy. Without some food to start the day, you risk an energy dip, brain fog, and downright hanger. Which, let’s be honest, we don’t need in a kitchen overflowing with dirty dishes and extended relatives.

According to recent reports, I have an easy solution. Making breakfast on Thanksgiving (or any day, really) doesn’t have to be a last-minute hassle. It can be quick to assemble and still feel special—like you’re really taking care of yourself, because you are. Take this overnight oats–chia pudding hybrid, which comes together in barely 10 minutes the night before you blueprint to eat it.

Open up a can of pumpkin purée—odds are you bought extras that didn’t become a pie. Mix it with oats, maple syrup, and whichever milk you have in the fridge. A scoop of chia seeds adds bonus nutrition and prevents the oats from turning gluey as they hydrate overnight.

Industry observers note that the next morning you’ll be rewarded with a lightly sweet, mousse-like treat that’s actually good for you. It’ll keep you full and firing on all cylinders for a day of turkey roasting, potato mashing, and vibe managing. It may not be the most notable meal of the day—at least on Thanksgiving—but it will be delicious.

Only-in-Anchorage Winter Traditions

📅 23 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (867 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Atlasobscura

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Winter brings out the best of Anchorage.
  • Sources indicate that translating to “winter” in Dena’ina Athabascan, the name of this month-long celebration honors Anchorage’s First People — “heyi” is the Dena’ina word for winter.
  • In a recent development, alaska’s biggest celebration of independent film is a can’t-miss event for filmmakers and cinephiles alike.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Winter brings out the best of Anchorage. Under a blanket of snow, the city comes alive with festivals exploring regional history, lively tributes to Indigenous culture, decades-old sled dog races, and comfort food best enjoyed with friends and family. Here, Alaska’s adventurous spirit is felt in the traditions of diverse communities and seasonal occasions that offer a little something for everyone. Whether you’re taking in the shimmering colors of the aurora borealis from a snowmobile or enjoying films by up-and-coming artists at the Bear Tooth Theatrepub, there’s no shortage of events to make a winter in Anchorage one for the books.

Sources indicate that translating to “winter” in Dena’ina Athabascan, the name of this month-long celebration honors Anchorage’s First People — “heyi” is the Dena’ina word for winter. It’s prime time to enjoy winter outdoors, check out local arts markets, and enjoy seasonal community events like solstice. There’s also delicious food left and right, from Alaska halibut tacos to Himalayan curries and steamed dumplings best enjoyed by an outdoor fire. While unique events unfold each day, the whole city comes alive with lights and music. Many parks host ice rinks and ski loops, some of which give you an up-close look at Anchorage’s wildlife, from moose to hares to foxes.

In a recent development, alaska’s biggest celebration of independent film is a can’t-miss event for filmmakers and cinephiles alike. Along with screenings of short and feature-length projects, guests can attend Q&A sessions and panel discussions or participate in workshops and networking events. While artists from all over the world screen their works here, the festival is especially focused on growing and sustaining Alaska’s film community, as well as providing a greater platform for Indigenous voices.

Hosted by the Nordic Skiing Association of Anchorage, this winter solstice celebration turns Kincaid Park into a winter wonderland, with visitors passing dozens of decorated trees and colorful lights in the park’s Mize Loop (just remember your skis or snowshoes!). After finishing the 1.5-mile loop, guests are encouraged to grab free hot chocolate and s’mores, enjoy live music, and vote on their favorite tree. Younger attendees can crawl through illuminated tunnels set up throughout the park while adults sip drinks from Raven’s Ring Brewery by the warming barrels.

For 37 years and counting, this free event has showcased up-and-coming artists and helped build community through music. During “Folk Week,” venues around town host local and visiting artists, while music workshops are held on the weekends at University of Alaska Anchorage’s Wendy Williamson Auditorium. There are many other folksy events to participate in, too, from a barn dance to a ukulele jam to a banjo contest. Also, an annual fundraiser concert helps support future editions of the festival, with tickets starting at $20.

It has been revealed that anchorage is a city that loves its brews, so it’s only right that they be celebrated! Each year, the Brewers Guild of Alaska partners with Peak 2 Peak Events to host this epic ode to beers, ciders, wines, meads, and more. Award-winning brewers from across the state converge at the Dena’ina Center for a day of beverage tasting, hearty grub, games, and live music. Over 200 different drinks are available to try, including a wide selection of nonalcoholic options. Plus, there’s a chance to take home fun swag like beanies, socks, koozies, and stainless-steel pint glasses.

For more than 90 years, “Fur Rondy” has brought Anchorage to life with events and activities all over the city. The festival is inspired by the rendezvous that Alaska’s fur trappers and miners had each winter, sharing stories and drinks after months of isolation in the wilderness. Fur Rondy celebrates the region’s unique history through all kinds of annual traditions, from sled dog races to snow sculptures to the Frostbite Footrace (where wintery costumes are encouraged). The fest is even home to the world’s largest Outhouse Races, which requires teams to push festive latrines through a race course.

Each year, hundreds of dogs gear up on the first Saturday of March for the ceremonial start of the “Last Great Race on Earth”: a 1,000-mile course that starts on 4th Avenue and D Street in downtown Anchorage and goes all the way to Nome. There are plenty of spots around town to watch the action, from Cordova Street and 16th Avenue (the steepest hill of the day) to the scenic University Lake near the University of Alaska Anchorage campus. Also, many mushers open up their kennels to the public for tours (and sometimes even tutorials!) all year long.

Anchorage is the perfect place to take in the awesome beauty of the aurora borealis, a.k.a. the northern lights, with prime viewing locations all over the city. From Point Woronzof, a coastal park on the northwestern edge of town, to the Eagle River Nature Center at one of the entrances to Chugach State Park, you can easily pick and choose the viewing experience that works best for you. There are also numerous tour services to help visitors make the most of their Anchorage winter experience, including adventures that combine the lights with dogsledding and snowmobiling.

#90. In praise of the dilettante

📅 30 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3267 w)

In praise of the dilettante

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3267 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Aeon

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Why, of all people, defend the dilettante?
  • Merriam-Webster defines the dilettante as ‘a person having a superficial interest in an art or a branch of knowledge’.
  • According to recent reports, clearly, the dilettante is no aspirational character.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Why, of all people, defend the dilettante? An amateur at best, a flighty rascal at worst: why take an interest in someone whose own interests are never more than a passing hobby? These are serious times – why take seriously someone for whom nothing is serious?

Merriam-Webster defines the dilettante as ‘a person having a superficial interest in an art or a branch of knowledge’. Encyclopedia.com calls the dilettante someone who cultivates an interest ‘without real commitment or knowledge’. Cambridge settles for someone whose understanding ‘is not very deep or serious’. Collins gives us someone who ‘seems interested in a subject … but does not really know very much about it’. None of it is flattering.

According to recent reports, clearly, the dilettante is no aspirational character. No university markets itself as training the next generation of dilettantes; no magazine runs a ‘dilettante of the year’ concern (except, perhaps, for the excellent Idler publication). He – for the dilettante is, historically and in popular imagination, so often a ‘he’ – is in essence an amateur, a role defined by wide interests and narrow expertise.

Such is the reputation of the dilettante, assigned and maintained by a culture that treats a single-minded devotion to one pursuit as the only route to a meaningful life. Pick something and stick with it, we are told. It’s not so much an explicit campaign against dilettantism I’m challenging, but rather the diffuse yet relentless pressure to narrow one’s interests, to specialise, to gain expertise, to forgo breadth for the sake of depth. We hear it in the barrage of imperatives to follow your dreams or find your passion uttered at graduation speeches, in self-help guides, and similarly corporate-sounding pep talks. Under this scheme, the specialist is the hero and the dilettante is but a cautionary tale: the person who never committed, never finished, never got good enough at any one thing.

It has been revealed that but what if the scheme has it backwards? What if the dilettante’s perpetual movement from one thing to another is not a failure of nerve but a different and defensible way of being, one whose exploratory zeal turns out to be just what a hyper-specialised, over-optimised and all-too-serious world needs most? Then the dilettante would turn out to be not a capricious buffoon but a kind of modern anti-hero. That, I argue, is a dilettantism worth defending.

First, let’s consider how ‘dilettante’ relates to some of its conceptual cousins: the amateur, the dabbler, the jack-of-all-trades, etc. First, the dilettante is by nature an amateur, ie, a non-expert, a non-professional. But amateurism is a necessary though not sufficient condition of dilettantism. Anyone can be an amateur at any particular thing: woodworking, birdwatching, astronomy, etc. The dilettante’s amateurism is wide-ranging over several interests, and tends to orient around the production and/or appreciation of art and beauty. Like the jack-of-all-trades, the dilettante is a multi-dimensional amateur. But the dilettante’s amateurism is typically of the aesthetic variety.

Further, the dilettante is no dabbler. The dabbler scratches the surface of interests, whereas the dilettante, I argue, can and does go deep – without, however, anchoring a sense of self in any one interest. This also sets the dilettante apart from the flâneur, Charles Baudelaire’s urban wanderer strolling through the city’s offerings, sampling everything, invested in none of it. The dilettante is deeply engaged in interests, and more an active participant than a passive spectator.

The term originally referred to someone who pursues an interest, particularly an artistic one, for the sake of ‘delight’.

Industry observers note that in this respect, the concept is closest in spirit to the ‘Renaissance man’, minus the gender specification and historical context. The dilettante is one who is moved by enjoyment rather than necessity, professional obligation or the pursuit of credentials, and who purposefully cultivates a plurality of distinct, often aesthetic interests beyond mere surface familiarity.

One reason to defend the dilettante, then, is for lexicological justice. The term has been unfairly burdened with an overly negative connotation. It wasn’t always this way. From the Baroque-era Italian dilettante, the term originally referred to someone who pursues an interest, particularly an artistic one, for the sake of pleasure, or ‘delight’. Even as the term evolved, it stayed largely neutral, distinguishing enthusiasts from professionals in a given practice. The pejorative connotation familiar to us today is more recent, shaped by what I’ll call a ‘deficiency’ model, in which amateurism is viewed negatively as a lack of something: skill, seriousness, focus, expertise. This is the meaning ascribed by cultural gatekeepers like Theodor Adorno, who in 1929 dismissed the dilettante as one ‘unable to establish any standards’.

Recent findings suggest that the more important aim, however, is to show dilettantism as a way of living that offers more than we might think. It is a life liberated from specialisation, instrumentalisation and meritocratic bean-counting, as well as from a Protestant work ethic that is suspicious of pleasure for pleasure’s sake. Arguments denigrating specialisation in education and vocation are well known, as are those championing well-roundedness and the virtues of the liberal arts. Though similar in spirit, this defence of dilettantism is less about the purpose or outcomes of academic or professional life and more about making the mental switch away from the socially conditioned pressure to find your thing and stick with it to an open and exploratory pursuit of pluralistic interests. Reclaiming this sense of joyful experimentalism is intended to show dilettantism as a mode of abundance rather than deficiency.

Recent findings suggest that A good place to start is the essay ‘On Dilettantism’ (1799) by J W von Goethe and Friedrich Schiller. This fragmentary, never-completed project by the literary dream-team of Weimar-era Germany paints a deeply ambivalent portrait of dilettantism, praising the dilettante over here for ‘cultivat[ing] something serious in man’ and condemning him over there as a ‘plagiarist’ and a ‘bungler’. Viewed retrospectively, however, its almost scientific treatment of the ‘advantages’ (Nutzen) and ‘disadvantages’ or ‘harms’ (Schaden) of dilettantism helps give a clear-eyed view of the potential virtues and vices of dilettantism today.

Industry observers note that crucially, Goethe and Schiller’s analysis is squarely situated in the cultural context of Weimar classicism. This means that, first, the question of the dilettante arises (as it does in its original Italian usage) exclusively in relation to the arts. They treat the dilettante as a distinctly aesthetic figure, ‘a lover of the arts who wishes not only to contemplate and enjoy them, but also to participate in their production.’ This aesthetic dimension has (regrettably, I think) faded from the meaning of ‘dilettante’ over time. But nor does it need to be narrowly inscribed in 18th-century anxieties about who can and cannot properly be called an artist. Artistic engagement isn’t essential to dilettantism. But it is worth reasserting, maybe even foregrounding, the sense in which the ‘delight’ of dilettantism involves, to some extent, the experience of aesthetic pleasure, broadly understood. The dilettante, that is, pursues what Søren Kierkegaard calls an ‘aesthetic life’: the ongoing, everyday activity of observing, valuing, and participating in art and beauty.

The dilettante is comfortable in the garb of an amateur. For the dilettante, every night is karaoke night.

Recent findings suggest that though rooted in classicist aestheticism, some of Goethe and Schiller’s criticism of the dilettante still resonates today. They worry, for example, that the dilettante ‘jumps over the steps’, gliding too glibly through the creative process and claiming victory too early. There’s something to this. Similar to Oscar Wilde’s concern about the ‘sentimentalist’ in his 1897 epistolary essay, De Profundis, who ‘desires to have the luxury of an emotion without paying for it’, the authors voice a reasonable objection to those willing to cut the line in chasing laurels. Progress is earned through practice, and those of us who have put in the work are right to protect it, as any trained therapist, frustrated with the quackery that passes for therapy on YouTube and TikTok, will gladly testify.

According to recent reports, studies of Søren Kierkegaard (c1850) by Vilhelm Pedersen. Courtesy the SMK/Copenhagen.

In a recent development, but due to their idealisation of the ‘true artist’ as a manifester of Truth and Beauty, Goethe and Schiller cannot help but view the dilettante as lacking in both aim and ability. To be fair, no practice is a total free-for-all, and some practices are less permissive of dilettantism than others (who wants to live in a house built by a dilettante architect?). But the notion that the dilettante tries and fails to follow the ‘true objective rules’ of art and beauty the way legit artists do rests on outdated and Eurocentric assumptions about what both artists and dilettantes are actually up to. In other words, take away the neo-classicist presumption, and suddenly the dilettante appears less like an imitator and more like a liberated creator. It’s not that the dilettante falls short in any given practice but, rather, has a different orientation toward it. Indeed, an overly goal-oriented attitude, especially in the realm of pastimes and pleasures, cuts against the very spirit of dilettantism. Part of its appeal is its ethos of open-endedness, its willingness to do something for the sake of delight rather than achievement. The dilettante is comfortable in the garb of an amateur. For the dilettante, every night is karaoke night.

From our Germans, we glean a sense of where the dilettante goes wrong. But they can also help us make the corrective mental switch from seeing the dilettante as a wannabe practitioner to someone who chooses a more experimental, exploratory orientation toward a given practice.

Recent findings suggest that goethe in the Roman Campagna (1787) by Johann Heinrich Wilhelm Tischbein. Courtesy the Städel Museum.

The key to perceiving dilettantism as abundance instead of deficiency is to appreciate the sense of freedom it affords. It is, in the first place, a negative freedom, a freedom from the constraints that otherwise bind professional practitioners. More precisely, it is a freedom of mobility within a practice.

First, the dilettante has greater freedom to engage in a given practice. For Goethe and Schiller, one of the most important ‘advantages’ of dilettantism is that it ‘stimulates a certain taste for art, and extends it to where the artist would not be able to reach’. Generalising a bit, the point holds well beyond art: the dilettante can act as a liaison between expert and layperson, closing the gap between high practice and everyday curiosity, introducing otherwise cloistered practitioners to wider audiences and extending an invitation to anyone who might otherwise feel shut out.

It has been revealed that A personal example. A few years ago, I joined Mountain Haulers, a cycling group that meets on Tuesday evenings for a ride through Asheville, North Carolina. It is a ‘no drop’ ride: cyclists wait at points along the way for everyone to catch up, however slow or struggling, and the first ride of the month is always a chill ride along the river. This openness sets the group apart from a cycling culture of notorious cliques of devotees clamouring to outdo each other’s worship of the sport. Welcoming the less-experienced and the less-committed seems a more genuine way of loving the thing you claim to love. If biking is your thing, surely you want more butts on bike seats. The dilettante cyclists who show up for Tuesday-night rides make cycling better.

The modern admonition to ‘stay in your lane’ stems from assumptions about the commitment required to claim an interest as one’s own.

Recent findings suggest that the further sense of the dilettante’s freedom involves mobility between different practices – a freedom from the barriers dividing them. The dilettante maintains a certain detachment, or intentional separation, between who one is and what one does, to live the life of a cultural itinerant. Painting, gardening, MIG welding, beekeeping, language learning, comic-book collecting, dancing, swimming, printmaking, powerlifting, pickleballing, sourdough baking, accordion playing, brisket barbecuing – all exciting destinations to travel and explore without seeking citizenship or even permanent residence in any one. The dilettante is a wayfaring cosmopolitan whose sense of freedom is found in never being stuck in one place.

And yet, this mobility is also part of a positive freedom to satisfy the basic human need to explore and make one’s mark on the world. Goethe and Schiller credit the dilettante for activating this natural impulse toward curiosity and creativity, a drive they compare with children’s innate desire to playfully imitate their surroundings. Going further, I would say that dilettantism offers not only the satisfaction of scratching the Homo faber itch; making and exploring for the simple sake of joy and curiosity is a freedom that is every bit as valuable to self-discovery as any commitment or singular pursuit.

However, from the outside, mobility may look like mere lack of commitment. No doubt this drives some of the allegations of superficiality commonly lodged against the dilettante. Pulling up anchors and moving on from an interest gets flagged as surface-skimming. I’m speculating here, but such criticism seems rooted in a work ethic that tells us that investment in certain interests ought to yield dividends: authority, credibility, permission to enter culturally guarded spaces, etc. Just as the neo-classicist wants to set the ‘true artist’ apart from the poseurs, the modern admonition to ‘pick a lane’, or (more aggressive) ‘stay in your lane’, stems from assumptions about the level and length of commitment required to claim an interest as one’s own.

Dilettantism rejects this quasi-capitalist mindset. The petty territorialism common to social, academic and cultural spaces (think record stores, cocktail bars, art galleries, philosophy classes, etc) is unnecessary but, more importantly, at odds with a genuine interest in the thing itself. A crucial part of the switch from deficiency to abundance is learning to see the dilettante as an asset to a given practice rather than a threat to it. Even Adorno, snob par excellence, allows a version of this, arguing that the expert critic needs the dilettante around ‘in order to prove to himself that he isn’t one’.

More than simply escaping sickness, the dilettante’s movement is a headlong rush at vitality and vigour.

Also crucial to making this mental switch is seeing the dilettante’s curiosity as equal in intensity to the expert’s, but different. Picture the dilettante as the love-child of two very different philosophical figures: Kierkegaard’s aesthete in Either/Or (1843) who finds and cultivates interests with an intensity that is abandoned before it hardens into obligation, and Friedrich Nietzsche’s ‘free spirit’, the fiercely curious, light-footed nomad whose restless pursuit of intellectual and artistic treasures provides a profound, if rootless, freedom. From Kierkegaard, the dilettante acquires an innate aversion to boredom (‘the root of all evil’) which is achieved by what he calls ‘rotation of crops’: perpetually changing ‘the method of cultivation and the kinds of crops’. From Nietzsche, the dilettante inherits a rejection of convention coupled with perpetual motion, a sense of permanent ‘homelessness’ that propels an unfettered perusal of interests. Passionate enough to go deep, detached enough to eventually leave, such a figure shows the possibility of being intensely invested in various ways of knowing, doing and making, but never content to let a sense of self form too firmly around them.

Sources indicate that in a memorable scene from the Spike Jonze film Adaptation (2002), the journalist Susan Orlean (Meryl Streep), who is writing a book about the orchid thief John Laroche (Chris Cooper), is at once intrigued by his hunt for a rare hallucinogenic ‘ghost orchid’ and baffled to learn that it is only the latest in a lifetime of obsessions: turtles, prehistoric fossils, 19th-century Dutch mirrors, etc. How can he detach so abruptly from something in which he’s invested so much? He can only offer an anecdote. A profound and consuming love for tropical fish ended suddenly with the realisation that the passion had simply run its course. ‘Fuck fish,’ he tells her, disrupting her assumption that loving something means sticking with it forever.

Industry observers note that the difference is that, unlike Kierkegaard’s aesthete, the dilettante doesn’t rotate crops out of despair. Dynamism, detachment and insatiable curiosity are constitutive of the dilettante’s free and full subjectivity, rather than a stage on the way to achieving selfhood. The dilettante chooses aesthetic life over the life of commitment that Kierkegaard’s ‘either/or’ dichotomy presents, and fully owns that choice. Nor is the dilettante simply recovering from existential illness, as Nietzsche’s free spirit seems to be. Rather than running the risk of relapse – or worse, the ‘cankerous vice’ of pessimism – dilettantism is a healthy embrace of this freedom; more than simply escaping sickness, the dilettante’s movement is a headlong rush at vitality and vigour.

In the dilettante’s genes is a compulsion to pursue passions, deeply coupled with a refusal to shape a life or identity permanently around any one of them. The dilettante possesses a unique capacity to dive deep into an interest, then surface and plunge into the depths of the next, each one an exploration, an adventure, but not a lifelong, life-defining project. It is precisely to hold open the possibility of the next reconnaissance mission that the dilettante rejects any dogmatic principle of stick-to-itiveness. Sometimes, the dilettante is a devout hobbyist parked on one interest for years at a stretch; sometimes, a juggler of several overlapping projects at once; and sometimes, a serial enthusiast on the hunt for the next novelty – what holds these modes together isn’t any fixed duration or rhythm of arrival and departure, but a disposition toward perpetual motion. The dilettante’s talent, energy and passion are constantly rechannelled through latest outlets. Far from deficiency, dilettantism is a constant quest for abundance.

Industry observers note that the life of the dilettante, so described, is not an especially easy one. It is a life of perpetual searching and fleeting satisfaction, in which accomplishment often arrives without accolades. Until breadth of interest is held in higher esteem, today’s dilettante will largely have to forgo public recognition and settle for a private life of pursuits and pleasures. Rarely is the dilettante widely celebrated as such. Consider someone like Susan Sontag, a novelist, critic and political activist whose wide-ranging work has earned both praise for its unconventional contributions to the intellectual life of 1960s New York and criticism for lacking rigour, for lacking substance. A ‘Win’ in the dilettante’s column, in other words, often comes with an asterisk – a conditional victory at best.

Further, the dilettante is also no pack animal; however much a part of a group one may feel, the dilettante will likely always be something of a tourist within it. The dilettante has to be comfortable travelling as a lone wolf at the margins of any community organised around a shared interest.

No, dilettantism is not for everyone. For anyone whom the universe has called to pursue a single passion – congratulations! Stay the course! But for those of us compelled by something closer to FOMO for the sheer variety and abundance the world has to offer, the dilettante’s path can lead to a genuine quality-of-life upgrade. If courage means overcoming the fear of new beginnings, without the reassurance of a title or a track record to show for it, then dilettantism may have much to offer. After all, not every crop is a monoculture, sowed and tilled to maximise output. Some of us need to cultivate our gardens through crop rotation. A defence of the dilettante is thus a call to follow the forked path of varying interests to a life made meaningful through abundance rather than acclaim.

According to recent reports, A perfectionist known for his ability to become the characters he drew, Tytla chose to go in another direction to satisfy his vision. He reshot references using the movieâs art director Wilfred Jackson as his model. Chernabogâs dominating gestures and sinister demeanor stem from Jacksonâs performance. He helped define the sequence that sees Chernabog raise the dead to gallivant with demons. Cavorting through flame and darkness, these figures danced a line between the mortal and spiritual worlds.

What makes Chernabog so terrifying is Tytlaâs attention to his devilry. He is a nightmarish allusion to Satan. This is shown clearly through his winged depiction, the unfurling of his darkness, his control over spirits and creatures of hell, and his diminishing once morning comes and the church bell rings. He has dominion over the night and all the sordid evils that pass through it. Tytla masterfully portrays his malevolence and control to hair-raising perfection.

Recent findings suggest that âThe Night on Bald Mountainâ is a feast for the eyes supported by an instrumental that sweeps the audience along with the winds of Chernabogâs whims. The song, which gives the sequence its name, is a tone poem composed by Modest Mussorgsky in 1867. Leopold Stokowski arranged the poem for the film and conducted the Philadelphia Orchestra through the movements.

But it is not all chaos and fire and smoke. As the sun crests over the horizon, the music transitions to âAve Mariaâ by Franz Schubert. It is the signal that Chernabogâs reign is over as he shrinks back from the light. He is forced into slumber by the breaking of day and laid to rest. Itâs a reminder that all things must end.

While Fantasia brings Chernabog into the fantastical imaginings of an animated short, he is actually based on Chernobog, a Slavic deity whose name translates to âBlack God.â He is the god of misfortune and the opposing figure to Belobog (âWhite Godâ).

According to recent reports, during the Witchesâ Sabbath, or Walpurgis Night, Chernobog is mentioned to lord over the night, sowing ruin and discord. But in practice, northern Europe and Scandinavia see the day as a holiday to celebrate on April 30. According to Britannica, the Swedes sing traditional spring folk songs and light bonfires on the night. Germans dress up in costumes and prank each other. They make loud noises to keep evil away. Revelers in the countries that celebrate Walpurgis Night hang blessed sprigs of foliage in their homes and barns to ward off evil spirits. They also leave phantom hounds offerings of buttered and honeyed bread.

Sources indicate that fantasia takes a decidedly ghoulish interpretation of the holiday, but in actuality Walpurgis Night takes its cues from pagan celebrations of springâs arrival and fertility rites. For Chernabog, however, itâs a night when he and his minions can get into mischief and spread mayhem for as long as darkness has its hold on the land.

8 Gargoyles and Grotesques Hiding in Plain Sight

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (782 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Atlasobscura

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • While most of these creatures are made in a similar style, with recognizable bodily features, expressions, and poses, there are a handful around the globe that are unapologetically unique: sometimes familiar, sometimes offbeat, and always worth a closer look.
  • Both are ornate stone figures carved into buildings; however, gargoyles also double as waterspouts to drain rainwater off a building, whereas grotesques are purely decorative.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, what’s more wondrous than towering spires on a building? Stained glass? Vaulted windows, or garden roofs? One word: Ghouls. Nothing jazzes up a normal old cathedral or mansion more than a mischievous face etched in stone, smiling (or, more likely, grimacing) at those passing below. Gargoyles and grotesques, in their own endearingly ugly way, are one of the best ways for architects to let their creations stand apart from the pack and inspire reflection for centuries to come.

While most of these creatures are made in a similar style, with recognizable bodily features, expressions, and poses, there are a handful around the globe that are unapologetically unique: sometimes familiar, sometimes offbeat, and always worth a closer look.

A Note on Gargoyles vs. Grotesques.

Both are ornate stone figures carved into buildings; however, gargoyles also double as waterspouts to drain rainwater off a building, whereas grotesques are purely decorative.

Industry observers note that D.C.’s National Cathedral is the largest in the U.S. and the sixth largest in the world, but it has another, less obvious claim to fame: a small carving of Darth Vader among its spires. When the cathedral underwent constuction in the 1980s, it held a contest for schoolchildren to submit designs, and this infamous villain took third place, earning it a spot on the exterior. For the best view of the Dark Lord, grab your binoculars and head to the northwest parking lot. Near the top of the northwest tower, Vader is just above a large skull.

Polish-Ukrainian architect Vladislav Gorodetsky, “the Gaudí, of Ukraine,” intended for this animal-themed building to be his permanent residence; however, he was forced to vacate it when his pocketbook ran dry. The house, located in Kyiv’s historic Lypky neighborhood, is right across the street from the Ukrainian president’s office and has been used for diplomatic ceremonies since 2005. Its gargoyles and grotesques were inspired by Gorodetsky’s love of hunting, and inside is even filled with stuffed versions of many of these same animals.

According to recent reports, architect Changiz Tehrani designed this mixed-use structure with 22 different WhatsApp emoji faces that stare out at passersby, including fan favorites like the smile, the wink, the heart eyes, the kissy face, and the winking face with tongue out. Tehrani drew inspiration from an Amsterdam building called “The House with the Heads,” which depicts the faces of six Greek gods.

Recent findings suggest that an officer who died in the line of duty is memorialized on the south-facing outer wall of Carlisle Cathedral, surprisingly inconspicuous beside the medieval gargoyles and grotesques. Police Constable George Russell’s stone likeness wears a helmet and star badge, marking his life’s dedication to service and safety. Russell is buried in Carlisle and also honored by a plaque at the Oxenholme Lake District railway station.

It has been revealed that among the Duomo’s many easy-to-miss intricacies is this stone bull’s head facing Via Ricasoli and right over the Porta della mandorla, the door that allows one up into the grand dome. There are two explanations for the bull’s origin: One holds that it was the builders’ tribute to the draft animals used to construct the cathedral. The other (far more fun) theory is that a stonemason designed the bull to look straight into the shop of his girlfriend’s husband, a daily reminder that it was the stonemason she truly loved.

For over a century, this deformed rabbit has sat at the back of St. Nicholas Cathedral, but no one can say why or how it came to be. Some say it represents the coming of spring (à la the Easter Bunny), whereas others insist it was built to scare away grave robbers. Still others believe the creature was intended to be a normal rabbit but, unfortunately, its ears were accidentally put on backward.

Sources indicate that when Paisley Abbey underwent renovations in 1993, 13 of its gargoyles were removed and replaced with updated versions, though one of the stonemasons on the job took some major creative liberties. His contribution to the facade looks strikingly like H.R. Giger’s Xenomorph from the “Alien” franchise, though it’s never been confirmed whether this was his exact intention or a happy coincidence.

E.E. Roberts designed a number of homes in this sleepy Chicago suburb, working in styles that ranged from Victorian to Tudor to Prairie. Perhaps his most fanciful building, Park Grove Manor is adorned with playful, chubby-faced gargoyles and grotesques. Above the service entrances to the building are sculptures depicting an architect and a bricklayer, both of them amusingly cartoonish. This may have been Roberts becoming less self-serious in his older age, joyfully deriding the pretensions of modern architecture.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Everyone knows the best part of Thanksgiving is the sidesâand the sideshow. For a few hours every November, the main meal makes room for the annual Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, a feast for the eyes featuring colorful character balloons, festive floats, and a whole lot of helium.

In a recent development, since 1924, the parade has been a revolving door for America's favorite pop culture icons, from classic Mickey Mouse to Gen Alpha's beloved Bluey. As silly as the giant Snoopy and Spider-Man shadows over Manhattan's West Side may seem, it's this very spectacle that keeps millions glued to their screens every Thanksgiving morning. Here's a look back at the cartoon characters and blockbuster balloons that shaped the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade over the last century.

According to recent reports, before we had colossal character inflatables and live television coverage, Manhattan's biggest holiday celebration was known as the Macy's Christmas Parade. Released on November 24, 1924, for a crowd of just 10,000 spectators, the event featured horse-drawn floats like this 1925 Santa Claus carriage and even live animals from the Central Park Zoo to usher in the holiday shopping season.

From Disney's animation studio to the streets of Manhattan, the balloon adaptation of this beloved Disney character was introduced to the parade in 1934. Walt Disney designed the original Mickey Mouse balloon, which saw four more tweaks over the years.

Sources indicate that while Macy's halted the parade from 1942 to 1944 during World War II, all was right by the late 1940s, when oversized helium friends passed by Central Park once again. Quirky figures like Harold the Firemanâa play on Herald Square, where the route famously ran throughâbecame massive names thanks to broadcast networks increasingly covering the parade, with CBS putting it on screens nationwide for the first time in 1948.

As television turned the parade into a pre-pie living room tradition, live broadcasting brought unscripted drama. During the 1956 parade, the Mighty Mouse balloon tragically collided with a street sign, collapsing and slowly deflating at Columbus Circle in front of millions of viewers at home.

Snoopy first joined the festivities in 1968 as an aviator. Most of the 1970s saw the Peanuts pup as an astronaut, while the '80s featured an ice-skating Snoopy. Broadcast on NBC, the debut started a half-century run that would eventually make Snoopy the most frequently featured character in parade history.

The success of Sesame Street and The Muppet Show led to Muppetmania amidst the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in the late '70s. Kermit the Frog debuted in 1977 as the parade's first major puppet-based balloon, marking the start of an era where Saturday morning TV staples ruled the route.

According to recent reports, america's favorite comic books came to life in more ways than one in the '80s, thanks to the success of Christopher Reeve's hit films and the return of the latest and improved Superman balloon. Measuring 104 feet long and 35 feet wide, the massive character balloon made its mark on the Macy's Parade as the largest in history at the time. With its detailed, humanoid design, the 1980 "Man of Steel" also served as the final balloon manufactured by Goodyear, before DC's rival Marvel eventually took over the superhero slot with Spider-Man by 1989.

It has been revealed that soaring superheroes made way for skateboarding sitcom stars as quirky cartoons characterized cable TV in the '90s. The Bart Simpson balloon cruised through the decade for the most partâsave for a split seam in 1993. The Cat in the Hat, on the other hand, faced a different fate in 1997, when heavy winds caused the inflatable to strike a lamppost and permanently change how the parade handles safety.

One bright yellow cartoon character led to the next as the new millennium commenced, with the SpongeBob SquarePants balloon floating through Times Square for the first time in 2004. From PokÃ©mon's Pikachu to the M&M crew, the parade's Y2K era was a manifestation of modern animation come to life. While far from the first quirky character to fly over Central Park, the SpongeBob balloon was the first square balloon in the history of the Turkey Day spectacle.

Recent findings suggest that thanksgiving might have started stateside, but the parade's pop-culture reach blew up beyond borders by the tail end of the 2010s. In 2018, Goku from Dragon Ball made history as the first Japanese manga character to join the festivities. Casting jagged shadows over the city with his spiky cyan hair, the Saiyan warrior helped introduce Macy's to a more worldly audience. For the franchise's 40th anniversary in 2024, the balloon got a makeover complete with Goku's classic black hairâplus back-up from fellow manga character Monkey D. Luffy's balloon.

According to recent reports, even a global pandemic couldn't stop the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade from livening up the streets of Manhattan, with a scaled-down return in 2021 followed by an influx of fresh pop-culture characters in the years following. Featuring blown-up fan favorites like Blueyâthe animated Australian pupâand Stuart the Minion, the late-November skies above New York basically doubled for a Roku screen.
