The self-making world

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4743 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Aeon

⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The French naturalist Jean-Baptiste Lamarck was 65 when his great treatise on the transformation of life was published.
  • But if you’ve heard anything at all about Lamarck, it’s probably how wrong he was about one animal in particular, the giraffe, and how this giraffe fiasco epitomises his wrongness about everything.
  • According to recent reports, illustration from Histoire naturelle, générale et particulière (1749-1804) by Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The French naturalist Jean-Baptiste Lamarck was 65 when his great treatise on the transformation of life was published. With Philosophie zoologique (1809), translated a century later as Zoological Philosophy, Lamarck intended to establish an entirely newly introduced science, one built on the idea that all living beings are constantly transforming themselves, from the tiniest microbes to the most complex mammals, gaining new forms and new abilities. It wasn’t the bodily structures of organisms that determined their ways of life, Lamarck stated, but just the opposite: their ways of life in response to their circumstances gave rise to their changing bodily forms. ‘Can there be any consideration in natural history more important,’ he demanded, ‘or deserving of greater attention, than the one I have just set forth?’ (My translation.).

But if you’ve heard anything at all about Lamarck, it’s probably how wrong he was about one animal in particular, the giraffe, and how this giraffe fiasco epitomises his wrongness about everything. Lamarck suggested that, by stretching to reach leaves in high tree branches, giraffes slightly elongated their necks, creating tiny changes that were then handed down to their offspring, accumulating over many generations to produce the long necks we see today. Around the turn of the 20th century, Lamarck’s giraffe idea became a laughing stock when biologists roundly rejected the notion that bodily changes undergone in the course of an individual lifetime could be inherited in the next generation.

According to recent reports, illustration from Histoire naturelle, générale et particulière (1749-1804) by Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon. Courtesy the Linda Hall Library.

It wasn’t only his ideas about long-necked mammals that came under attack. Lamarck’s interest in giraffes was just a passing mention in the midst of his voluminous writings, which set out a revolutionary, field-founding theory: organisms, he claimed, transform themselves and, in doing so, they remake the world. That idea has drawn scorn for more than two centuries.

Though Lamarck is often overlooked, his science was foundational to modern biology and informed the theory of evolution that Charles Darwin later developed. Darwin followed Lamarck in believing in the agency of living beings to transform themselves and their environment. But most people don’t know about Lamarck’s influence on Darwin because, around the turn of the 20th century, Darwin’s followers expurgated every trace of Lamarckism from their neo-Darwinist version of evolution, rendering living beings the objects of random variation and outside forces. For the neo-Darwinists, living things played no direct role in the evolutionary process. Evolution happened through random genetic variation and external environmental pressures. For Darwin’s followers, organisms were just as passive as they had been for the creationists, who saw them as products of divine will.

It has been revealed that throughout the history of modern biology, most powerful figures in science and politics have ridiculed and repressed Lamarck’s radical idea that organisms have agency in the evolutionary process. In mainstream biology today, a neo-Darwinian view of living things as passive still largely dominates, though research in several areas has been challenging its reign.

Sources indicate that this is the story of how Lamarck’s radical idea was cast aside by mainstream science, and why it was overlooked for so long. It is also the story of a surprising reversal: in recent decades, some biologists have begun turning back toward Lamarck’s view of life.

It has been revealed that while many people think of giraffes when they hear Lamarck’s name, few know that he coined the word ‘biology’, in 1802. He needed a name to designate a fresh science he thought should exist: a science of all living beings, and only living beings. At the time, there was no such field. There were broader sciences, such as natural history, which included inanimate things like rocks, rivers and mountains; and there were narrower sciences, such as botany or zoology, which covered subsets of the living world. But Lamarck thought there should be a science of life. At the heart of his new science, he developed the first theory of what we now call ‘evolution’, although he didn’t call it that. He simply referred to ‘change’.

Lamarck lived and worked in the Jardin des plantes (Garden of Plants) in Paris from 1788 until his death, aged 85, in 1829. His life was tumultuous, to say the least. He lived through the French Revolution, then under Napoleon, then during the Bourbon Restoration. He survived the Reign of Terror, as well as the withering disdain of Napoleon and his circle of scientific advisors, and the return of the monarchy; he also outlived three wives and four of his eight children. In the last decade of his life, he was blind and frail but carried on working with the help of his daughter Rosalie. At the end of his long career, he had identified and named more than 6,000 species, and for more than two decades had taught a legendary course in the Garden of Plants, drawing students from all over the world. The course grew so famous that even fictional characters attended it, such as the lovelorn young Amaury, hero of Sainte-Beuve’s autobiographical novel Volupté: The Sensual Man (1834).

The Garden of Plants, Paris. Courtesy Wikipedia.

France’s National Museum of Natural History, located in the Garden of Plants.

By daring to usurp God’s monopoly on Creation and reassign it to mortal beings, Lamarck provoked the ire of the mighty and powerful. He wrote that life originated in spontaneous generation, brought about by natural forces such as electricity and heat acting upon inanimate matter. This led to the emergence of the simplest organisms: single-celled protozoa and algae. From that point, a property intrinsic to living matter exerted itself, a tendency to complexify, which Lamarck named ‘the power of life’. As organisms grew more complex, another cause of transformation came into play: their responsiveness to the environment. In the simplest beings, this responsiveness was rudimentary – an irritability or sensitivity, and reflexive reaction. But in birds and mammals, Lamarck argued, it rose to the level of ‘acts of will’, through which creatures could form ‘habits’ and ‘ways of life’ in response to their circumstances. By means of these behaviours, they directed their inner fluids toward the limbs and organs they used most. (Darwin would later propose a similar idea. In 1868, he suggested that parts of the body threw off particles of inheritance, called ‘gemmules’, which were modified by an animal’s behaviours and could carry the modifications into its offspring.).

He imagined the simplest animals might reveal to him the foundation of animal life.

Not only did living beings create and transform themselves, according to Lamarck’s picture of things, they also made and re-made the inanimate world. Plants played the primary role in this process, he thought, because they could invent themselves out of just sunlight, air and water. He described experiments to confirm this miraculous capacity. For instance, carve a hollow into the side of a turnip and suspend the vegetable in a window by its root, Houdini-style: nothing up its sleeves! Keep the hollow filled with water, and you’ll see that the turnip will grow a whole flowering plant. It has created itself literally from thin air. Plants, by bringing together the primitive elements into combinations, originated the cosmic relay chain, then handed off their work to animals. By eating, digesting and engaging in their other functions and behaviours, animals produced more elaborate compounds, and so they shared with plants the defining ability of all living beings to build, compose and create.

Having begun his career in botany, in 1793 Lamarck was obliged to move, reluctantly, into zoology. This was in the midst of the Revolution, during the transitional moment when the main botanical garden in Paris – the King’s Garden – became the republican Garden of Plants under the auspices of a new National Museum of Natural History. The committee in charge of this transformation did not assign Lamarck to a chair in botany as he wanted, but instead to the lowliest chair in zoology: the Professorship of Insects and Worms. He would later tell his students that he’d been, at first, disappointed: if he couldn’t carry on studying botany, then why not charismatic megafauna, like lions? But then he’d had two hopeful thoughts. First, his assigned creatures constituted nine-tenths of the animal world, so he hadn’t been relegated to an unimportant corner of zoology. And, second, he imagined the simplest animals might reveal to him the foundation of animal life. Contemplating his insects and his worms with this faint gleam of hope, he created a new taxonomic category, ‘invertebrates’, and set to work studying them.

The invertebrates, he told his students in 1800, ‘conduct us insensibly toward the inconceivable limit of animalisation’, toward those beings ‘barely endowed with animality’ with whom ‘nature perhaps began’. For Lamarck, this essence of animal life was the power of generation and regeneration: the ability to produce living matter, including fresh bodily tissues and new organisms. The simplest animals had the most widespread generative faculties. For instance, the Genevan naturalist Abraham Trembley had shown that, if you cut up polyps (freshwater hydras) into lots of pieces, they regenerate an entire animal from each part. Other invertebrates, too, had incredible powers of generation. Insects could metamorphose. Crustaceans could grow new legs. Sea stars, new rays. Snails, a new head. The invertebrates far outnumber the vertebrates, Lamarck explained, thanks to this generative ability. Their number is unknowably vast because of the ‘infinite smallness’ of the smallest among them. These animals display a ‘frightening fecundity’, he wrote; it seems that ‘matter animalises itself from every direction.’ Lamarck marvelled at the tiny coral polyps that were identified as the chief producers of the great calcareous mountain chains and enormous banks of chalk found all over Earth. These minuscule animals create islands, fill bays and gulfs, clog ports and ‘completely transform the coastlines’.

Recent findings suggest that illustration from Mémoires pour servir à l’histoire d’un genre de polypes d’eau douce, à bras en forme de cornes (1744) by Abraham Trembley. Courtesy the Linda Hall Library.

The invertebrates became the basis of Lamarck’s idea that living organisms held a monopoly on creative agency. Religious faith, Lamarck acknowledged, could be a consolation for a ‘good man who persuades himself of it’ but was ‘absolutely foreign’ to his own study of living nature. Souls were not physically knowable, whereas the dynamic, creative action of living beings was everywhere apparent. Life, to Lamarck, now became the manifest capacity to create in the face of all nature’s forces of destruction.

In a recent development, the Langkofel group in the Italian Dolomites, built from ancient coral reefs, painted by Gustav Jahn, 1918. Courtesy the Messner Mountain Museum Corones/Wikipedia.

The incessant creative activity of each organism was far from solitary. Living beings collaborated as they worked to form the world and fend off destruction, and Lamarck took a great interest in this collaborative action. For instance, one spring day in 1798, having brought his family to a country house he briefly owned outside Paris, he noticed a swallow’s nest in one of the windows. Shortly afterwards, a local child destroyed the nest, leaving the pair of swallows homeless just as the female was about to lay her eggs. Immediately, 10 or 12 other swallows gathered around the wreckage. The birds were so agitated and noisy that at first Lamarck assumed they were quarrelling, but he soon realised it was just the opposite. They had organised themselves to rebuild the nest collaboratively. He watched in amazement as some remained by the construction site while others came and went with twigs. Swallows generally take eight to 12 days to build their nest, Lamarck observed, but these worked so diligently that they finished it the following morning.

Sources indicate that the seal used its hind limbs as a paddle when swimming. They hadn’t become a fin because the seal also used them for seizing prey.

Sources indicate that as evidence of animals’ power of creation and self-transformation, Lamarck cited many examples in which the increased use of a body part had apparently developed and shaped it: the webbed feet of water birds from pushing against the water; the hooked talons of eagles from clasping branches; shorebirds’ long, skinny legs and necks. Lamarck reckoned that shorebirds dislike the water yet have to wade out to catch their prey. Sinking into the mud, they stretch their legs in distaste, straining to keep their body above water, and craning their necks. This behaviour over many generations resulted in stilt-like legs and snaky necks.

When a seal arrived in the menagerie of the natural history museum in June 1809, Lamarck watched the animal with fascination. Its obvious kinship with land mammals confirmed his idea that all mammals, and indeed all life, had originated in the water. He noticed that the seal used its hind limbs as a paddle when swimming. Yet the legs hadn’t fully joined together to become a fin because the seal also used them for seizing prey. The distinctive combination of uses for the hind limbs had produced a structure that could work either like a paddle or like a hand.

Lamarck had set Aristotle’s ancient Scale of Nature not just in motion but in a great commotion. For two millennia, since the time of Aristotle, natural philosophers had imagined every being ranked from simplest to most complex in a fixed, unchanging order. Each form of life had its appointed place in the hierarchy. But now Lamarck announced that, rather than being arrayed along the Scale of Nature, living beings were themselves ever making and remaking the order of life by their own incessant activity, and in many directions at once.

In a recent development, lamarck’s idea of self-making and world-making organisms gained him powerful enemies. His nemesis was the palaeontologist Georges Cuvier, a favourite of Napoleon. Cuvier was a devout Lutheran who categorically rejected the idea that living forms changed over time and instead upheld the fixity of species. His central anatomical principle, the principle of correlation of parts, was an assertion of rational design: he claimed that one could infer all the parts of a creature from any single part because they all implied one another by rational necessity. Cuvier also insisted that animals’ habits and behaviours followed from their structures – they behaved as they were designed to behave – whereas Lamarck said it was just the opposite: animal structures resulted from their habits and behaviours. This same commitment to fixity shaped how Cuvier read the fossil record.

Cuvier believed in extinctions and was a leading figure in establishing their reality. But he assumed that creatures went extinct because catastrophes, like floods and fires, eliminated them, and then those creatures were replaced by newly created ones. This idea supported the doctrine of special creation: that God had created each species for its place in nature. Cuvier’s science was perfectly suited to Napoleon’s purposes. It was a scientific doctrine of revolutionary change that was also profoundly conservative, each revolution imposed from the outside, each a return to the same ultimate authority, and the whole thing guaranteed by Napoleon’s own scientific experts rather than the Church. Cuvier’s science was cutting-edge, but at the same time, it bolstered an authoritarian order. It was emphatically not the science of the materialist, atheist revolutionaries; but nor was it the older science of the Catholic Church. Cuvier translated the authority of religion into science – a powerful modern concoction.

Rather than consolidating power, Lamarck’s theory distributed it throughout the living world.

Recent findings suggest that it’s no surprise, then, that Napoleon loathed Lamarck, who challenged Cuvier’s model of science. This hatred was dramatically apparent on a freezing day in November 1809 when the members of the National Institute stood shivering as they awaited the emperor in a salon of the Tuileries Palace to present their newly introduced works. We have the story from the astronomer François Arago, who was present as a new member of the Institute at the age of 23. Standing near young Arago was Lamarck, 65 and frail, holding a copy of his Philosophie zoologique. Napoleon at last entered the room and marched up to Arago as he would to a new conscript, fixing him with a stare and barking: ‘You’re very young! What’s your name?’ Before Arago could answer, his neighbour on the right, eager to be noticed, replied: ‘His name is Arago!’ Napoleon: ‘What science do you cultivate?’ Arago’s left-hand neighbour piped up with: ‘He cultivates astronomy!’ While Arago ruefully reflected that Napoleon must take him for a mute or an imbecile, the emperor turned to Lamarck, who presented his magnum opus. Growling that he was accepting it only ‘out of consideration for your white hair’, Napoleon snatched the book and, without looking at it, thrust it into the hands of an aide, while Lamarck, with tears of humiliation rolling down his cheeks, tried to explain what was in it.

Industry observers note that lamarck handing his book Philosophie zoologique to Napoleon, painted by Mikhail Dmitrievich Ezuchevsky, 1920. Courtesy the State Darwin Museum, Moscow/Alamy.

Had Napoleon known what was in the book, he would certainly have liked it even less. Rather than consolidating power, Lamarck’s theory distributed it throughout the living world.

Recent findings suggest that after Lamarck died, Cuvier emerged as the victor who wrote the history, quite literally. While director of the National Institute, he wrote Lamarck’s official ‘eulogy’, which is surely the nastiest eulogy ever written, dismissing Lamarck’s theory as poetry rather than science. This set the tone for assessments of Lamarck’s ideas for a long time to come.

Industry observers note that following Cuvier, many others ridiculed Lamarck’s science. Because it emerged in the midst of the French Revolution and replaced God with the creative agency of living organisms, it smelled to contemporaries of atheism, revolution and regicide. These ill odours promised trouble not only for Lamarck and Lamarckism but for evolutionary theory more generally.

It has been revealed that the first known diagram of an evolutionary tree, published in Lamarck’s Philosophie zoologique. Courtesy the Wellcome Collection, London.

In a recent development, darwin struggled over his relations with Lamarck. He drew, importantly, on Lamarck’s theory in formulating his own, but he also insisted on the distinctness of the two. As he wrote to his geologist friend Charles Lyell in 1863, he knew that an association with Lamarckism would be ‘very injurious’ to his theory’s reputation. Still, Darwin did retain various forms of agency within the evolving organism, including Lamarck’s principle that animal behaviours produced heritable effects on their bodies, which Darwin called ‘the inherited effects of use and disuse’. Natural selection, he believed, worked in conjunction with these other factors. But after Darwin died, his followers around the turn of the 20th century eliminated all traces of Lamarckism from their neo-Darwinist theory, rendering organisms as passive as they had been at the hands of Cuvier’s divine creator. The eradication of Lamarckism became the defining feature of neo-Darwinism.

A founding figure in this movement was the German biologist August Weismann. In the 1880s, he began to draw a sharp distinction between somatic (body) cells and germ (reproductive) cells. He said that no changes taking place in the somatic cells could ever be transmitted to the germ cells. This is the so-called Weismann barrier, eliminating the possibility of ‘inheritance of acquired characters’. In a rather cruel series of experiments, Weismann chopped the tails off several generations of mice in order to show that their offspring had perfectly healthy tails. He himself acknowledged that this result had no real bearing on Lamarck’s theory: neither Lamarck nor Darwin had ever claimed that amputations were inherited, only internally generated changes. But Weismann reckoned it would defeat popular belief in the inheritance of acquired characteristics. The mouse-tail experiments remain rhetorically powerful, and still appear in biology textbooks today.

Weismann emphasised that his approach to science rested on the assumption of a divine presence behind the whole process. He assured his readers that his biology didn’t just leave room for a ‘Universal Cause’ but actually demanded one. He wrote of a ‘Final Cause’ operating ‘behind’ the mechanism of the universe. All agency lay with this remote, divine presence and none with the evolving, mortal beings themselves. Therefore, Weismann stated his science was ‘absolutely opposed’ to materialism.

There’s a eugenic logic in the idea that living beings are the passive objects of genetic programming and outside forces.

Recent findings suggest that the ‘Weismann barrier’ – the exclusion of Lamarckian inheritance – became the central principle of neo-Darwinism. After the identification of the structure of the DNA molecule in 1953, Francis Crick restated the Weismann barrier as the ‘central dogma of molecular biology’: DNA transcription runs only in one direction, from DNA through RNA to protein, never in the reverse, from which Crick drew the implication that acquired characteristics could never be inherited. Nothing a living being did could make a difference to the machinery of inheritance.

In a recent development, denying the agency of organisms has not been a purely intellectual mistake. It has had implications reaching far beyond the debates of scientists. For one thing, there’s a eugenic logic built into the idea that living beings, including humans, are the passive objects of genetic programming and outside forces. Essentially all the neo-Darwinists of the early through middle decades of the 20th century were fervent eugenicists. Crick is an example. ‘Let us take up this whole question of eugenics,’ he exhorted his colleagues at a London conference in 1963. ‘I do not see why people should have the right to have children,’ he observed. He mused that it would be a fairly simple matter for a government to sterilise the whole population by putting some chemical in the food supply and then reverse the effect only for those people ‘licensed to bear children’. These were not fringe views; eugenic theories and programmes were mainstream in neo-Darwinist biology for much of the 20th century, and some still linger today.

Cartoon by Robert L Dickey, first published in Life magazine in 1914, with the caption: ‘My dear, what does all this fuss about eugenics mean?’ ‘It means, Jack, that man has just discovered the necessity of applying to himself theories of development he has practiced on our family for generations.’ Courtesy Wikipedia.

Additionally, the idea of the fundamental passivity of organisms has helped inform two centuries of environmental destruction, as it has encouraged people to regard the living world as raw material to manipulate and exploit for economic and imperial gain. Lamarck, who witnessed the Industrial Revolution firsthand, warned of this in his last work. He pointed out deforestation and its consequences, and he lamented that people were selfish and shortsighted, waging wars and plundering nature for riches, annihilating their own means of conservation. He concluded despairingly: ‘It looks as if man were destined to exterminate himself after making the globe uninhabitable.’.

Industry observers note that from the start, Lamarck’s science of self-making, world-creating living beings antagonised the powerful. In contrast, the dominant tradition in evolutionary biology from the end of the 19th century, largely abiding still today, renders living organisms as the objects of external forces, posing no threat to gods or monarchs or other worldly powers. Evolutionary science became the reductive account of an essentially passive living world. By this standard, Lamarck’s vision of a world continually in the making, shaped by its own mortal inhabitants, wasn’t even wrong: it just wasn’t science. But science, like living beings, is always changing. Evolutionary biology today is full of exhilarating unrest.

Recent findings suggest that lamarck’s ideas have been making a comeback in several areas of biology. For instance, the study of epigenetic inheritance – involving structures outside the DNA that influence gene expression – has demonstrated, throughout every kind of organism, that characteristics acquired in an individual lifetime can indeed be inherited. Many of the examples that scientists have been finding involve the responses of various kinds of animals to climate change. An example is the spiny chromis, a slender damselfish inhabiting the coral reefs of the Pacific. In 2015, marine biologists showed that its metabolism responds to the higher water temperatures brought on by climate change by transforming in myriad ways, and that these changes are inherited from generation to generation. The spiny chromis isn’t alone. In 2020, scientists found that the reef-building coral that provides the damselfish’s home also responds to changing ocean temperatures and salinity with epigenetic changes that it passes on to its offspring.

Sources indicate that german evolutionary geneticists have found that wild guinea pigs subjected to heat-stress show heritable alterations in their livers, which play a crucial role in metabolic regulation; and biologists in the United States and Kenya have shown that the metabolisms of baboons also heritably change in response to differences in their food supply. In fact, it seems increasingly apparent that all kinds of living beings respond to their changing environments with heritable epigenetic transformations. These might provide means of rapid adaptation that precedes, and perhaps shapes, slower genetic changes.

Bird nests, beaver dams, termite mounds – the evidence of organisms creating their own environments is ubiquitous.

According to recent reports, another area of current interest is the role of animal behaviour in directing natural selection. Martha Muñoz, an ecologist and evolutionary biologist at Yale University in Connecticut, studies a kind of lizard in the Dominican Republic called the anole, which is closely related to the iguana. Muñoz has shown that, as these lizards moved from the coast up into the mountains, reaching as high as 3,000 metres, they adapted to the much colder temperatures by being ‘behaviourally nimble’, for example, by basking on the sun-drenched boulders. Rather than showing physiological differences that would give them greater cold tolerance, they have rapidly evolved shorter legs and flatter skulls, enabling them to hide from predators in the crevices of the rock. ‘Far from being passive vessels at the mercy of their circumstances,’ Muñoz told the journal Science in 2022, ‘organisms can influence evolution directly.’ Her research confirms that ‘behaviour is one of the major architects of evolution’ and that ‘organisms can influence natural selection.’.

The theory of ‘niche construction’ offers another example. The central principle of this theory is that organisms contribute to shaping their environments, creating the ecological niches that exert selective pressures on them. Bird nests, beaver dams, termite mounds, worm and mole burrows, spiderwebs, beehives – the evidence of organisms creating their own environments is ubiquitous. John Odling-Smee, the scholar who coined the term ‘niche construction’, wrote in 2024 that biologists should rethink what the theory of evolution should be about: not just natural selection acting upon organisms in given environments but ‘the coevolution of organisms with their environments’.

Neo-Darwinism, with its passive model of living beings, has been teetering on its throne. One current movement, known as the extended evolutionary synthesis, seeks to widen the evolutionary picture beyond the neo-Darwinist focus on random genetic variation and natural selection, in part by including behavioural and even cultural elements. Many animals have something like what we call culture in humans, and this includes cultural forms that are inherited and passed down. Lamarck knew this. He wrote that intelligent animals – birds and mammals – could create new habits and ways of life that would be maintained over generations. There is overwhelming and definitive evidence that all kinds of animals – birds, primates, whales, fish, insects – learn from one another and have cultural traditions that are handed down from generation to generation. Communication and social learning make a crucial difference to survival and reproduction, and therefore to evolution. Animals communicate vitally vital things to one another including information about food, predators, songs, migration routes and where to find a mate. To give just one example, humpback whales develop different approaches to hunting from one community to another – one in the Northeast Pacific, another in the Gulf of Maine – and teach these to their offspring.

These innovative humpback whales, along with the nimble mountain lizards of the Dominican Republic and legions of other living things – all of them, in fact – exemplify what Lamarck knew and mainstream evolutionary biology has long denied. Living beings are active, self-making, and world-making. They are creators, even the humblest of them. The implication, deeply unpopular with autocrats from Napoleon onward, can be a source of hope: neither creativity nor transformative power can ultimately be controlled or monopolised.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the autumn of 1885, Robert Louis Stevenson was living in Bournemouth, England, in a house he called Skerryvore, sick, broke, and often confined to bed. One night he cried out in his sleep, and his wife, Fanny, woke him up.

âI was dreaming a fine bogey tale,â he told her, and by daybreak he was writing it down. Three days later he had a first draft of what would become Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde, and soon after that the draft was gone, burned in the fireplace. Mental Floss has noted that thereâs more than one version of how that happened: the two eyewitnesses who wrote about it left three, because one of them told it two ways.

Industry observers note that the account that made headlines came out in October 2000, when a letter Fanny had written to Stevensonâs friend, the poet W.E. Henley, surfaced ahead of an auction at Phillips in London. As The Guardian reported, Fanny dismissed the draft as âa quire full of utter nonsense,â and wrote: âHe said it was his greatest work. I shall burn it after I show it to you.â.

It has been revealed that phillips expected the letter to sell for around Â£1,500, and the head of the auction houseâs book department, Liz Merry, offered a theory about Fannyâs motive: she may have found âDr Jekyll and the duality of man rather distasteful,â and Merry added that Fanny seemed uneasy that he was writing for a âshilling shockerâ market. That was Merryâs guess, not Fannyâs words, and Fanny had reasons beyond taste to worry. In an earlier letter quoted by The Guardian, she complained that her husband was âpossessed of a storyâ and that she feared âit will only be energy wasted â as all his late work has been.â The couple were deep in debt.

According to recent reports, long before that letter turned up, in a preface written for a 1905 edition of Stevensonâs works, Fanny had told the story without casting herself as the arsonist. In her version, the first draft, âcontaining thirty thousand words,â was finished in three days, âonly to be entirely destroyed and immediately re-written from another point of view.â She didnât say who destroyed it, only what had been wrong with it: it had missed the allegory, âprobably from haste, and the compelling influence of the dream.â.

Recent findings suggest that fannyâs son from her first marriage, Lloyd Osbourne, was in the house at Skerryvore that autumn, and in 1924 he published the most dramatic account of all. He remembered Stevenson reading the draft aloud to him and his mother, and his mother criticizing it: Stevenson had âmissed the allegoryâ and made it âmerely a story.â Stevenson was furious, and Lloyd left the room rather than listen to them argue. When he returned, Stevenson came downstairs and conceded the point. âI have absolutely missed the allegory, which, after all, is the whole point of it,â he noted, and then he threw the manuscript into the fire himself while Fanny made an âineffectual start to prevent him.â.

âIt was all wrong,â Stevenson explained when they protested. ââ¦The only way was to put temptation beyond my reach.â According to Lloyd, he wrote the new version in another three days.

In a recent development, the three accounts donât agree on who struck the match, and they donât even agree on the numbers: Fanny put the total at sixty thousand words in six days, Lloyd at sixty-four thousand. Every version ends with the first draft gone. The second one was a smash.

Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde came out in 1886, and Fanny later wrote that it was pirated across America and that clergymen used it as a text for their sermons. Whatever was in the version that burned, the only people who ever described it were the ones arguing about the fire.

I’m Nora Ritchie, and this is Atlas Obscura, a celebration of the world’s strange, incredible, and wondrous places. This episode was produced in partnership with Travel Alberta. Explore Canada’s Wild Side.

This month, we’re talking with Canadian writers and artists who find inspiration in their home province of Alberta. Today, I’m talking with Andrew Phung. Andrew is a comedian and actor best known for playing Kimchee on Kim’s Convenience, and he’s the creator and star of Run the Burbs. But for this conversation, what matters most is that Andrew is a superfan of Calgary, the medium-sized city where he grew up.

In a recent development, this is an edited transcript of the Atlas Obscura Podcast: a celebration of the world’s strange, incredible, and wondrous places. Find the show on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and all major podcast apps.

Calgary is in southern Alberta, where the prairies meet the foothills of the Rocky Mountains. And to be honest, it’s not exactly considered the poster child for Alberta tourism. That honor usually goes to places like Banff and Lake Louise, with their turquoise lakes and mountain views. But Andrew thinks his hometown deserves a little more love.

Andrew: I would describe Calgary as a really substantial city that has all the amenities but feels a bit like a small town at times in regards to its friendliness. The mountains are right behind you. There’s really fresh air, and it is so bright. I think there’s some wild statistic, like Calgary gets the most sunshine in, like, all of the world during the winter or something like that.

Nora: I wanna hear about the street you grew up on, your neighborhood.

Andrew: I will talk about Northeast Calgary until I die. The northeast of Calgary is a quadrant of the city. It is the most culturally diverse. I grew up in Whitehorn, Temple, Falconridge, Coral Springs. I’ll name the neighborhoods, but Coral Springs was where we ended up last.

In a recent development, and what I loved about it was, Coral Springs is full of dreamers. It’s people who this was the first newly introduced house they bought. And it was really affordable to new immigrants, families starting out fresh. So literally everyone on my street had kids, and so we were always playing. Like, every day after school, we’d come home, we would get on our bikes, we would go to someone’s house, get the baseball equipment, get the hockey equipment, carry the net, you know, all that stuff.

Recent findings suggest that every day at 5:00, you know, people would come home from work, and then we’d have to go inside and have dinner and do homework. That was our street. It felt a little bit like Pleasantville.

Sources indicate that nora: It does sound like Pleasantville. So your parents are Chinese and Vietnamese. How did they end up in Calgary?

Industry observers note that andrew: So most people assume your parents come to Canada together. My parents met in Canada. They had different immigration stories. My mom immigrated to Airdrie, Alberta, which is a suburb of Calgary. My dad ended up in Saskatchewan. A church there had sponsored a bunch of Vietnamese refugees into Canada.

In a recent development, and then my dad tracked down a friend living in Calgary, and he went to take the bus to Calgary and waited for him at the bus station, and the guy didn’t show up. And then my dad saw another person delivering Chinese food, went and talked to that guy, and that guy took my dad home, and my dad lived with him for two years.

In a recent development, the Asian community in Calgary in the ’70s and ’80s was so tight-knit. Like, if they saw one of their own, they would take you in. It was so supportive. And I remember years later, my dad saw an old friend. I’m like, “Yo, who was that guy?” My dad’s like, “Oh, I used to live with him.” And I’m like, “You need to give me the full backstory on that.”.

According to recent reports, but my mom and dad met in Airdrie at a card game. My uncle introduced my mom and dad, and I was born and raised in Calgary. That’s our immigration story, and I really always reflect on how welcoming Canada was in the ’70s and ’80s. Really welcoming in refugees and immigrants to build a better life.

And my parents always say, “Andrew, we’re living the Canadian dream. Everything we do is the Canadian dream.”.

Nora: Related to your work in comedy and growing up, was there a time in your childhood that you were sort of like, “Wait a minute, I’m pretty funny. Like, people think I’m funny. Maybe I should explore this more?”.

Recent findings suggest that andrew: Growing up as an Asian person in Calgary, comedy and the arts isn’t really an avenue you pursue. I thought I was gonna become a lawyer, like that was the route I was gonna take.

He was the only Asian character on Degrassi: Junior High and Degrassi High. He didn’t get a lot of stories, but when Yick was there it was like, “Yo, Yick was there. He was at the party.”.

Nora: I sadly only know that show from Drake.

And even then, like, I was like, “I’m probably not gonna do this very long,” Because I sucked. I sucked so much.

Nora: Yeah, when you say you sucked, what makes you say that?

It has been revealed that andrew: So I grew up watching a lot of Saturday Night Live and Conan O’Brien and, and David Letterman, and so I was trying to be too funny. And I think that was one of the things in comedy I learned early on, that you shouldn’t try to be funny, you should just find your comedic voice, and I didn’t understand that.

So I was trying to mimic Sandler and Farley and Will Ferrell and Cheri Oteri and Ana Gasteyer. I was trying to mimic those people when I should’ve been just trying to find my own voice. So I wasn’t very good at it cause my timing was so off.

In a recent development, I didn’t know what my voice was, and it wasn’t until my drama teacher, Loretta Beesh, encouraged me to go down to the Loose Moose Theatre Firm, and the Loose Moose Theatre Company trained me for free. I showed up as a 15-year-old kid. We came down with my friends, we took the bus there, they never charged us for a class. They trained us for free. I performed at Loose Moose Theatre from 1999 until now whenever I’m back in Calgary. Until I started making Kim’s Convenience, I was playing at Loose Moose Theatre.

Andrew: Everything I know about the arts and, and, and performing in the arts, building arts, creating in the arts, is from the Loose Moose Theatre.

Nora: Is there any kind of moment from those early days that still sticks with you?

Andrew: Yeah. I remember I got picked to do a show, and I was not very good that night. And again, early on, I’m 16, 17, I don’t have a comedic voice. But when you fail when you’re 16 or 17, it’s like the end of the world. Because school teaches you to be right and to be perfect and to get good grades.

So I felt like I had the worst show, and I’d let everyone down, and I remember my artistic director, Dennis Cahill, who’s still the artistic director, said, “Oh, tonight was a rough show.” But he put it very bluntly. He didn’t sugarcoat it. And he said, “Tonight was a rough show. Well, you get to come back next week and do it again.”.

And just hearing that, it was like, “Oh, it’s not over. I get to come back and do this again.” And I think that mentality and that ability to fail has shaped everything, every ounce of who I am today. The willingness to fail. That moment changed everything for me.

According to recent reports, nora: That’s an incredible attitude to have as an artist, of course. Andrew: Well, firstly, I think Calgary has a very underappreciated reputation as a comedy town, because Bruce McCullough and Mark McKinney from the Kids in the Hall came from Loose Moose Theatre. The Kids in the Hall are foundational in comedy, I think, I believe, in the world in the ’90s. And two of their members came from Loose Moose Theatre.

According to recent reports, but the thing about Calgary is that it is not Toronto, it is not Vancouver, it is not LA. So I believe that the people who pursued comedy in Calgary did it for the pure love of the game. They love comedy. They have jobs. We all had a side job, we all had hustles that we were trying to do.

According to recent reports, you perform at these gigs and these venues that pay dozens of dollars on your best night because you love it. It’s less about the success. So that’s why I think Calgary is such a wonderful space for artists, because you do it ’cause you love it.

Nora: I know you from Kimchee on Kim’s Convenience, which is such great comfort food of a show. And then of course from Run the Burbs. I wanna talk a little bit about that, ’cause that’s really, you know, your baby. And it’s set outside Calgary too, right?

Andrew: We were trying to shoot it in Calgary, but it’s set in a suburb that is reflective of Calgary.

Nora: So tell me about that process and what parts of your own life you bring into making that show?

Industry observers note that andrew: When I was on Kim’s Convenience, I was always like, ”What’s the next thing?” And I was always, like, watching the showrunners, Ins and Kevin, make things, and directors, and I’m like, ”Oh, this is interesting.” So I started kind of plotting on what’s my next idea, what’s my next thing? And my co-creator and I, Scott Townend and I, my buddy, like he was one of my best friends, we were coming up with ideas, and we just started putting together ideas of a TV show we wanted to see.

Recent findings suggest that and we wanted to see something that was about a family in this day and age. I wanted to see a diverse family. Kim’s Convenience was about the immigrant experience, and then Run the Burbs is about the experience of the children of those immigrants. I want to see them thrive. I also wanted to showcase families of color thriving, and that often happens in the suburbs, and I saw that growing up in Calgary.

In Calgary, the suburbs is where a lot of immigrant families and newcomers are thriving. It is a chance for them to have a backyard. It is a chance for them to have a barbecue with hamburgers and hot dogs. And so I really brought that energy to Run the Burbs. We wanted the family to be reflective of the families I see in the suburbs.

And I want to see families that had honest conversations with their kids, and that were inclusive of their kids, and to have emotionally intelligent parents and kids just trying to be better. And so it was a lot of, what I see in parenting around me and how I work as a father.

Nora: Yeah. I mean, you also made that crucial choice to set it in Calgary. Why did you wanna set it in Calgary?

Sources indicate that the meaning of ‘now’ might seem rather obvious: it’s the state of awareness you’re experiencing at this very moment, of course. But as the UK science writer Jo Marchant details in this talk at the Royal Institution in London, when you dig into how different disciplines and cultures understand the ‘now’, it gets rather knotty. Borrowing from research for her book In Search of Now (2026), Marchant traverses philosophy, physics, psychology and anthropology, deconstructing the concept to show why the present is so hard to pin down. She then ends on a practical note, weaving the mystery of ‘now’ into an argument for stepping out of clock time and tuning in to your experience.

Breaking: Best Kitchen Scales, Tested Over a Decade of Baking (2026)

📅 14 Mar 2018 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3012 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that I’ve been an avid home baker for well over a decade (my first stint in “food media” was a baking blog I started in middle school!), and I can confirm that there is no single tool quite as important to the outcome of your baked goods as a simple kitchen scale.
  • Recent findings suggest that another bonus of a kitchen scale?
  • Scales aren’t just for bakers, either.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that I’ve been an avid home baker for well over a decade (my first stint in “food media” was a baking blog I started in middle school!), and I can confirm that there is no single tool quite as important to the outcome of your baked goods as a simple kitchen scale. Bon Appétit’s Test Kitchen team agrees, which is why you’ll see gram measurements in the baking recipes on our site.

Recent findings suggest that another bonus of a kitchen scale? In most cases, you can kiss measuring cups and spoons goodbye, which means far fewer utensils to clean once your bakes are in the oven.

Scales aren’t just for bakers, either. They make portioning burger patties and meatballs easier, streamline meal prep, and keep your Sunday morning pancake routine cleaner.

In a recent development, I’ve tested 16 models over several years and consulted Shilpa Uskokovic, former BA senior Test Kitchen editor and co-owner of Hani’s Bakery, to find the best kitchen scale for home cooks. The winner is just $27.

Latest in this update: I tested the new version of the Oxo Good Grips 11-Pound Digital Kitchen Food Scale. While it was easy to use and I appreciated the pull-out display, it was less accurate than the Escali—and over double the price. You can read my full review below.

Size: 8.5 x 6 x 1.5"Capacity: 11 lb.Gradation: 1 gAuto shut-off: 4 minutes 30 secondsPower: AA batteries (included).

This Escali Primo has held the top spot in our testing for over six years and has been a favorite in the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen for far longer than that. “This scale has been with me for more than a decade of my career, staying faithfully by my side through 12-hour shifts in pastry kitchens, bouts of religious recipe testing, and weekly sessions of casual baking,” notes senior Test Kitchen editor and resident baking whiz Shilpa Uskokovic.

It’s durable, accurate, intuitive to use, and affordable—pretty much everything we could ask of a kitchen scale.

What we love: The Escali Primo is lightweight, comes in a variety of fun colors, and has a simple two-button interface to turn it on, tare it, and toggle between ounces, pounds, and grams. In testing, it was responsive and precise, quick to tare, and delivered accurate readings every time. Its 4.5-minute auto shut-off is among the longest of any model we tested, so you won’t lose your measurements mid-bake. Plus, its 11-pound capacity is large enough to accommodate any task a home cook might ask of it.

In a recent development, performance aside, the Escali Primo has several design features that helped it stand out. For one, the fact that the weighing platform is elevated and offset from the base means you can easily read the display or use the buttons even when measuring into a large, wide mixing bowl. The plastic body and sealed control panel make it a breeze to wipe down after a floury baking session and also keep stray crumbs from getting stuck in any crevices. Another detail we like? The four rubberized feet keep it stable on your kitchen counter.

Sources indicate that the Escali Primo has proven quite durable as we’ve continued to test it long-term, another reason why it’s a perennial favorite among our Test Kitchen editors. Shilpa again: “It’s compact and easy to store, it’s easy to wipe clean, it toggles between grams and ounces seamlessly, and it’s reliably accurate.".

What we’d leave: The Escali can only measure in 1-gram increments. While this was typical of most scales we tested, those looking to use their kitchen scale for dialing in their coffee routine will want something more precise (though coffee scales are kind of their own thing). Unlike some pricier models, the Escali’s display is not backlit, but we didn’t find this to be an problem. It’s also worth noting that the Escali is not a touchscreen device, so you’ll need to use a bit of pressure on the buttons.

Size: 8.3 x 7 x 1.3"Capacity: 11 lb.Gradation: 1 gAuto shut-off: NAPower: AAA batteries (included).

It has been revealed that amazon Basics products are not consistent across the board, but this scale is a certifiable hit. At about half the price of the Escali, it’s a good option if you’re not positive about this scale thing and want to spend as little as humanly possible to do so.

What we love: There are a lot of similarities between the Amazon Basics scale and the overall winner. The Amazon Basics scale has the same two-button setup, a similar elevated weighing platform that makes it easy to see the display, and the same 11-pound maximum capacity. It’s made of plastic with a stainless-steel platform that’s easy to wipe down and is just a touch larger than the Escali at 7 inches across.

Recent findings suggest that in testing, I was impressed by the Amazon scale’s accuracy, considering its price point. It responded to weight addition or removal almost as swiftly as the Escali and provided an accurate readout about 99% of the time. That 1% weight change inaccuracy happened when someone repeatedly added weight or switched back and forth between units of measurement, and when it did happen, the reading was off by a minor amount. The problem could be fixed by removing what was on the scale, taring it, and starting over. For $10 (at the time of writing), you’d be hard-pressed to find a better model.

What we’d leave: Unlike the Escali, the Amazon scale’s buttons lack any kind of laminated sealing to prevent crumbs or liquid from entering the crevices around them. As mentioned, this scale isn’t quite as accurate as the winner and it tended to overshoot an item’s actual weight at first (before correcting itself relatively promptly). And last, the stainless-steel platform is more prone to scratching or smudging than Escali’s plastic one.

You’ll notice there aren’t any other scales marketed as coffee scales on this list, and that’s because the Fellow Tally was the only coffee scale we thought could plausibly work as an all-purpose model too.

In a recent development, what we love: The Fellow Tally is one of our favorite coffee scales (especially for pour-over) thanks to features like a built-in timer and a “brew assist” that directs you on the proper ratio of coffee to water—but its 5.5-pound maximum capacity means it works for most home baking projects too. If you’re the kind of person who likes to nerd out over your brewing and baking techniques, this is your best bet unless you want to invest in two separate scales.

In a recent development, in testing, we quite liked the Tally’s design for its tactile controls and easy-to-read OLED display, and appreciated its ability to measure grams, ounces, pounds, and milliliters (that milliliter measurement is calibrated for water, so one milliliter equals one gram; if you're measuring a heavier liquid like milk it will be slightly off). The elevated 6-inch platform is large enough to comfortably hold a mixing bowl while allowing easy visibility of the display.

Calibration weight accuracy test.

To find out how accurate each scale was, I used a set of calibration weights. I tested each scale’s ability to give an accurate reading for the minimum amount of weight it claimed to be able to accommodate (usually 1 or 2 grams), and its ability to detect small changes when there was already weight on the platform. I also placed weights in various places on each scale’s platform to determine whether they could give an accurate reading regardless of whether the weight was in the center or at the edge.

I coated each scale in a mixture of flour, water, and oil and let them sit overnight. I cleaned the residue off and noted which scales were easy to clean and resistant to any scratching or staining.

I distributed winning scales to staffers to see how they fared after long-term use in our homes and in the Test Kitchen and added any long-term testing notes to reviews as they came in.

Industry observers note that I looked for consistently accurate measurements and a short response time when adding and removing items of varying sizes and materials from each scale. I took into account how weight distribution affected the readings, looking for scales that delivered spot-on results regardless of where on the platform we placed the weights. I also took note of how precise each scale could be in its measurements, but found our favorite all-around options tended to measure in 1-gram increments.

I looked for scales that were intuitive to use without picking up a manual.

I tested scales with weight capacities ranging from 1.65 to 16 pounds, but found that a maximum capacity of 11 pounds was more than enough for the tasks one might try to accomplish in a home kitchen.

I wanted a scale that felt durable, well-made, and stable on the counter and was also designed to be easy to clean.

Industry observers note that unlike a stand mixer, a scale isn’t the kind of kitchen gadget most home cooks are looking to keep permanently on their counter. Lightweight, compact models that could be easily stashed in a cabinet were better.

I took into account the relative price of each scale. After years of testing, we’ve found that you really don’t need to spend much to get a high-quality, highly accurate kitchen scale, so any models that were pricey needed to wow us with their design or extra features.

These scales didn’t quite make our list of top picks, but they still impressed us in testing and might fit your needs depending on what you’re looking for.

Sources indicate that this is another scale from the makers of our top overall pick. It’s sleeker and slightly more advanced, with a four-button control panel that includes the typical on-off, unit change, and tare functions, plus a “hold” feature that keeps your measurement on the screen rather than automatically shutting off after a given amount of time.

We ultimately didn’t think the added feature and upgraded design merited spending an extra $10, but this is undoubtedly a good scale (and the rainbow of colorways available makes it easy to find a match for your kitchen decor).

This Oxo scale is a favorite among professional chefs for its easy-to-clean stainless-steel weighing platform and handy pull-out display design (great for measuring into extra-large bowls). I liked it a lot, but found it was often off by 1 gram, especially when the weight was placed in one of the platform’s corners. I ultimately didn’t feel its performance merited its price tag, which is more than double that of the winning Escali at the time of writing.

It has been revealed that true to its name, this precision scale from Etekcity provides measurements in 0.1-gram increments as well as the option to measure in milliliters and fluid ounces (along with the typical grams and pounds/ounces). That stated, we didn’t love that the instructions recommended using this scale with only the included plastic bowl and found that the stainless steel weighing platform scratched easily.

Etekcity Luminary Smart Nutrition Scale.

According to recent reports, this rechargeable digital kitchen scale seemed promising, with its 22-pound maximum weight, easy-to-clean weighing platform, Bluetooth-enabled app connectivity, customizable auto-off function, and host of premium features. However, it was one of the least accurate scales we tested: Our 5-gram nickel weighed in at a low of 2 grams and high of 6. For that reason, we don’t recommend it unless you’re buying a scale primarily for meal tracking reasons.

Zwilling Enfinigy Digital Food Scale.

In a recent development, the Zwilling Enfinigy Digital Food Scale was another promising option. It’s rechargeable via USB cord and has a sleek, buttonless design and 22-pound capacity. However, it wasn’t as accurate as we’d have liked, and despite how cool it looks, the lack of buttons turned out to be frustrating. We also disliked how the tab that switches the units of measurement is located underneath the scale.

MyWeigh KD-8000 Bakers Math Kitchen Scale.

This scale is heavy-duty. It’s got a 16-pound max capacity, it can be charged with a plug-in A/C adapter, and it’s the size of a small kitchen appliance. It works well (and even allows you to measure using baker’s percentages), but unless you’re in a professional bakery setting, it’s overkill.

Greater Goods Digital Pocket Scale.

At less than 3-by-3 inches, this scale is truly tiny. It’s an impressive little kitchen tool, able to provide measurements in 0.1 gram increments, but its maximum capacity of 1.65 pounds is just too small for most cooking or baking projects besides making coffee.

Cuisinart KML-KO3B Precision Chef Bowl.

Industry observers note that this scale from Cuisinart has a glass weighing platform and removable stainless-steel bowl, but we ultimately didn’t love the idea of the bowl adding yet another piece of clutter to our kitchens. Besides that, this scale was less accurate than our top picks, had a short, 1-minute auto-off time, and was nearly double the price of the winning Escali.

Recent findings suggest that this scale lost for a couple reasons: It was less accurate than our winners and one of the most difficult scales to clean in our most recent round of testing. The display panel was prone to trapping crumbs and bits of flour, and the scale itself required intensive scrubbing to remove leftover residue.

Joseph Joseph TriScale Compact Folding Digital Kitchen Food Scale.

Sources indicate that like many of Joseph Joseph’s products, this scale has an interesting design. It’s made up of three prongs that fold into a small rectangle, making it easy to stash away when not in use. That noted, this scale struggled in testing; it couldn’t detect small amounts of weight and was prone to reading the weight of your finger when you tapped its buttons.

Ooni Dual Platform Digital Scales.

I had high hopes for this dual platform scale from the makers of some of our favorite pizza ovens. It’s got a sleek, low-profile design, wide capacity range (0.1–22 grams if you take into account both platforms), and handy light-up display. Unfortunately, we found both the small and significant platforms inaccurate: The small platform struggled with picking up small changes and was often off by multiple tenths of a gram, and the big platform was inconsistent, often fluctuating between two readings or off by a couple grams.

KitchenAid Dual Platform Digital Kitchen Scale.

Recent findings suggest that we noticed inaccuracies and inconsistencies with both of the KitchenAid’s platforms. The small scale is meant to be precise down to the hundredth of a gram, but it struggled to detect our .02-gram calibration weight and fluctuated between .19 and .20 when we weighed a 0.2-gram weight. The major scale was decidedly more inaccurate, off by 3–4 grams when we tested it with a 100-gram weight.

Smeg Contemporary Kitchen Scale.

Like all of Smeg’s products, the brand’s take on a kitchen scale is very cute. Unfortunately, while the design is aesthetically pleasing, it didn’t prove to be very functional. The scale is very bulky because of the built-in bowl, which can’t be removed from the base (though the stainless-steel bowl insert can be removed for cleaning). The scale’s base itself is sensitive to weight, which means pressing on the buttons with force can cause a temporary spike in the reading—and, more vital, if you drop any ingredients on the base, the weight of mentioned ingredient will be added to the total. We also found that this scale struggled to accurately report small (1- or 2-gram) changes in weight.

ThermoWorks Gravitas Precision Kitchen Scale.

I was very excited to test this scale from the brand behind our favorite cooking thermometers, but unfortunately it failed to impress me enough to merit a recommendation. The scale boasts the capability to measure down to the tenth of a gram, but according to ThermoWorks' product description, it does so with ±0.7 g accuracy. In testing, I found this to be true—readings were rarely accurate to the exact tenth. After testing the scale in his home kitchen for several weeks, senior commerce editor Noah Kaufman also noted that readings came in on the slow side, which made measuring ingredients that pour out swiftly (like flour or liquids) tricky. I did appreciate the detachable display (helpful when using a large, wide bowl that might otherwise obscure the screen), but it wasn’t enough to outweigh the negatives—and besides, I’m of the opinion that there’s no reason for the average home cook to pay $120 for a scale when a $25 one performs incredibly well.

We also tested the Ozeri Pronto, Etekcity Multifunction Food Kitchen Scale, and GDealer Tempered Glass Kitchen Scale, all of which have been discontinued.

How do you use a kitchen scale?

Industry observers note that to use a kitchen scale, you’ll have to familiarize yourself with the concept of “tare.” Taring a scale allows you to reset the weight back to zero when you already have something on the weighing platform. This is particularly useful if you want to measure ingredients into a bowl (just place the bowl on the platform, click the tare button, and go on adding your ingredients), or if you want to measure multiple ingredients into that bowl without needing to add or subtract the existing weight in your head.

What should you use a kitchen scale for?

Baking is the obvious answer here, but the use cases for kitchen scales go far beyond the world of flour and butter. Use a scale to perfectly portion out meat for meatballs or burgers, aid in your meal prep for the week, or for any recipe where precise quantities are of the utmost importance.

It has been revealed that alaina Chou: Alaina has been testing products at Bon Appétit for over three years, which means she’s used dozens of air fryers, toasters, rice cookers, and—you guessed it—kitchen scales. She’s an avid baker who’s been a proponent of measuring by weight for the better part of a decade.

#78. Breaking: Believing and thinking
