Breaking: Believing and thinking

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3962 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Aeon

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the idea of separating church and state – now entrenched in many modern liberal democracies – is in some ways strange.
  • Recent findings suggest that separating church and state appears strange from other perspectives as well.
  • We’re fans of Jefferson’s principle, one of us (Neil Van Leeuwen) being a philosophy professor who grew up in the Christian Reformed Church, and the other (Jacob Eisler) being a law professor who regularly attends synagogue.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the idea of separating church and state – now entrenched in many modern liberal democracies – is in some ways strange. After all, governments must keep themselves informed and inform their citizens. That’s why they turn to the science of meteorology to predict weather patterns, to economics to understand patterns of growth and decline, and to the medical sciences to improve public health. So why wouldn’t governments also keep close alliances with religious institutions to know what’s going on with God?

Recent findings suggest that separating church and state appears strange from other perspectives as well. In the historical sweep of large-scale human societies, it’s a relative newcomer, often associated with the United States’ founding father Thomas Jefferson. In 1802, Jefferson asserted the principle of separation in a letter to the Danbury Baptist Association in Connecticut:.

We’re fans of Jefferson’s principle, one of us (Neil Van Leeuwen) being a philosophy professor who grew up in the Christian Reformed Church, and the other (Jacob Eisler) being a law professor who regularly attends synagogue. But Jefferson’s letter makes putting the principle into practice sound simpler than it is – as though governments could be entirely hands-off when it comes to people’s beliefs, or ‘opinions’. That, however, can’t be right: engaging with and shaping political, social and other kinds of beliefs is actually a core function of government. Public education guides what people believe about everything from mathematics to history to astronomy. Governments also shape beliefs for policy reasons. If fire department officials learn that people believe a building is safe when it isn’t, they will try to change what people believe about the building’s safety. Belief is also a category of legal interest. If a psychotherapist, for example, believes a patient is a danger to himself or others, the therapist is obligated by law to report that belief.

All this means that Jefferson’s ‘wall of separation’ can’t sensibly prohibit governments from intervening on beliefs of any type whatsoever. Rather, Jefferson – along with advocates of the principle who came after him – must have presupposed that there is something distinctive about religious beliefs that makes it reasonable to give them a different legal status.

Industry observers note that but what is this distinctive thing? Is it that religious beliefs concern God? No, because Buddhism is a religion with its own beliefs, yet Buddhism has no supreme deity. Is it that religious beliefs concern the supernatural generally? No, because many superstitions that aren’t part of a religion concern the supernatural too. Is it that religious beliefs concern morality, as the biologist Stephen Jay Gould once suggested? No, because many religious beliefs aren’t about morality, and many moral beliefs aren’t religious. In any case, any system of government must presuppose some moral beliefs – eg, that murder is wrong – to be a government at all. These considerations might make one despair of articulating the psychological distinction of interest – what’s different about religious ‘belief’? – that’s needed to make sense of separating church and state in the first place.

In a recent development, such attempts at characterising religious belief fail, we think, because they focus on belief contents, or what the believing is about. But since any given idea can be believed in a religious way or not, that won’t work. Our suggestion, then, is that religiously believing is a different attitude from ordinary matter-of-fact believing – a different way of relating to ideas – and that this is what’s distinctive about religious belief. In other words, sacralising an idea is different from just taking it to describe how things are. Furthermore, empirical research in cognitive science and anthropology of religion, along with accompanying philosophical analysis, can help reveal characteristic features of the difference in attitude we’re after. To have specific terms, we call that the difference between religious credence and factual belief. Understanding this difference, we’ll see, helps make sense of Jefferson’s wall of separation, and supports the rationale for separating church and state in liberal democracies more generally.

Whatever they are, ‘beliefs’ come in different varieties. The word ‘belief’ is polysemous – meaning it can refer to a range of different-but-related things – and it subsumes a motley crew: from humdrum factual beliefs (say, about where the ice-cream store is) to superstitions (like those found in astrology), and from moral beliefs about murder to philosophical beliefs about how ‘all is one’. As mentioned earlier, beliefs can also be categorised by their contents (what is the belief about? Is it about politics? Or maybe about a probable scientific theory?) Or by the attitude they embody (how does a person relate to given ideas or contents?) Here, however, we focus on the differences between matter-of-fact believing and religious credence as distinct ways in which people process ideas. There are, of course, more varieties of belief-like attitudes. But we home in on factual belief and religious credence since the differences in those attitudes matter most to the psychology of separating church and state.

Ethnographies of religion, like the anthropologist Tanya Luhrmann’s When God Talks Back (2012), feature the devout talking of their ‘beliefs’ as a matter of choice. One of the congregants from the Vineyard Church whom Luhrmann interviewed told her: ‘There is always a choice to believe what it is.’ And a common theme in the Vineyard is choosing Jesus, which means choosing to believe in Jesus. Nor is choosing ‘belief’ unique to Christianity. People around the world switch religions for reasons of romance or for other social incentives, which means voluntarily choosing what religious credence to have.

But suppose someone offered you $1 million to believe, in a matter-of-fact way, that lions are vegetarians. Could you do it? We doubt it, even if you wanted the money. You could voluntarily imagine that lions are vegetarians, or you might pretend to believe it. But if you know that lions eat meat, you can’t just choose to believe the contrary. This is one illustration of how factual belief is not under voluntary control. Or, as one of us (Neil) has put it in Religion as Make-Believe (2023): if you factually believe it, you can’t help believing it. Try for a moment to factually believe that New York City is in Quebec, that Iceland is in the Southern Hemisphere, or that Justin Bieber speaks Swahili as his mother tongue.

This gives us our first processing difference between religious credence and matter-of-fact belief:.

Difference number 1: religious credence is voluntary, while factual belief is involuntary.

But if matter-of-fact belief isn’t voluntary, or responsive to the will, what does it respond to? Numerous psychological pressures come into play, including distortions like biases and misremembering. But that shouldn’t obscure the main driver of factual belief: evidence. Examples are so simple they’re easy to overlook. If you think, in a matter-of-fact way, that you started the washing machine and then, an hour later, see that the clothes you loaded are dry and still dirty, the evidence of your eyes extinguishes your prior factual belief. If you think the supermarket is open and then arrive to find its lights are all out, that evidence changes your factual belief.

Noah was an exemplar of faith for building an enormous boat when there was no evidence of an impending flood.

Empirical research reveals such evidence-responsiveness already in children and even infants. According to The Scientist in the Crib (1999) by the developmental psychologist Alison Gopnik and colleagues, young children and even babies learn about the world by forming mini-theories in different domains, and testing them – much like scientists do. According to the research of the developmentalists Paul Harris and Melissa Koenig, children are also evidentially discriminating in how they learn from other people. Among other things, children are more likely to believe sources that have been accurate in the past than sources that have been inaccurate.

Is religious credence similarly responsive to evidence?

Consider faith. In Hebrews 11:1, we read: ‘Now faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen.’ If that’s right, then religious credence doesn’t depend on evidence in the way factual belief does. In the Gospel of John, for example, we read about Doubting Thomas, who demands evidence that the man before him is Jesus resurrected; he consequently is an exemplar of what faith is not. In the Old Testament, Noah was an exemplar of faith for building an enormous boat when there was no visible evidence of an impending flood. Examples can be multiplied. If faith is to stand strong, religious credence must endure the slings and arrows of absent, or even contrary, evidence.

Sources indicate that contemporary cognitive science of religion bears out this point. In a series of cross-cultural studies, researchers have found that, from a young age, people, even in religious societies like Iran and the US, report lower levels of confidence in the invisible religious entities they profess, like God and angels, than in invisible scientific entities, like germs and oxygen. That difference in confidence is presumably due to the felt poverty of evidence for the invisible religious entities. Yet people in some sense nonetheless ‘believe’ (read: religious credence) in the invisible religious entities. The psychologists Emily Liquin, S Emlen Metz and Tania Lombrozo conducted studies finding that participants indicated a lower need for explanation when it came to religious beliefs as opposed to scientific beliefs, while at the same time having a higher mystery acceptance for religious beliefs. So people are often fine treating their religious credences as inexplicable and mysterious.

That gives us our second difference between religious credence and matter-of-fact belief:.

Difference number 2: factual belief is highly vulnerable to evidence, while religious credence is not vulnerable to evidence.

It has been revealed that there are, of course, complications here. Religious apologists, for example, claim evidence for the stories and doctrines they profess. But claiming evidence is not the same as having one’s credences be vulnerable to it, and apologists are outliers anyway against the broad background of faithful who don’t usually pretend to treat their religious credence in an evidence-based way.

Industry observers note that those differences, voluntary choice versus evidence-responsiveness, are differences in how religious credence versus factual belief arise in the first place. But what about downstream differences, like how they bring about action and behaviour?

This brings us to the third difference. Have you ever heard the expression ‘once-a-week Christian’? The phrase describes people who act as though their Christian ‘beliefs’ are true one day a week – and then largely leave them dormant otherwise. Having grown up and participated in different religious traditions ourselves, we can say from personal experience that more people fit this compartmentalised model than would like to admit. Even those who practise devotion daily may act as if God is real specifically in sacred or ritual times and places, but then not really act this way otherwise. If one asks religious people whether God is ever-present in their lives, they might say yes. But such probes might be like opening the refrigerator to see whether the light is always on. In Breaking the Spell: Religion as a Natural Phenomenon (2006), the philosopher Daniel Dennett highlights this behavioural pattern in even blunter terms. He points out that people do things with God watching that they wouldn’t do with their own mothers watching, and then asks pointedly: ‘Do you really believe God is watching you? Perhaps not.’ We would say that people who profess to religious credence do typically have religious credence in a watchful deity – but, to Dennett’s point, not factual belief.

It has been revealed that empirical studies and ethnographic observations further exemplify the compartmentalisation of religious credence. According to one study, people in the Bible Belt start subscriptions to pornography sites at the same rate as in less conservative regions of the US – though not on Sundays, when the rate is significantly lower. According to another study, charitable giving among the religious is not significantly different from among the secular – except for on Sundays. Turning to a different religious context, the experimental economist Erik Duhaime found that, in an economic game, 100 per cent of Moroccan shopkeepers in the Medina of Marrakesh chose the most charitable option while the call to prayer was audible, dropping to 50 per cent in the 20 minutes following it.

Even if one pretends that a slab of concrete is a soft bed, one still stretches out on it slowly so as not to injure oneself.

Another way of putting the point about compartmentalisation would be to say that religious credences tend to guide people’s symbolic actions – prayer, liturgies, rituals or even charity – but not their everyday instrumental actions, like commuting to work or feeding the dog. In those cases, the world is just a world, and supernatural beliefs are largely dormant. And even if a religious tradition says its religious ‘beliefs’ should govern actions all the time, the fact that such norms exist and are hard to follow is actually evidence that such religious credences usually don’t guide action outside of sacred settings. (If they did, why have such a norm?).

Matter-of-fact believing, however, is not compartmentalised in this way. Factual belief, in the sense at work here, is a person’s default cognitive map of the world, and it is always on, whenever we act. Examples of ideas most people factually believe help to illustrate this point. Dried concrete is always hard. Electricity just exists. Wood comes from trees. And so on – at least for people who believe those things in a matter-of-fact way. This lack of compartmentalisation can also be illustrated through a contrasting reference to pretend play: even if one pretends that a slab of concrete is a soft bed, one still stretches out on it slowly so as not to injure oneself, rather than flopping down on it. That’s because the factual belief that concrete is hard still guides action even when one is pretending otherwise. Whenever you perform actions, you act on a mental model of how things just are, and a person’s default mental model of what the world is like is what we are calling factual belief.

Difference number 3: religious credence is compartmentalised, while factual belief is uncompartmentalised.

Industry observers note that this is all just a snapshot of some of the psychological processing differences between religious credence and factual belief. There are, of course, complications and details to sort out – including hard-to-categorise examples, like conspiracy ‘beliefs’, along with quasi-religious ideological credences – but those shouldn’t obscure the overall picture. Religious people, by and large, have a two-map cognitive structure with factual belief and religious credence playing distinct roles. Factual belief is the evidence-responsive default cognitive map that guides action across settings, and religious credence is a chosen, compartmentalised cognitive map that becomes active in sacralised ritual settings. Those settings may occur as often as several times a day, just one day a week, or even more rarely than that, but compartmentalisation is there in any case.

Before returning to the concern of separating church and state, let’s just address one more question about this overall psychological picture: are lay people (not just people who read and write essays like this one) aware of the psychological difference between factual belief and religious credence?

The answer, the evidence suggests, is yes – at least in a vague way.

It has been revealed that to start, people often express their religious credences by saying things like ‘I personally believe…’ But one would not express a matter-of-fact belief, say, that their bicycle is in the garage, by saying: ‘I personally believe my bicycle is in the garage.’ They would rather say: ‘I think my bicycle is in the garage’ or just ‘It’s in the garage.’ The inclination to use ‘personally’ suggests people have an intuitive awareness that the kind of ‘belief’ being expressed is a different attitude, a different way of relating to ideas from matter-of-fact belief. And there is more systematic empirical evidence for this point, as well. One of us (Neil) together with colleagues has conducted experimental studies showing that English speakers tend to use the word ‘believes’ when it comes to describing religious attitudes but just ‘thinks’ when it comes to describing matter-of-fact beliefs.

Furthermore, such linguistic differentiation has parallels in other languages, including Fante (a dialect of the Akan people of Ghana), Thai, Mandarin and Bislama (a creole spoken in Vanuatu). Further studies show that people’s use of the word ‘believes’ correlates with seeing an attitude as being held voluntarily and not for evidential reasons – for example, out of loyalty – and as giving rise to symbolic action, like public pronouncements. People’s use of the word ‘thinks’, on the other hand, correlates with seeing an attitude as being held for evidential reasons and as giving rise to truth-dependent instrumental action (like buying property or making investments). All of that suggests that most people are at some level tracing the differences that the foregoing theory makes explicit – and they’re often using the words ‘believe’ versus ‘think’ to report religious credence versus factual belief.

Sources indicate that let’s return to Jefferson’s idea and to the political realm more generally. How does the psychological difference between factual belief and religious credence support the political principle of separating church and state? We think that understanding the difference – psychological dynamics and all – helps us see two justifications that we couldn’t have articulated clearly otherwise.

It has been revealed that first, the fact that religious credences are not vulnerable to evidence helps justify the idea that liberal democracies should not establish state religions, in the sense of compelling people to adhere to them. (This is the part of the ‘wall of separation’ captured in the so-called ‘establishment clause’ of the First Amendment to the US Constitution.) The reasoning here is simple. It starts by recognising that any actions a government takes will, in point of fact, be based on, and justified by, ‘beliefs’ of some sort. For example, quarantining people who return from the Democratic Republic of Congo at the time of an Ebola outbreak is based on officials’ factual belief – justified in this case – that those people risk spreading the disease.

Importantly, if the beliefs in question are vulnerable to evidence, as we argued that factual beliefs are, then they will be susceptible to change through the kind of dialogue-based argument and reasoning that is the deliberative heart of democracy. Basically, factual belief-based reasoning and policy-making allows everyone to participate, since factual beliefs respond to evidence, and evidential reasons are the property of everyone.

Sources indicate that but, conversely, if a ‘belief’ is not responsive to evidence, as we argued religious credences are not, then it won’t be movable by falsification-oriented argumentative reasoning. Only people who already have the ‘belief’ will be convinced by decisions based on it. Thus, a policy explicitly religious in nature – imposing religious practice, for example – would lack tractability to the defining practices of democratic decision-making. In short, liberal democracies should exclude religion-establishing policies in order to safeguard the rational communal deliberation that is at their centre.

Private motivation and public justification are different things.

Recent findings suggest that this perspective illuminates why policy is justified the way it is in liberal democracies. Even when they happen to be motivated by spiritual convictions, citizens tend to, and legislators must (if they are to be constitutionally respectable), frame the descriptive claims in their arguments in terms of matter-of-fact, universally tractable evidence. Such framing yields public explanations that are better suited to liberal democratic coexistence than the mere direct clash of disparate religious ‘beliefs’. This is apparent in one of the most controversial areas of contemporary policymaking: abortion law. Right now in the US, abortion policy runs from fairly permissive in some states to materially restrictive in others. Yet, while it’s true that many political actors are motivated to take positions on this matter that align with their spiritual beliefs and religious affiliations, they still attempt to justify those positions by appeal to beliefs that can be contested by reason and evidence. As a result, debate over how to respect ideals like sanctity of life can, at least in principle, be a matter of public dialogue that includes everyone.

According to recent reports, we’ve focused on the US case here, because it is prominent in the history of separating church and state. But commitment to the kind of separation spelled out in the US with the First Amendment is mirrored across the globe, from Japan to Mexico and from Portugal to Namibia. Even the United Kingdom, which has state religions in the form of the Church of England and the Church of Scotland, places strict limits on what those state religions can and can’t do in the public sphere. Importantly, again, none of this prevents citizens and leaders from being motivated to prefer one policy over another due to their religious commitments. But private motivation and public justification are different things. Our present point is that the psychological difference between factual belief and religious credence helps explain why a principle that teases apart those two things makes sense.

Second, the fact that religious credences are psychologically compartmentalised helps justify the idea that, in a liberal society, ‘free exercise’ of religion is a reasonable ideal. (This is the other side of the ‘wall of separation’, also captured in the First Amendment: government shouldn’t stop people from choosing which religion to follow, if any.).

It has been revealed that here’s how this argument works. The compartmentalisation of religious credence, along with the fact that it operates as a ‘map’ distinct from factual belief, means that people who have religious credences are at least capable of setting them aside when it comes to interacting with people outside their own religion. (For example, people who have religious credence in the existence of demons don’t typically perform exorcisms on strangers in the supermarket.) So, since people are capable of setting their religious credences aside in the public sphere, they should be free to keep and venerate them in private, in light of general considerations of privacy and autonomy. Public deliberation can then proceed on the basis of evidence-responsive factual beliefs, as well as moral beliefs that respond to reasons. In short, the default compartmentalisation to which religious credence is prone makes it possible for people with a plurality of religious ‘beliefs’ to co-exist in a free society without a need for the state to challenge any of those ‘beliefs’ per se.

According to recent reports, to put this all together, our argument is this: the deal that separation of church and state offers to the religious – namely, that everyone gets religious freedom in exchange for abiding by a constitution that prevents government from establishing their specific religion – can work only because religious credences are psychologically compartmentalised and operate at a different level from factual belief. But the very fact of that default compartmentalisation is precisely what makes such a deal worth striking. Jefferson, we suspect, intuitively sensed this, when he composed his letter to the Danbury Baptists, quoted at the outset, assuring them that they wouldn’t be oppressed for their religious commitments. And perhaps we hear a foreshadow of the very idea of compartmentalisation in his line: ‘religion is a matter which lies solely between man and his God.’.

The possessive pronoun in that phrase (‘man and his God’) bespeaks the personal nature of religious credence. Religious credence, after all, is voluntary. That personal nature makes religious credence inapt for entry into public deliberation, but it also makes it ripe for receiving the freedom from government interference into private lives that characterises liberal societies generally.

Industry observers note that in 1915, a 23-year-old Oxford graduate named J.R.R. Tolkien published a poem called "Goblin Feet" in the annual anthology Oxford Poetry, and it's about as far from Legolas as you can get: it's full of "enchanted leprechauns" and "the padded feet of many gnomes," and he wrote it to please his future wife, Edith Bratt. Tolkien came to hate that kind of fairy so much that when he was asked to let the poem be reprinted in 1971, he reportedly mentioned he wished "the unhappy little thing" could be "buried for ever.".

In his 1939 lecture "On Fairy-Stories," he called Michael Drayton's fairy poem Nymphidia "one of the worst ever written" and blamed it for the "flower-fairies and fluttering sprites with antennae that I so disliked as a child." Mental Floss has noted that Tolkien took elves from tiny to human-sized, and the material he used to do it was already on his own shelves.

Recent findings suggest that tolkien read Old Norse, and the most famous description of elves in it comes from the Prose Edda, written by the Icelandic chieftain Snorri Sturluson in the 13th century. Snorri describes a heavenly place called Alfheim and splits the elves in two: "The light-elves are fairer than the sun to look upon, but the dark-elves are blacker than pitch," and the dark ones live down in the earth.

Industry observers note that tolkien gave his own elves a split along the same line: in his mythology, the elves who made the journey west and saw the light of the Two Trees of Valinor became the Calaquendi, or Elves of the Light, and the ones who never got there were the Moriquendi, the Elves of Darkness. The Tolkien scholar Tom Shippey has argued that this division was Tolkien's way of making sense of Snorri's, with history doing the sorting instead of skin color.

The same Norse tradition handed him his dwarves. A section of the poem VÃ¶luspÃ¡ known as the Dvergatal lists dozens of dwarf names, including Ãorinn, FÃ­li, KÃ­li, Dvalinn, BÃ¶mburr, GlÃ³inn, Ãinn, and Eikinskjaldi, a name that means the one with the oaken shield. Mental Floss has covered that borrowing, but the list has one more name on it: a dwarf called Gandalfr, which ends in Ã¡lfr, the Old Norse word for elf.

According to recent reports, tolkien became a professor of Anglo-Saxon at Oxford in 1925, and the Old English he taught didn't treat elves as cute. In Beowulf, the descendants of Cain include "eotenas ond ylfe ond orcneas": giants and elves and a third kind of creature usually translated as something like demon-corpses. An Anglo-Saxon medical charm called WiÃ° fÃ¦rstice, meant to cure a sudden stabbing pain, blames the injury on "ylfa gescot," the shot of elves, among other culprits: the pain could be something an elf had fired into you.

They were also beautiful, in a way that made people nervous. Old English had the word Ã¦lfscÄ«ne, meaning "of elfin beauty" and poets used it for Abrahamâs wife Sarah and for the biblical heroine Judith. The scholar Alaric Hall argues that the word meant beautiful in a dangerous, seductive way, and Tolkien seems to have read it that way too: in the 1920s, he wrote his own Old English poem, "Ides ÃlfscÃ½ne," about someone seduced and carried off by an elf-woman.

In a recent development, in 1937, when Tolkien sent his elf mythology to the publisher Allen & Unwin, the firm's reader complained about its "eye-splitting Celtic names," a story Mental Floss has told before. Tolkien wrote to Stanley Unwin on December 16 with a correction: "Needless to say they are not Celtic! Neither are the tales.".

The folklorist Dimitra Fimi doesn't entirely buy it. In Irish myth, the Tuatha DÃ© Danann are a semi-divine people who arrive in Ireland by ship, burn their ships so thereâs no going back, and win their first battle at a cost that includes their king Nuada's arm. In The Silmarillion, the rebel elves called the Noldor sail to Middle-earth, burn their ships on arrival, and win their first battle, and one of their leaders, Maedhros, is later hung from a cliff by his hand until it has to be cut off to free him.

The Tuatha DÃ© Danann were finally noted to retreat into ancient mounds or to lands across the sea, and Tolkien's elves end their story sailing west. In that same letter, Tolkien admitted he knew Irish and Welsh stories "in their original languages," said they were "mad," and added, "but I donât believe I am.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Standing in the historic North End of Sydney, Nova Scotia, Cossit House is the city's oldest surviving residence and one of the oldest buildings on Cape Breton Island. Built in 1787, the house has witnessed more than two centuries of history, and according to local ghost stories, some of its earliest residents may never have left.

According to recent reports, the house was built for Reverend Ranna Cossit, a Loyalist Anglican minister who served as the garrison chaplain for the colony of Cape Breton Island. As the first Protestant minister assigned to the colony, Cossit played an important role in its early political and social development. He lived in the house with his wife, Thankful, and their growing family. Of the couple's 13 children, six were born within its walls.

Over the years, Cossit House has gained a reputation for paranormal activity. Staff have reported smelling unexplained pipe smoke in areas associated with Reverend Cossit, while visitors have described encounters they believe involve the spirit of his wife, Thankful, who died in the house during childbirth. Paranormal investigators and mediums have also visited the property, reporting unusual sounds and sensations.

Today, Cossit House has been carefully restored to reflect life between 1787 and 1800 and operates as a living history museum. Costumed interpreters demonstrate everyday activities of the late 18th century, including stitching samplers and churning butter, offering visitors a glimpse into domestic life in early colonial Cape Breton.

Whether the reported spirits are real or simply part of the house's enduring folklore, Cossit House remains a fascinating reminder of Sydney's early history, with a few ghostly stories lingering within its walls.

Recent findings suggest that cossit House Museum is located at 75 Charlotte Street in Sydney's historic North End, Cape Breton, Nova Scotia. The museum operates seasonally, generally from early June to mid-October.

#75. Inside Sugar House Hotel, Marriott’s All-Electric Bet on the Future of Hospitality

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1620 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Matadornetwork ↗ Open Full Page

Inside Sugar House Hotel, Marriott’s All-Electric Bet on the Future of Hospitality

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1620 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Matadornetwork

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the most radical thing about Sugar House Hotel is how ordinary it feels.
  • Industry observers note that developer Doug Nedde and his team are pursuing LEED Zero Energy certification, and the building is designed to use 54 percent less energy than a standard code-compliant hotel of the same size.
  • “There’s no economic case study to whether investing that extra money towards LEED certification and all the sustainability initiatives is going to pay off,” Nedde told me on a tour of the property.” But I think five, 10 years down the line this will be the norm.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the most radical thing about Sugar House Hotel is how ordinary it feels. The 115-room hotel in Winooski, just across the river from Burlington, is entirely electric. Its designed around sustainability, yet nothing about a stay here is gimmicky. It feels like Vermont: maple trees in the lobby and a creemee at check-in, with a nature park out the back window. That balance may turn out to be its biggest innovation. I visited the hotel and found my stay to be exactly what I’d expect from a boutique property targeting visitors to a state rife with outdoor adventure and a booming local-first mandate. Its ability to hit that mark without sacrificing sustainability is an inspiring look into the future of hotels. Here’s what its like to stay here.

Industry observers note that developer Doug Nedde and his team are pursuing LEED Zero Energy certification, and the building is designed to use 54 percent less energy than a standard code-compliant hotel of the same size. Rather than rely on offsets, the hotel went all-electric. There’s no gas anywhere on property, including in the restaurant kitchen. Onsite solar supplies part of the power, while a geothermal well system behind the hotel, beside the adjacent wildlife area, handles heating and cooling.

“There’s no economic case study to whether investing that extra money towards LEED certification and all the sustainability initiatives is going to pay off,” Nedde told me on a tour of the property.” But I think five, 10 years down the line this will be the norm.”.

Nedde’s modeling projects an 82 percent reduction in heating energy, a 69 percent reduction in HVAC energy use, and 65 percent lower emissions than similar-sized hotels. Low-flow fixtures keep water use down, and reclaimed water helps restore the wetlands in the Casavant Nature Park. Running latest buildings on renewable energy is increasingly common in city centers; doing it at a full-service hotel with a restaurant and event space is a significant undertaking.

Industry observers note that when I first learned about Sugar House Hotel, I wrote in Matador’s Substack newsletter about why this project matters, not only for the Burlington area but for hospitality as a whole. By adding the hotel to its heavily curated Tribute Portfolio collection, Marriott, the world’s largest hotel company, signaled that it’s willing to test a lower-impact model. If it succeeds, expect the company to bring the concept to other locations. In effect, Sugar House could become proof that sustainability works at scale, for individual owners and corporate boardrooms alike.

Nedde and the team initiative to add local excursions to the slate of offerings, including a sleighride through Casavant Nature Park and an in-house sugaring experience.

“We really want to tell the story of sugaring in Vermont,” Nedde says.

Industry observers note that the sugar maple defines the building’s look from the front entrance on. Two large maple trunks, one from Nedde’s property and the other from a neighbor’s, anchor the staircase from the lobby to the second-floor reading area. A wall of maple syrup jars backs the front desk, and the adjacent gift shop sells Vermont’s most famous foodstuff alongside a collection of locally made goods. The lobby hearth, shaped like the state of Vermont, incorporates the mantel of a historic Vermont barn, and reclaimed farmhouse wood appears throughout the property.

I was picked up at the airport in an electric VW ID Buzz van emblazoned with the word “MAPLE” in large letters on its side. Nedde told me that a second van is coming that will read “SUGAR,” and that he plans to park them in line out front of the hotel. Rooms at the hotel start around $234 per night.

Recent findings suggest that after check-in, I was invited to try a creemee, Vermont’s signature maple soft serve, as velvety as it was sweet. The machine in the lobby is open to guests throughout their stay, the attendant told me. I wished I could bring some home to my five-year-old daughter; a jar of maple syrup had to suffice.

Industry observers note that each room is named after a Vermont sugar house. Mine, room 702, Beldock’s Sugar House, had windows on two sides: to the east, a panoramic view over downtown Winooski and across the river to the University of Vermont campus; to the north, the Casavant Nature Park. Nedde’s slogan for the hotel is “city out front, nature out back,” and I can’t think of a more fitting line. The local aesthetic carries inside, too. On the bed was a custom throw blanket made from repurposed materials, and I slept soundly both nights on the plush queen mattress. A bench runs beneath the window along one wall, beside a dining table that doubles as a laptop desk.

An afternoon walk through the nature park felt like a near-complete escape from the town center. As a Coloradan, I recognized the town-to-trail lifestyle the two states share, and this hotel puts it on fine display.

The bathroom has a single vanity and a walk-in shower that heats swiftly, and an armoire holds jackets and clothes and offers a spot to set a bag down on the way in. In the shower is house-branded shampoo, body wash, and conditioner commisioned from local materials. My one gripe: the in-room Keurig came with only single-use plastic pods. Commercially compostable pods, or a reusable K-Cup with a jar of ground coffee, would be a welcome upgrade. Water and coffee are also available at the elevator landing, and house-brewed coffee is served downstairs at Moss Cafe & Bar. When the weather allows, a cup on the cafe’s patio is a great way to start the morning.

On Level 2 there’s a gym and dog wash as well as tables and seating ideal for posting up on a laptop or with a book. From here, I was able to look out over the lobby and feel the energy of the space from above. Some rooms include a kitchenette and a separate bedroom, and this does feel like the type of place one could spend some time, if their budget allowed.

According to recent reports, the hotel is powered partly by rooftop solar and partly by a geothermal heat well in the adjacent Casavant Nature Area. A trail rings the acreage, and the hotel built a bridge connecting its property to the nature area as part of its efforts to revitalize of the watershed – sending people over the creek rather than through it. Photo: Tim Wenger.

The top floor holds event space and Treetops, the hotel’s restaurant, where I ate on my first night. I had the local trout, and our crew split several appetizers; the lentil cakes were my favorite. Diners who look for locally sourced ingredients or plant-based dishes will find plenty to choose from. Craft beer culture is another thing Vermont and Colorado share, and I enjoyed sampling a few local brews over the course of the meal. The bar itself is built from reclaimed timber from a historic drawbridge to North Hero Island, north of the city.

In a recent development, biophilic design is seen in both the restaurant and the lobby, each rich in greenery and repurposed wood. It’s incredible how calming it is to walk into an open lobby and know that its designed around the best of local artisans and materials — I felt this sitting in the lounge at Moss, and while going through emails in the admittedly quirky-named Poetry Nook (ample locally-inspired literature is available for read, so the name does earn its keep).

Industry observers note that A maple syrup tasting is available in the lobby. Also, my five-year-old daughter loved her “maple syrup gingerbread man.” Photo: Tim Wenger.

Zero-emission hotels aren’t brand new. Populus, a brand conceived by Denver-based developer Urban Villages, runs what it calls “carbon positive” hotels in Denver and Seattle. I’ve stayed at both, and while Sugar House shares their ethos, it differs in one notable way: Nedde and his team built a hotel that lives its purpose without overstating it. The low-impact features are easy to spot if you know what to look for, but the first impression is simply that of a thoughtfully curated boutique hotel.

In a recent development, outwardly, the vibe is more “Vermont” than “sustainable.” This is the hotel’s innovation. For low-impact business operations to become a societal norm, they must be presented not as an outlier but as simply the best way to do business. Sustainability shouldn’t be a marketing gimmick so much as a smart long-term investment. Nedde projects that the all-electric design will cut the hotel’s energy costs by 62 percent, and he believes the extra up-front investment will pay off and give other developers a case study to build from.

Nedde, a developer and former owner of the small Bolton Valley ski resort east of Burlington, extends the environmental mandate beyond the hotel itself. He also built an affordable housing complex next door, where some of the hotel’s staff now live, cutting commutes and giving employees a stake in the neighborhood they serve. It’s a reminder that sustainability means people as much as power sources.

I left Winooski with that jar of maple syrup for my daughter and found myself thinking about the hotels she’ll stay in someday. If Sugar House works the way Nedde expects, she may never think to ask whether they run on gas or geothermal – they’ll just be good places to stay. Progress is inevitable in every industry, and that progress requires forward-thinking businesses to take calculated risks. In my view, that calculation leads to easy math, and Sugar House will be the innovator that solved the equation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it was late at night outside Burns, Oregon, and the Milky Way shone overhead as I soaked in 100-degree waters at Crane Hot Springs. I soaked in those same springs at sunrise, watching the mist rise off the water. This was not the Oregon I’d always pictured.

Sources indicate that until a recent fall visit, I’d associated the state with its coast, lined with sea stacks and rugged beaches. But on this trip, instead of heading west from Portland, I traveled east, trading green foliage for gold sagebrush — past the Columbia River Gorge’s waterfalls, through the Hood River Valley’s orchards, and on to the cowboy town of Pendleton before reaching the high desert. What stayed with me was the spirit of the American West, where working craftspeople, Indigenous culture, and contemporary expression intertwine.

Sources indicate that the Columbia River Gorge has one of the largest concentrations of waterfalls in North America. Many line the winding Historic Columbia River Highway, known as the “King of Roads.” Some require a hike, while others, such as Shepherd’s Dell, sit just off the highway. Multnomah Falls, Oregon’s tallest waterfall, is perhaps the highway’s most recognizable. It drops 620 feet in two tiers, and the 1914 Benson Bridge crosses between them.

Recent findings suggest that more than 2,500 apple varieties are cultivated in the United States, and Kiyokawa Family Orchards in the Hood River Valley grows more than 120 of them. The Kiyokawa family has farmed the valley since 1911 and works to preserve rare and heirloom varieties. Browsing the wooden bins at the orchard’s store, or picking your own directly from the orchard, gives you the chance to discover less-common varieties that don’t keep long enough for grocery stores.

Recent findings suggest that kiyokawa is one of about 30 stops on the Hood River Fruit Loop, a 35-mile drive past orchards, farms, and wineries. Along the loop, you can sip crisp pinot gris at one stop and bite into a pink-fleshed Mountain Rose apple or Anjou pear at another (Hood River County is the world’s leading producer of Anjous). I promptly learned to pace myself while sampling.

Kiyokawa Family Orchards: 5625 Hutson Dr, Mt Hood, OR 97041.

It has been revealed that for views of the Hood River Valley, ride the Mount Hood Railroad, which departs from downtown Hood River. The line opened in 1906 to haul lumber from a mill at Dee and later carried the valley’s fruit to market. About three miles out of town, the train reverses direction on a switchback to climb the grade, one of only five railroad switchbacks still in use in the US. Today, the train carries passengers up the valley to The Fruit Tech giant, where you can taste wine, tour a fruit-packing museum, or wander among rows of grapevines and fruit trees beneath Mount Hood. If you visit in the fall as I did, you’ll ride past the valley’s changing foliage.

Mount Hood Railroad: 110 Railroad Street, Hood River, OR 97031.

A post shared by Nicole Stevens (@in_the_nic_of_time__).

In a recent development, pendleton captures the spirit of the West. Every September, during the second full week, the town’s population swells from about 17,000 to more than 50,000 for the Pendleton Round-Up, one of the most prestigious rodeos in North America. The rodeo’s rallying cry is “Let ’er Buck!” Since the first Round-Up in 1910, local tribes including the Cayuse, Umatilla, and Walla Walla have set up a tepee village next to the stadium and taken part in the rodeo and its festivities.

Sources indicate that interwoven, a upcoming fashion and culture festival celebrating Indigenous and Western makers, debuted in October 2026. It featured multiple runway indicates, including one on horseback, along with artisan markets and a fashion-inspired brunch pairing local chefs with designers.

Pendleton Round-Up: 1205 SW Court Ave, Pendleton, OR 97801 Interwoven: 601 Westgate, Pendleton, OR 97801.

Sources indicate that you don’t have to visit during one of Pendleton’s festivals to experience its culture. A walk through historic downtown indicates that this is a city of makers. Cowboy boots, belts, saddles, and much more are made here. Stop by Stapleman Custom Boot Shop, where Richard Stapleman, a former bull rider, still builds boots largely by hand (although you’ll face a yearlong wait for a custom pair). Take some time to explore Hamley & Co., the sprawling Western store that started as a saddle shop. I made my way to the back, where you can still watch saddle makers at work. End the day at the Rainbow Cafe, which claims to be Oregon’s oldest continuously operating bar, dating to 1883 (the claim is disputed by the Pioneer Saloon in Paisley, Oregon). Cowboy hats are common but not required.

Stapleman Custom Boot Shop: 7 SE Court Ave, Pendleton, OR 97801 Hamley & Co.: 30 SE Court Ave, Pendleton, OR 97801 Rainbow Cafe: 209 S Main St, Pendleton, OR 97801.

Recent findings suggest that descend a set of stairs you probably didn’t notice from the sidewalk, and you’ll explore historic basements and sidewalk vaults with a guide from Pendleton Underground Tours. Guides recount stories of speakeasies, Chinese laborers’ living quarters, and opium dens (though historians writing for the Oregon Encyclopedia have challenged parts of the tour’s account of the city’s Chinese community, including the idea that Chinese immigrants built the tunnels).

After about an hour underground, watching the feet of passersby through a few surviving purple-hued prism-glass panels, known as vault lights, you’ll head upstairs to Madam Stella Darby’s Cozy Rooms. Darby, the city’s most famous madam, ran a brothel here from 1928 to 1967. Guides tell stories of buttons dropped from above to entice customers, police raids, and the priest who delivered a sermon every Sunday in the bordello’s private parlor. They also credit Darby as a generous supporter of the community.

Pendleton Underground Tours: 31 SW Emigrant Ave, Pendleton, OR 97801.

Crane Hot Springs sits in the state’s expansive high desert, about 20 miles outside Burns. Eastern Oregon is also one of the country’s top locations for dark-sky viewing, with many areas in the region achieving Bortle Class 1 — the darkest classification for night skies. With little to no light pollution, the Milky Way is easily visible on clear evenings while you’re soaking in the mineral-rich waters. The area is also a stopover point for migratory birds. Nearby Malheur National Wildlife Refuge is worth visiting during the spring and fall migratory months. Crane Hot Springs also has trails encircling the ponds that make birdwatching easy.

Crane Hot Springs: 59315 OR-78, Burns, OR 97720 Malheur National Wildlife Refuge: 36391 Sodhouse Ln, Princeton, OR 97721.

A post shared by Brigham Fish Market (@brighamfishmarket).

It has been revealed that overlooking the Columbia River in Cascade Locks, Brigham Fish Market is run by sisters Kim Brigham-Campbell and Terrie Brigham, members of the Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation. Their family has fished the river for generations, and the market sells whatever the river provides: coho, sockeye, chinook (the most popular, according to Terrie), and steelhead. Take smoked fish to go, or grab a seat on the outdoor patio for a smoked salmon po’boy and a huckleberry lemonade.

Brigham Fish Market: 681 Wa Na Pa St, Cascade Locks, OR 97014.

Alia, the restaurant at the Lightwell Hotel in Hood River, opened in fall 2026 and pairs Mediterranean dishes with Northwest ingredients. Chef Dalton Jones’ menu features dishes like charred octopus skewers, malfouf mahshi (stuffed cabbage rolls), and Northwest salmon, all complemented by local Hood River wines. Save room for the baklava.

Alia: 201 Cascade Ave, Hood River, OR 97031.

For lunch with a volcano view, visit Grateful Vineyard, where rows of grapes draw your eyes to Mount Hood (an active stratovolcano that’s right now dormant) in the distance. Its salads and fig, pear, and arugula pizza highlight the region’s produce. Pair either with one of the wines, ciders, or beers made on site.

Grateful Vineyard: 6670 Trout Creek Ridge Rd, Mt Hood, OR 97041.

A post shared by Hamley Steakhouse & Saloon (@hamleysteakhouseofficial).

Industry observers note that after a day of “letting ’er buck,” head to Hamley Steakhouse & Saloon for dinner. Next to Hamley & Co.’s Western store, the restaurant serves USDA Prime beef (and lots of other non-beef options) in the building Hamley’s has occupied since 1905. The steakhouse opened there in 2007, and the Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation have owned the business since 2019. Its 100-year-old mahogany bar, stained glass, and Western memorabilia evoke the Old West. Order a Midnight Manhattan, made with Pendleton Whisky.

Hamley Steakhouse & Saloon: 8 SE Court Ave, Pendleton, OR 97801.

Industry observers note that if you’re looking for pizza (Detroit-style, Chicago-style, or Neapolitan), look no further than the Oregon Grain Growers Brand Distillery. Located in a former Cadillac and Oldsmobile dealership, the distillery serves arguably the best pizza in Pendleton and some of its most interesting cocktails. I couldn’t say no to trying the pickle-brine vodka in a Curious Martini with coconut and lime.

Oregon Grain Growers Brand Distillery: 511 SE Court Ave, Pendleton, OR 97801.

Sources indicate that CORAZÓN Artisan Kitchen (open Friday through Sunday and located on the Crane Hot Springs property) is conveniently located if you want a bite to eat without having to step out of your bathrobe. Janne Valdez serves small-batch, handmade tortillas; house-made chorizo; chicken tinga; al pastor; tamales; fresh salsas; and seasonal specialties. Be sure to ask her if she has any cheesecake available; I’m already planning a trip back to get some more.

CORAZÓN Artisan Kitchen: 59315 OR-78, Burns, OR 97720.

The Lightwell Hotel is a convenient base for exploring the Hood River Valley. Located in downtown Hood River, it’s steps away from the Mount Hood Railroad and Oak Street, lined with artisan shops and boutiques. The rooms have been recently updated. The hotel features a rooftop patio with Columbia River views, and the lobby has a baby grand piano and comfortable sofas for relaxing. End a busy day of chasing waterfalls and sampling wine by visiting the subterranean spa with a sauna and a hot soaking tub.

Lightwell Hotel & Spa: 201 Cascade Ave, Hood River, OR 97031.

The Hotel Pendleton, a 1962 motel renovated in 2023, puts you within walking distance of the city’s makers and shops. Hamley & Co. sits across the street, and Stapleman Custom Boot Shop is half a block away.

The Hotel Pendleton: 105 SE Court Ave, Pendleton, OR 97801.

It has been revealed that for a more intimate stay, the six-room Pendleton House Historic Inn Bed & Breakfast sits just across the Umatilla River. Affectionately known as the “pink house,” the 1917 Italian Renaissance-style mansion is one of the colorful historic homes in the neighborhood.

The Pendleton House Historic Inn Bed & Breakfast: 311 N Main St, Pendleton, OR 97801.

If you’re really taken with the Pendleton Underground tour, stay at the Working Girls Hotel, where Pendleton Underground Tours converted part of the former bordello into a suite and four guest rooms in 1991. The rooms are furnished in Victorian decor, with 18-foot ceilings.

Working Girls Hotel: 17 SW Emigrant Ave, Pendleton, OR 97801.

Don’t let the private airstrip deter you. For all its luxury, The Retreat at Silvies Valley Ranch is down-to-earth and casual, and the property is still a working cattle ranch, spread across 150,000 acres. On McVeigh’s Gauntlet, a seven-hole course, you can have a goat as a caddie (yes, they really do have goats that carry your golf clubs). There’s also a spa, and the night skies are free of light pollution.

The Retreat at Silvies Valley Ranch: 10000 Rendezvous Lane, Seneca, OR 97873.

Recent findings suggest that at Crane Hot Springs, you can sleep steps away from the hot spring pool. The property has a number of accommodation types, including traditional tepees, cabins, suites, and camping pads. The suites and tepees each have a private soaking tub that can be filled with mineral spring water. The springs are open for overnight guests 24 hours a day. I practically lived in my swimsuit and the plush bathrobe provided by the property, enjoying multiple soaks.

Crane Hot Springs: 59315 OR-78, Burns, OR 97720.

This trip covers a lot of ground. Oregon is the ninth-largest state in the country, and Portland International Airport (PDX) is the most practical gateway. A rental car is essential for the long distances between stops, but you’ll be rewarded along the way. The Historic Columbia River Highway was the first scenic highway in the US designated a National Historic Landmark. As you head east, rainfall drops and the forests give way to sagebrush. Our route between Pendleton and Crane Hot Springs passed through the Umatilla and Malheur National Forests and across wide, sweeping plains.

It has been revealed that getting around requires a vehicle, as most locations are separated by large distances. However, the cities of Hood River and Pendleton are both very walkable and best explored on foot. First Nature Tours also provides custom itineraries and guided tours in the region.

#70. Methodical/mercurial

Methodical/mercurial

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2946 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Aeon

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Buzzing on your own brilliance at finding the answer to all of your problems, your true calling in life and, basically, frigging nirvana, you are desperate to wake your beloved, who is lying beside you, blissfully unaware that their world is about to be rocked.
  • Industry observers note that but as you sit impatiently waiting for an acceptable hour to rouse your beloved and blow their mind, your whole self shifts sideways, like someone just turned the TV over to another channel or a changeling took over your mind.
  • What idiot thought that any of this was a good idea?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Buzzing on your own brilliance at finding the answer to all of your problems, your true calling in life and, basically, frigging nirvana, you are desperate to wake your beloved, who is lying beside you, blissfully unaware that their world is about to be rocked. You think about waking them because you can’t contain all this excitement alone and need to share it, but it’s only 6 am and you know from experience that this wouldn’t end well. So you sit, fidgeting, watching the clock until 6:30 am. Surely, that’s late enough? Perhaps if you bring them coffee, they won’t be so mad. Yet how could they be mad, when what you’re about to reveal to them will make them say: ‘Why didn’t you wake me up sooner, you genius?’.

Industry observers note that but as you sit impatiently waiting for an acceptable hour to rouse your beloved and blow their mind, your whole self shifts sideways, like someone just turned the TV over to another channel or a changeling took over your mind. You suddenly realise that your previously designated Best Idea Ever is full of holes and is actually a Terrible Idea. You are puzzled that you didn’t see this sooner. What were you thinking? You can’t move house because your kids are in school here, you have a full-time job and bills to pay, and you don’t have the attention span to read your horoscope, let alone do a master’s. And you can’t even swim.

What idiot thought that any of this was a good idea? Oh… it was me. OK… time to cancel it all and hope that you didn’t lose too much money and that it will all be back in the bank account before ‘they’ wake up.

And hope that you don’t do the same thing again tonight.

You will likely have come across the term AuDHD used as a shortcut to describe those given the dual diagnosis of autism and attention-deficit and hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). It is a relatively new label and for good reason – until recently, no one individual was clinically permitted to be given both diagnoses and therefore there was no one to whom the term ‘AuDHD’ could officially apply.

Recent findings suggest that in 1994, a mere 32 years ago, the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 4th edition (DSM-IV), included Asperger Syndrome for the first time. In 2013, the diagnosis was removed from the 5th edition (DSM-5) and subsumed under the broader category of ‘autism spectrum disorder’. Asperger Syndrome had identified individuals who met the social and behavioural aspects of the diagnostic criteria for autism but who did not have intellectual disability or the language-development differences then associated with an autism diagnosis. As a result, an autistic person reading this magazine today would have been unlikely to receive an autism diagnosis in the past: there was simply no diagnostic category that fit their profile. That helps to explain the huge rise in adult diagnoses in recent decades.

Autism and ADHD were long considered mutually exclusive.

It has been revealed that alongside this, diagnosis of ADHD in adults has been a similarly recent arrival. Having been considered a predominantly childhood condition for most of its history, the idea that children can continue to experience ADHD features into adulthood was not seriously considered until the early 2000s. Earlier versions of the DSM required that symptoms had to have been present prior to the age of seven years, and focused almost entirely on childhood behaviours to form the diagnosis. In 2013, with the publication of the DSM-5, the onset age of ADHD symptoms was raised to 12 years, and fewer symptoms were required for adults to meet the diagnostic threshold – which took into account development changes and challenges within adult settings, such as work – thus opening up ADHD diagnosis to adults.

This means that a person without intellectual disability and with relatively typical language development has been eligible for an autism diagnosis for only 32 years. And the ADHD criteria have been explicitly adapted to better recognise the disorder in adults only since 2013. That history is one part of the AuDHD issue.

In a recent development, the second part is that autism and ADHD were long considered mutually exclusive. It was thought that their apparently contradictory traits of rigidity and impulsivity effectively cancelled each other out. This meant that a person – either child or adult – could not be officially diagnosed with both conditions until 13 years ago, when the DSM-5 removed this exclusion and allowed both diagnoses to be given to the same person – opening the way for what is now widely called AuDHD.

Sources indicate that at first glance, existing diagnostic criteria for each condition may look like contradictions of each other. While a stereotypical autistic person may present as socially awkward, precise and cautious in language and behaviour, requiring predictability, sameness and calm, our ADHDer looks like the complete opposite. ADHD diagnostic criteria typically present as someone socially driven, scattered and impulsive in language and behaviour, seeking novelty, variety and stimulation. How can it be that both of these seemingly opposing traits can exist in one person, and what is it like for that person when they do?

Sources indicate that given the relatively recent formal recognition of this comorbid profile, research into its impact is unsurprisingly scarce and, aside from a small handful of papers, has been focused on children and adolescents. The earliest research into this overlap I could find was published in 1999; those investigators concluded that autistic features were common in those with ADHD, and that a dual diagnosis should be considered in some cases, even though this was not clinically permitted at the time. This overlap has been one of the most frequently studied aspects of AuDHD.

Recent findings suggest that A 2023 systematic review identified 9,050 articles and ultimately included 23 studies; across these, estimates of the prevalence of ADHD symptoms in autistic young people without intellectual disability ranged from 2.6 per cent to 95.5 per cent. Another paper suggested that 50 to 70 per cent of autistic people present with comorbid ADHD. If you are reading this article with a diagnosis of autism or ADHD, you may want to think about whether you may be both, because it’s looking increasingly likely that you are.

It has been revealed that of course, there have always been differing opinions and concerns about the pathologising nature of diagnosis in neurodiversity. Where does one neurodivergent condition end and another begin? Can we really separate these aspects of ourselves into neat clinical categories – often deemed necessary to permit access to a particular support service, therapy, fund or setting to meet the often-disabling needs of being neurodivergent in a neurotypical world? The reality is that no one knows the answers, so here we are with our rigid clinical diagnostic criteria, which – as we can see from the alterations in the DSM-5 – are changing as understanding grows. Forgive me for working within these uncomfortable neat boxes, but they are all we have right now; and, for at least some people, they can be a helpful way of understanding the contradictions of living with AuDHD.

My former life had failed to meet my autistic need for routine but had satisfied my ADHD need for novelty.

The example at the top of the article is one from my own life and it has resonated with many of the 69 AuDHD adults and parents of AuDHD children whose stories and words I had the privilege to gather for my new book, The Complete Guide to AuDHD (2026).

Sources indicate that my own AuDHD story is a typical one. I was diagnosed as autistic in my 40s after having written five books on autism and neurodiversity and achieving an MA in autism – I knew my stuff, and myself, or at least I thought I did. Yet I had led a chaotic life of multiple jobs, house moves and intends and schemes of one kind or another – I am known for it by those who know me; they take bets on how long I will stay in one place/job/course/project – which upsets me, but which is hard, logically, to take umbrage at.

I had never considered that I would meet the criteria for ADHD diagnosis because I was too logical, too organised and too set in my ways. I am the Queen of the Spreadsheet, the Mistress of the Initiative. After bringing up two kids, I worked as a trainer and speaker for 15 years, travelling the country and overseas on a crazy schedule of driving, hotels and public speaking. Not surprisingly, I crashed horribly into years of panic attacks, agoraphobia and severe physical and mental burnout. Eventually, I gave it all up and began working locally and remotely, removing 90 per cent of the stress and unpredictability of my former life. At first, it was wonderful, I remembered what it was like to wake up without a brick of dread and anxiety on my chest. I slept in the same bed every night and knew what each day would bring. Perfect. Until… a few weeks into this blissful new existence I recall a feeling that I verbalised at the time as ‘I feel like I’m dead.’ I felt flat, blank, nothing, emotionless. Over a period of reflection, I realised that I had never actually sat still my whole life. While my former parenting and working lives had failed to meet my autistic need for routine and predictability, they had entirely satisfied – what I now understood to be – my ADHD need for constant dopamine in the form of novelty, variety and excitement.

Recent findings suggest that those who have the same experience of a second diagnosis of either autism or ADHD share the same feeling I did – it’s the final piece of the puzzle. The first diagnosis made sense of a lot, but it didn’t explain it all. There were questions and gaps: ‘I’m too social to be autistic.’ ‘I need too much order to be ADHD.’.

This sense of two selves, of the push and pull of opposing wants and needs, is the core of the experience.

Sources indicate that since the dual diagnosis of the two conditions is fairly recent, it is still unusual for both diagnoses to occur at the same time, with most adults right now having received one diagnosis first and the second at some point later, as did I. And although autism and ADHD were deemed contradictory for much of their joint history, both sets of diagnostic criteria need to be met for each diagnosis to be given: there is no allowance made for ADHD characteristics masking those of autism, for example – which they often do – during the diagnostic assessment.

Sources indicate that which diagnosis comes first varies from person to person, with either autism or ADHD often appearing as the primary profile. Perhaps ADHD appears more ‘visible’ for a child challenged by sitting still at school, or autism for an adult struggling with the social and flexibility requirements of a job – with the other lurking behind ready to throw a spanner in the works or offer a helping hand. Given that the second diagnosis was simply not an option for so long, the thought of it was generally never given the time of day, although a number of AuDHD people I have assessed often say they’d felt that the first diagnosis had answered some of the questions they’d had throughout their lives about why they were different, but not all. For others, it was a complete surprise. As one person I interviewed for my book explained:.

According to recent reports, for many, this ‘primary’ profile is not fixed. Female hormones are known to affect the severity of ADHD. The time of day and associated stress and fatigue play a role. And the impact depends on the activity contemplated – does it require speed and creativity, or accuracy and focus?

The idea of the autistic and ADHD selves as separate entities is hardly definitive, and experts differ here. Some research finds autism and ADHD symptoms to be largely segregated along existing diagnostic boundaries; others that they have overlapping features; while others suggest that the co-occurrence of autism and ADHD may represent a distinct combined phenotype. Regardless of the thoughts of academics, this sense of two selves, of conflict and contradiction and the push and pull of opposing wants and needs, is one that formed the core and essence of the experience of the participants in my own research.

An article by Siân Boyle in The Guardian in 2024 described this contradiction in the AuDHD label as one of ‘oxymoronic nature, perpetual internal war and rollercoaster of needs’, which nicely sums things up.

The realisation that there is a name and an explanation for the persistent inconsistency that accompanies the AuDHD lived experience can be liberating – it’s a relief to know that you are not actually crazy, because that’s the way it can feel. In the words of my research participants, it is:.

Sources indicate that despite this sense of contradiction, the two conditions do share some characteristics. Both are highly heritable and run through families. As far back as 2009, a team led by the child and adolescent psychiatrist Aisling Mulligan at Trinity College Dublin found that autistic traits in children with ADHD ran in families, along with the ADHD itself. More recent research shows that mothers with ADHD are six times more likely to have a child with ADHD – and 2.5 times as likely to have an autistic child. Other studies suggest a shared genetic base between autism and ADHD, explaining the high prevalence of both conditions in the same families. Twin studies provide further evidence of this genetic overlap.

It has been revealed that people with either autism or ADHD may find it challenging to read subtle social nuances and engage in reciprocal conversation, making it harder to sustain friendships and relationships. Both often have intense passions and interests, although these tend to last longer in autism than in ADHD. And while sensory features are not mentioned in the diagnostic criteria for ADHD, both groups may have atypical sensory profiles. As a very broad generalisation, autistic people find sensory experiences overwhelming, leading them to avoid some sensations and seek out comfort. On the other hand, ADHD people may seek sensory input and stimulation to feel grounded and focused. Although it is early days for research and the number of papers looking at AuDHD are small and focused almost entirely on children and adolescents, the general consensus is that the combination of autism and ADHD makes things worse socially, adaptively, behaviourally and mentally. I could not find any research-based evidence that sought or found examples of the dual diagnosis making life better. It seems that, in academic studies, questions relating to the advantages and joys of AuDHD were not asked, and that the focus was entirely on problems, challenges and deficit, as is often, disappointingly, the case.

Every day needs to be filled with entertainment and stability, learning and fun.

The inconsistency brought by these apparently opposing sets of features does cause considerable frustration for the typical AuDHDer, who lives switching – often rapidly – between seeking both order and disruption, sameness and variety, impulsivity and risk-aversion, social motivation and solitude, single focus and multi-focus. When needs and wants shift so promptly and vary so wildly, decision-making and balance can feel impossible, leading to a far more chaotic life than would be expected from someone with an autism diagnosis. As one of the research participants stated:.

Yet the participants in my own research reported the joys of AuDHD as well. For me, the combination of the detail and diligence of autism and the creativity and impulsivity of ADHD have likely led to my deeply interesting and varied life, because I couldn’t have tolerated it any other way. Every day needs to be filled with entertainment and stability, learning and fun. Others in my research agree:.

In a recent development, for me, it feels like a life of two halves, like living as a pair of twins who argue a lot but now and again will sit on the couch together and watch a movie. We know we have to have a schedule, eat the same foods and get things done. We know we have to physically move – a lot – keep switching tasks, and force ourselves to stop when we’re just done. We know we find it hard to begin, hard to keep going and hard to stop, and we’re continually developing ways to work with all of that at any given time in all given circumstances.

In a recent development, and although Autism has to step in to keep ADHD in check, and force it to sit down and do the dull, vital things for a few minutes – rather than spending all day watching videos about giant tortoises on the Galápagos Islands – ADHD also needs to break through the rigidity of Autism’s need for productivity, tell it to lighten up – and come watch some of these great videos on giant tortoises on the Galápagos Islands. And then, once ADHD has piqued Autism’s interest with today’s Best Idea Ever, Autism can become a world authority on tortoises, research the climate, food, cheapest flights and best hotel on the islands, and build a spreadsheet to get this trip on the road. What a team!

We only have to hope that Autism knows where the passport is.
