Finding a Different Kind of All-Inclusive in Los Cabos

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1471 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Matadornetwork

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, I was explaining to my dinner companions what kind of fruit a mamey is.
  • Industry observers note that the setting matched the food.
  • In a recent development, but Pitahayas isn’t an independent fine-dining restaurant: it’s part of Hacienda del Mar Los Cabos, an all-inclusive resort.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, I was explaining to my dinner companions what kind of fruit a mamey is. Their sudden interest came after the chef at Pitahayas restaurant surprised us with mamey ice cream, served with pinole and buñuelo crumble for dessert. It was the last course of a long dinner that included octopus carpaccio, blackfin tuna tostadas, and short rib with Oaxacan black mole. Following the chef’s recommendations, we’d paired our appetizers with a chardonnay from northern Mexico and our short rib with a nebbiolo from Valle de Guadalupe, Mexico’s most prolific wine region. It was the kind of dinner against which you compare your dining experiences for the next year.

Industry observers note that the setting matched the food. Pitahayas sits under a large palapa overlooking the ocean, with high ceilings and dim lighting that make it feel like you’re dining on the beach. I could hear the surf breaking nearby and watched a couple of cruise ships departing Cabo San Lucas disappear into the distance.

In a recent development, but Pitahayas isn’t an independent fine-dining restaurant: it’s part of Hacienda del Mar Los Cabos, an all-inclusive resort. We paid extra for the upgraded bottles of wine, but the multi-course dinner and attentive service were included in our hotel rate.

According to recent reports, walking back to my room, I passed a now-empty pool where guests spent their mornings playing volleyball and joining fitness classes. Past the pools, a younger crowd was still dancing to a DJ at an outdoor kiosk, making good use of the all-inclusive drinks. Farther along, the main hotel buildings looked like something straight out of an old movie about a glamorous Mexican vacation. In the main patio, a band playing Queen covers launched into Bohemian Rhapsody, to the delight of the few guests still watching. I reached my room just in time to hear Freddie Mercury sing the final notes of the night.

It was an unlikely combination of old-school resort charm, lively entertainment, and surprisingly sophisticated dining — but one that seemed to capture how Hacienda del Mar has evolved since opening more than 30 years ago, when it was part of the first wave of upscale beachfront resorts that helped transform Los Cabos into an international luxury destination.

At first, Hacienda del Mar seems like a traditional Mexican resort — the kind of hotel my parents took me to when I was a kid growing up in Mexico City. Large, white villa-style buildings surround interior courtyards and gardens, while hand-painted tiles, stone passageways, and an extensive collection of religious art lend the property an old-fashioned charm without making it feel neglected.

It has been revealed that that traditional character extends to the rooms, which skew more toward hacienda-style details than the modern contemporary minimalism seen in newer properties. My room was spacious, with an enormous balcony overlooking the ocean furnished with a lounger, a dining area, and a separate sitting area. Inside, heavy wooden furnishings and terracotta tile floors reflect the resort’s original design, complemented by some contemporary touches like glass-walled showers. You can tell it’s been renovated, but it hasn’t lost the feel of Los Cabos of yesteryear, either.

Hacienda del Mar’s history began in the mid-1990s as a timeshare project in Cabo del Sol, when Los Cabos was just emerging as one of Mexico’s premier luxury resort destinations. Developed during an early wave of upscale beachfront construction along the tourist corridor, the property joined Sheraton in 2000 and became part of an early generation of large beachfront resorts competing for the growing luxury tourism market in Los Cabos. Its architecture drew on traditional Mexican haciendas, with villas arranged around courtyards, gardens, and fountains. These features, along with its expansive grounds and multiple pools, give Hacienda del Mar a distinct personality that sets it apart from many nearby properties.

The longtime Los Cabos staple was a Sheraton for 20 years, but joined Marriott’s Autograph Collection in 2020. Since July 2025, it’s been an all-inclusive.

However, unlike newer resorts designed around the all-inclusive model, Hacienda del Mar hasn’t forgotten it’s a property with three decades of history, famed restaurants, and a distinctly old-school character. The result is an unusual mix of traditional Los Cabos luxury and the lively atmosphere of a modern all-inclusive. It’s a combination that doesn’t always mesh, but gives the resort an inviting, distinct character of its own.

When I asked Fatyma Camacho, the hotel’s social media manager, what made Hacienda del Mar different from other all-inclusives in Los Cabos, she didn’t hesitate: “It’s all about the food.”.

The property has seven different restaurants, an extensive breakfast buffet, a coffee shop, a juice bar, a sports bar, and even an ice-cream shop, though that last one costs extra. The food program is led by chef José Lazcarro, originally from Puebla, Mexico.

Pitahayas is perhaps the best example of what distinguishes Hacienda del Mar’s dining program. The restaurant opened in 1995, before the resort became a Sheraton, and built a reputation for its Pacific Rim cuisine and oceanfront setting. Today, its menu emphasizes Mexican ingredients and regional flavors. That a restaurant with this kind of history is included in an all-inclusive package demonstrates that the hotel’s leadership places a strong emphasis on quality dining.

Even the breakfast buffet goes beyond the usual resort staples, with regional Mexican specialties such as molotes (fried masa pockets typically stuffed with potatoes, cheese, or meat), tetelas (triangular masa filled with beans), and panuchos, a Yucatán specialty of tortillas stuffed with refried beans and topped with meat and vegetables. Some experiences, like wine tastings or upscale bottles of wine, have an extra charge, but it didn’t feel like a requirement to enjoy the resort. My simple flat white at Molino Coffee Shop was better than most coffee shops near my home.

From my room’s balcony, I had a sweeping view of the Gulf of California and Faro El Encanto in the distance, along with the resort’s pools and gardens below. By late afternoon, the swimming pools were full of guests enjoying drinks from the bars or ordering from servers moving constantly between loungers. Farther away, a group had gathered around what looked like a board game competition, cheering whenever the host made an announcement. Live music drifted across the grounds. Almost everywhere I looked, people were taking part in some kind of activity.

This is the other side of Hacienda del Mar: a busy, family-oriented all-inclusive where much of the day revolves around the pools, organized activities, and entertainment. But mornings begin more quietly. I joined an early outdoor yoga class with about a dozen guests, stretching to the sounds of the ocean while the rest of the resort was still waking up. But by the time we finished, loungers were already being claimed and a speaker was announcing the next pool activity, all before 10 AM.

In a recent development, for those looking to escape the poolside commotion, Cactus Spa shows that the resort does have a quiet side. I arrived early for a massage and found myself wishing I’d discovered the hydrotherapy area sooner. The indoor courtyard, filled with tropical plants and covered by a wood mesh ceiling, was one of my favorite spa spaces I’ve visited in all my years traveling. Both male and female guests can relax before or after their treatments, soaking in small hot and cold pools. I was surprised by how much more intimate this space felt compared with some of the boutique hotel spas I’ve seen.

It has been revealed that the entertainment program also includes a weekly Mexican celebration, with mariachi music, folkloric dances, and an enormous dinner buffet. The event features a ceremony centered around the hotel’s patron figure, an upside-down representation of St. Anthony, followed by colorful performances drawing cultural traditions from different parts of Mexico. It’s exactly the sort of evening I’d expect at a traditional Mexican resort, and judging by the number of guests watching and participating, others felt the same.

It has been revealed that hacienda del Mar is hard to categorize. It’s not the kind of resort where every corner feels luxurious. And despite the quiet spaces, those looking for a quiet getaway could find the pools and entertainment a little too busy. But after three days there, I didn’t feel like I’d stayed at a resort trying to change what it was, and appreciated that it retained the old-school architecture and character that have defined the property since the 1990s. The different sides of the resort don’t always feel cohesive, but they give guests the freedom to choose the kind of Los Cabos experience they want. And in a destination increasingly defined by sleek, meticulously designed luxury resorts, there’s something refreshing about a hotel that doesn’t seem particularly interested in being another one of them.

At the intersection of State Road 3 and State Road 18, west of the town of Montpelier, Indiana, the former Tin Lizzy Ice Cream Shop features a large fiberglass man who once served as the shop’s mascot.

Famously, the ice cream man appeared in the opening credits of the first season of the television show “Parks and Recreation,” along with another nearby fiberglass statue. Now, the ice cream man has no banana cups, Dixie Pops, or Push-Ups, and the ice cream is missing from the cone in his left hand. Why, the poor bloke is no longer even a natty dresser, with his faded and peeling red cap and jacket!

The former shop closed around 2015, and the area around it is private property and should not be entered. For pictures, a quick stop along State Road 3 is recommended, since there is less traffic on 3.

According to recent reports, the official remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time debuted on November 5, 2026. The game faithfully follows in the footsteps of its predecessor, the legendary 1998 title of the same name.Â.

Sources indicate that at the heart of the story is Link, a young boy tasked with saving the kingdom of Hyrule from the Gerudo desert king Ganondorf. At his side is the ocarina, an instrument that Link uses to change elements of his world.

According to recent reports, ocarinas are a type of vessel flute belonging to a family of wind instruments. Their earliest ancestors are clay whistles, the earliest models of which have been found in Africa and date to some 30,000 years ago.

According to recent reports, early vessel flutes similar to the ocarina have also been found across Asia, including the xun, an egg-shaped flute noted to be roughly 7,000 to 9,000 years old that is still played today in China.Â These instruments are believed to have evolved from Stone Age hunting tools that people discovered made noise when air was blown through them. Some ancient ancestors of ocarinas have also been found in Europe. The oldest flute found in Europe is the âRunik Ocarina,â which was found in Kosovo and is thought to be around 8,000 years old.Â.

Industry observers note that modern ocarinas have roots in Central America. They may have originated in Costa Rica around 2000 BCE, and spread across the Mayan and Aztec Empires. They were often carved into elaborate shapes and served vital roles in rituals, ceremonies, gatherings, and funerals. Aztec musicians visiting Spanish King Charles V in 1527 are believed to have introduced the ocarina to Europe, along with songs and dances that accompanied it.Â However, Europeans initially perceived these sacred instruments as simple toys.

Sources indicate that yet they were much more than that, as anyone who has heard the instrument's mystical sound can tell. âThe material worldâof earth, of trees, of stone, of clayâis reshaped by the human world,â DavÃ­d Carrasco, Neil L. Rudenstine Professor of the Study of Latin America at Harvard Divinity School, told the Harvard Divinity Bulletin in a reflection on a collection of ocarinas at the Peabody Museum. âAnd out of that comes a third thing, which is music and sound and culture,â he continued. âSo what we have here are a number of sort of miniaturesâsmall, musical instrumentsâthings made out of the earth. Music has a sacred power, and in some ways, it is timeless. People can hear ancient music thousands of years old, and yet it will resonate with them today. So it is with this collection of ocarinas.âÂ.

The modern ocarina was invented in 1853 by a young Italian brickmaker named Giuseppe Donati, who created a version that could play melodies and scales inspired by the Mesoamerican models he encountered. He named his creation the âocarina,â which means âlittle gooseâ in a regional Italian dialect. Donati created the Gruppo Ocarinistico Budriese, or the Budrio Ocarina Group, an ensemble dedicated to spreading the ocarina around the world. It remains active today.

In 1928, Japanese sculptor Takashi Aketagawa added two more holes to the top of the ocarina that Donati invented, creating the model that is still used today. It became well-known worldwide after the Japanese musician Nomura Sojiro used the instrument to compose music for the documentary The Great Yellow River in 1986.

Industry observers note that still, the ocarinaâs popularity was waning by the time it appeared in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time in 1998. The game allowed players to compose songs on a digital version of the instrument and required them to use it to navigate various challenges.

Industry observers note that âThere are two prominent types of ocarinas: transverse and pendant,â Chicago composer Michael Barrera told WFMT. âThe instrument depicted in Ocarina of Time is a transverse or sweet potato ocarina. It has 10 to 12 holes and is held off to the side, with fingerings that are mostly linear.â.

Ocarinas soared in popularity after the release of Ocarina of Time in 1998, and Nintendo has released numerous special ocarinas tied to different milestones related to the game. Now, with the 2026 remake becoming the fastest-selling Nintendo Switch 2 game of all time, itâs likely that this instrument may see another wave of interest, and the world may hear more of its gentle, warbling call.

#66. Industry News: 13 Luxury Train Rides in the US Worth Splurging On

Industry News: 13 Luxury Train Rides in the US Worth Splurging On

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, when you think of luxury train rides, you probably imagine something along the lines of the famed Orient Express (the most expensive train ride in the world), or South Africa’s iconic Blue train, or even Switzerland’s GoldenPass Express.
  • It has been revealed that often believed to be the best option for luxury train travel in the US, the Rocky Mountaineer’s Rockies to the Red Rocks route is meant for those who want to take in the Southwestern scenery in extreme comfort.
  • The Royal Gorge Route Railroad runs daily throughout the year, taking passengers on a short but scenic journey along the Arkansas River, through the narrow 1,200-foot-deep Royal Gorge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, when you think of luxury train rides, you probably imagine something along the lines of the famed Orient Express (the most expensive train ride in the world), or South Africa’s iconic Blue train, or even Switzerland’s GoldenPass Express. But you don’t have to go all the way to Europe or Africa for luxury trains — luxury train travel in the USA is alive and well.

It has been revealed that often believed to be the best option for luxury train travel in the US, the Rocky Mountaineer’s Rockies to the Red Rocks route is meant for those who want to take in the Southwestern scenery in extreme comfort. Passengers can choose between two classes of service: SilverLeaf or SilverLeaf Plus, both of which offer a spacious car with oversized glass-dome windows, reclining seats, and seat-side service. SilverLeaf Plus, however, offers a little more: exclusive access to the lounge car and to a small outdoor viewing area, as well as elevated dining experience with wine pairings, premium alcoholic beverages, and signature cocktails. While the classic journey takes you between Denver and Moab, special packages allow travelers to start or end their journey in Las Vegas or Salt Lake City. The Rockies to the Red Rocks route is a two-day trip, but the Rocky Mountaineer is not a sleeper train. Instead, passengers disembark in Glenwood Springs, Colorado, where they stay in a luxury hotel for the night before getting back on the train the next morning.

Photo: Royal Gorge Route Railroad.

The Royal Gorge Route Railroad runs daily throughout the year, taking passengers on a short but scenic journey along the Arkansas River, through the narrow 1,200-foot-deep Royal Gorge. You can make your trip on board the Royal Gorge Route Railroad as casual or as luxurious as you want by choosing the class of service that suits you best. The fanciest way to ride this route is by booking the First Class Dinner Train in Vista Dome which lasts 2.5 hours. You’ll be served Champagne and an award-winning three-course meal while looking at the surrounding views from the huge panoramic windows. First Class Dinner Train passengers also have access to a private open-air car.

Photo: PT Hamilton/Shutterstock.

Sources indicate that the steam train of the Cumbres and Toltec Scenic Railroad runs from late May to late October, Tuesday through Sunday. The most luxurious way to ride the Cumbres and Toltec Scenic Railroad is by booking a seat in the adult-only, historic Parlor Car, where you’ll be served pastries, hot and cold beverages, and snacks by thoughtful train attendants. The Parlor Car is designed to provide the best views during the long train trip, with strategically placed seats and panoramic windows. Parlor Car passengers, alongside every other passenger on the train, have access to the open-air car. Note that the Cumbres and Toltec Scenic Railroad runs the single trip between Chama and Antonito once per day only. You can opt to take a luxury motorcoach back to the departing station or stay overnight in the arrival town and ride the train again the next day to get back to where you came from.

A post shared by Cape Cod Central Railroad (@capecodcentralrailroad).

Industry observers note that the Cape Cod Central Railroad’s most luxurious train ride offering is the Cape Cod Dinner Train, a three-hour ride during which passengers are served a candlelight four-course meal while traveling through the peninsula’s charming small towns. For the most exclusive seating, book Platinum Class (ages 21 and up), which seats you in a vintage 1917 lounge car; all classes include the same four-course dinner and differ only by seating. The Cape Cod Dinner Train is open to travelers aged 13 or older (children 3 to 12 are welcome in First Class only), but if you’d rather have an adult-only train journey, book Cape Cod Central Railroad’s Gourmet Wine Tasting Train in Platinum Class. The Cape Cod Dinner Train operates multiple times per week from late May through late October.

Recent findings suggest that the Green Mountain Railroad, also known as the Vermont Rail System, offers a Cocktails on the Rails ride every Saturday from late June to late October. This adult-only luxury experience takes place in a 1930s train car with plush leather seats and a full bar. The ride includes finger foods and snacks, and passengers can purchase drinks from the bar while listening to live music. The ride only allows for 18 passengers, making for a special evening.

According to recent reports, if it’s a fancy dinner aboard a train you’re looking for, the Green Mountain Railroad can do that, too. Every weekend between late June and late October, you can book the Champlain Valley Dinner Train, a three-hour roundtrip ride between Burlington and Middlebury that includes a three-course meal and all gratuities. Make sure you book a private table if you don’t want to share the space with your fellow passengers. (Note that the Champlain Valley Dinner Train is not an adult-only experience, it welcomes all passengers aged five and up.).

In 2025, the Virginia Scenic Railway introduced the Shenandoah, a vintage 1948 Budd Company dome car that once belonged to country music legend Merle Haggard. The refurbished car now offers panoramic views of the Shenandoah Valley and Blue Ridge Mountains on two scenic roundtrips — the west-bound Alleghany Special and the east-bound Blue Ridge Flyer. Passengers in the upper-level dome car can relax with regional drinks and light fare while taking in the scenery of the Blue Ridge Mountains and Shenandoah Valley.

Industry observers note that what makes Amtrak’s Empire Builder route unique is that from mid-April to mid-October, it serves East Glacier Park train station, located in the heart of Glacier National Park. And because the train station is just a few steps away from Glacier Park Lodge, you can go directly from the comfort of the train to that of a lovely hotel.

While you might think that traveling with Amtrak is far from luxurious, there are ways to make your train ride extremely comfortable. All you need to do is book a Bedroom Suite and you’ve got an all-inclusive and enjoyable train ride. A Bedroom Suite can sleep four travelers by turning the two sofas and chairs into sleeping berths when night comes, but if there are only two of you, you can enjoy all the extra space. There are also two in-room sinks, toilets, and showers so you don’t have to share the facilities with strangers. By booking a Bedroom Suite, you also get a dedicated First Class attendant, complimentary lounge access at the departing train station, priority boarding, and complimentary meals on board.

If you’re interested in visiting America’s national parks by train, check out Matador’s guide to the seven most scenic Amtrak routes through national parks.

The Grand Canyon Railway offers rides from Williams, Arizona, to the South Rim of the Grand Canyon daily throughout the year. The ride between Williams and the South Rim takes two hours, and passengers are given three hours on site to visit, making for a seven-hour day trip. With six classes of service available, you can make your ride with the Grand Canyon Railway as cheap or as luxurious as you want it to be. If you’re ready to splurge for a very comfortable experience, choose the Luxury Dome Class, reserved to travelers over the age of 16. The Luxury Dome Class consists of a two-story car: on top, there is a dome car with panoramic windows, while below is a parlor-style lounge car with very comfortable seats and a full bar. You’ll be served snacks and non-alcoholic beverages during the journey. (For complimentary sparkling wine, book the Luxury Parlor Class, the most exclusive seat on the train.).

Photo: Mount Rainier Scenic Railroad and Museum.

The Mount Rainier Scenic Railroad resumed excursions in 2023, offering steam-powered rides through the forests and foothills outside Mount Rainier National Park. The route follows the Nisqually River from Elbe toward Mineral, with clear views of the mountain on fair-weather days. Passengers ride in restored heritage coaches pulled by a 1922 Baldwin steam locomotive, combining classic rail travel with Pacific Northwest scenery on a short, comfortable trip. In 2026, the railroad added a second operating steam engine, Porter No. 5, built in 1925.

Sources indicate that the Napa Valley Wine train operates year-round and offers a variety of experiences to prospective travelers, all of which have an element of formal luxury for which you need to dress up. The most decadent of the experiences available is the Legacy Experience, a six-hour trip that includes three hours on the train, and three hours visiting vineries. Passengers on the Legacy Experience enjoy breakfast and lunch on board, as well as wine tasting. While most of the trip takes place in the restored vintage Pullman rail cars, the open-air car is also available to passengers.

For a shorter, but no less luxurious experience on board the Napa Valley Wine train, opt for the Vista Dome Dinner (a two-hour, multiple-course journey in the glass-dome elegant dining car), or the Afternoon Tea (a three-hour trip filled with cocktails, tea, finger sandwiches, miniature deserts, and more.).

It has been revealed that the Denali Star route, operated by the Alaska Railroad, is one of the most scenic train trips you can take in the US. Not only is the scenery between Anchorage and Fairbanks beautiful, but you can also take it in in extreme comfort if you opt for the Goldstar Service. The Goldstar Service includes a meal, soft beverages, and two adult drinks in the dining car. Goldstar passengers also benefit from comfortable forward-facing seats, and have access to outdoor viewing platforms and glass-dome cars from where you can enjoy the beauty of the Alaskan wilderness.

Sources indicate that another iconic Alaskan train route, the Coastal Classic is operated by the Alaska Railroad. The Coastal Classic is a much shorter ride than the Denali Star and is the perfect route for travelers with a tight schedule. Just like with the Denali Star route, those who want to make their train journey extra fancy should opt for the Goldstar Service — the views from the glass-dome cars never get old.

A post shared by Tennessee Valley Railroad (@tenn_valley_rr).

It has been revealed that the Tennessee Valley Railroad Museum operates its Chattanooga Dinner Train on select Friday and Saturday evenings from March through October. The train departs from Grand Junction Station in Chattanooga and travels along a historic stretch of track that includes the 1858 Missionary Ridge Tunnel. Guests are served a seasonal three-course meal while seated in fully restored dining cars, with the option to reserve a private car for small groups. The experience combines classic Southern dining with the atmosphere of mid-20th-century rail travel.

Yes, there are sleeper trains in the USA, all of them being operated by Amtrak. Amtrak’s overnight and long-distance routes have sleeper cars with multiple accommodation options to choose from, including Roomettes, Bedrooms, Accessible Bedrooms, Bedroom Suites, and Family Rooms. If you want to travel cheap, you can opt for a reclining seat in coach class.

Sources indicate that amtrak’s longest daily route is the California Zephyr, which runs 2,438 miles between Chicago, Illinois, and Emeryville, California, in roughly 51 to 52 hours. The longest route overall is the Texas Eagle: its thrice-weekly continuation from Chicago all the way to Los Angeles runs close to 65 hours.

The most luxurious train in the US is the Rocky Mountaineer with its Rockies to the Red Rock route that runs between Denver, Colorado, and Moab, Utah. The Rocky Mountaineer is not a sleeper train, and you can watch more details on the video below.

Sources indicate that the ubiquitous, ongoing discussions about machine learning and artificial intelligence and their impacts often leave out a crucial part of the equation – the cheap labour in the Global South that fuels these technologies. In his short documentary Their Eyes, the French filmmaker Nicolas Gourault spotlights the voices of several of these overlooked workers in Kenya, the Philippines and Venezuela. Throughout, they explain the tasks they perform to train self-driving cars, as well as the mostly precarious and low-paid working conditions they endure. Peering into the screens of these gig workers, the audience experiences how they parse images of unfamiliar streets, performing repetitive tasks so that cars in another part of the world can ‘see’. As viewers ultimately step out of the workers’ screens and into their homes, the film questions who gets to benefit from these technologies and at what cost, highlighting how they perpetuate and widen existing geographical inequalities.

Bob's Chicken Salad and More Recipes We Made This Week

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (933 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that it’s no secret that Bon Appétit editors cook a lot for work.
  • Every fall I stuff my pantry with cans of pumpkin purée.
  • There is a new vendor at my greenmarket who makes incredible buffalo milk yogurt.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that it’s no secret that Bon Appétit editors cook a lot for work. So it should come as no surprise that we cook a lot during our off hours too. Here are the recipes we’re whipping up this month to get dinner on the table, entertain our friends, satisfy a sweet tooth, use up leftovers, and everything in between. For even more staff favorites, click here.

Every fall I stuff my pantry with cans of pumpkin purée. And fortunately our annual Pumpkin Week tells me exactly what to do with the haul. I’m always in search of more savory uses for the ingredient, and my coworker Jesse Szewczyk’s Pumpkin Black Bean Enchiladas were right up my alley. I did a mix of black and kidney beans (what was around) and I toned down the spice for my toddler who—the universe laughs—refused to eat them anyway, instead opting to smear the sauce all over his clothes. C’est la vie! —Emma Laperruque, cooking director.

There is a new vendor at my greenmarket who makes incredible buffalo milk yogurt. My favorite is flavored with tangy, floral passion fruit. It’s not too sweet and works beautifully with fruit and granola. To showcase its power as a sauce, I made David Tamarkin’s apple olive oil cake (baked in an 8" round instead of a loaf) and served the yogurt underneath. For the cake, you shred a couple of apples then squeeze out their juices, which you can then drink for a baker’s treat. —Joe Sevier, senior editor, SEO & cooking.

Sources indicate that one of my favorite things is to use a banana bread recipe to make muffins and call it meal prep. I pack this gluten-free batter into tins, sprinkle on some flaxseed and pecans, and reduce the bake time. They can easily pass for breakfast, an afternoon snack, or dessert, and the recipe yields enough muffins to be enjoyed throughout the week with a scoop of yogurt or swipe of nut butter. —Kate Kassin, editorial operations manager.

With a recipe entitled Bob’s Chicken and Cabbage Salad, I’m sure you’re wondering: Who the heck is Bob? Author Melissa Broder’s late father, who happened to be fervently devoted to purple cabbage. Well, Bob, me too—especially after trying this one. Per the instructions, I chopped up half a head of cabbage, baby bok choy, scallions, bean sprouts, and water chestnuts, then tossed the roughage with pulled chicken. This time around, I did cheat with a store-bought rotisserie bird to jump-start cooking (it was 8 p.m. when I started, okay?). That also meant halving the heavenly soy-ginger dressing, since I no longer needed some of it for the marinade. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking.

My Test Kitchen buddy Rebecca Firkser has a wild little pasta up her sleeve that I can’t get enough of: Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates. When she first made it for the team, I was blown away. I would have never thought to throw dates into a pasta, but alas, it’s delicious. Each bite has something sweet, something creamy, a bit of crunch, and endless fun. —Jesse Szewczyk, senior Test Kitchen editor.

Industry observers note that since my son started daycare in September, our household has been sick more than it has been healthy. So it makes sense that I have been on a chicken soup kick. I have it for lunch and dinner and drink mugfuls of stock between meals. My latest batch was my colleague Rebecca Firkser’s Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup, which has a beautifully spiced broth and lots of nourishing spinach. It may not be a cure-all, but close enough. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director.

Sources indicate that delicata squash should be as popular as butternut. It’s far easier to cut (no hacks or hacking necessary), the thin skin is not only edible but tasty, and it’s got a sweet potato-like flesh that’s creamy and, well, sweet. I usually treat it simply (oil, salt and pepper, hot oven, done), but I treated myself to my former colleague Rachel Gurjar’s gussied-up Roasted Delicata Squash With Crispy Onions and I’m so glad I did. The squash itself takes no extra effort, but gathering up some toppings, like store-bought fried onions tossed with extra spices, juicy pomegranate seeds, and seasoned yogurt, transformed it into a dish I was proud to serve to guests. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor.

Sources indicate that we have a latest Friday tradition at our house: Pasta Alla Vodka and Caesar salad. Not rocket science, I know, but after a rough-and-tumble week of work and school, we are all reaching for some semblance of comfort. It is also easy enough to whip up that I can often beat the timing of our former Friday tradition, take-out pizza. The Caesar dressing is usually made in advance (I keep a batch in the fridge because my family lurves it) and the pasta of choice is usually rigatoni. It cooks in about the same amount of time as the sauce—I just love when that happens. —Hana Asbrink, deputy food editor.

It has been revealed that there’s nothing more perfect than a tuna melt. Buttery slices of sourdough or rye that leave a shine of grease on your fingers. Tuna salad mashed into tender flakes, speckled with crisp celery, onion, and herbs. A blanket of American cheese, so stretchy it’ll rival a mozzarella stick. And a mandatory pickle, to offer added tangy solace after each bite. I ate mine with salt-and-vinegar kettle chips stuffed inside because that’s how my favorite diner does it. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, there are in Truxton, Newly introduced York, three interrelated sites associated with legendary baseball manager John J.
  • Recent findings suggest that mcGraw’s father, also named John, emigrated to the United States in 1856.
  • Sources indicate that young McGraw had a difficult childhood.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, there are in Truxton, Newly introduced York, three interrelated sites associated with legendary baseball manager John J. McGraw, who was born in that Central New York town in 1873. The three are a monument to the native son, a baseball field named in his honor, and a sign memorializing the game played at John J. McGraw Field that funded the carving and installation of the memorial to McGraw.

Recent findings suggest that mcGraw’s father, also named John, emigrated to the United States in 1856. In his first fifteen years in America, John Sr. served in the Union Army during the Civil War, married and fathered a daughter, suffered the death of his wife, and relocated to Truxton. There, he married Ellen Comerfort, who bore seven children of which the younger John McGraw was the eldest.

Sources indicate that young McGraw had a difficult childhood. The family of ten was poor in an era before public assistance. When he was 12, a diphtheria epidemic struck the area, killing his mother and four of his siblings, including his older half-sister. John Sr. never recovered from the trauma of burying a second wife and became physically abusive to his namesake. McGraw fils ran away at 12 and a neighbor persuaded the father to let the boy live with her and her two sons.

McGraw had an early love of baseball and worked odd jobs—including walking the aisles of the Elmira, Cortland and Northern Railroad selling candy, fruit, and magazines—so he could afford to purchase sports equipment. A star pitcher locally at 16, McGraw talked his way on to a minor league baseball team in Olean, New York. In his first minor league contest, McGraw made eight errors in 10 chances at third base and was released after six games. It was a momentary setback.

Industry observers note that picked up by Wellsville, one of four squads competing in the sole season of the Western New York League, McGraw batted .364 in 24 games but more importantly, met former National League player Al Lawson, who brought the 17-year-old on a winter exhibition tour of Cuba. Returning home, the “American All-Stars” took on the Cleveland Spyders at the latter’s spring training camp. McGraw hit three doubles in five at-bats, garnering national notice in The Sporting News and thereby, multiple offers for the coming season.

McGraw signed with the Cedar Rapids Canaries of the independent Illinois-Iowa League, where he batted .276 in 85 games as the club’s everyday shortstop. At the request of the Baltimore Orioles, the Canaries released McGraw and he made his major league debut at age 18. McGraw played eight seasons with the Birds, then another nine as a player-manager with the Orioles, Cardinals, and Giants, becoming the full-time skipper of the Giants in 1908. He had a lifetime batting average of .334 and on-base percentage of .466, trailing only Ted Williams and Babe Ruth in career OBP, admittedly in far fewer games. He had five seasons in which he scored 100 or more runs and three seasons with 50 or more stolen bases, admirable statistics today even with a longer season.

That said, McGraw is primarily known as a manager. He was an innovator and tactician, for example popularizing the hit-and-run play first used by his mentor in Baltimore, Ned Hanlon. McGraw was the first baseball manager to hire coaching staff and use relief pitchers. Among his nicknames was “Little Napoleon” because (he was 5’-7” tall and) called every pitch from the bench, told players how to live their lives off the field, and was verbally abusive. Decades before football coach Vince Lombardi said winning is the only thing, McGraw managed according to that credo and his players by and large bought into the philosophy.

Industry observers note that mcGraw remains the longest-serving major league manager at 31 seasons. His 2,763 victories ranks third overall behind Connie Mack (3,731) and Tony La Russa (2,880). However, Mack was famously quoted as saying, “There has been only one manager, and his name is John McGraw.” For managers with more than 1,000 victories, his .586 winning percentage is second only to Joe McCarthy (.615), who managed for half as long. McGraw won ten National League pennants, tying him for first with Casey Stengel, and managed three World Series champions.

Four years after McGraw died from prostate cancer at age 60, the Newly introduced York Giants were permitted to play an exhibition game against a Truxton squad. The friendly match was scheduled to raise funds for a monument to the local lad made good who never returned to his hometown after leaving in 1890 to play baseball in Olean. Unsurprisingly, the professional ball players bested the amateurs, 8-1, but consistent with the game’s purpose, the contest raised the money needed to carve and install the memorial to McGraw.

According to recent reports, the monument is located in a small triangle on the main thoroughfare through town and can be easily overlooked, especially if one is focussed on the bend in the road. The face of the memorial includes a bust of McGraw in relief and the legend, “A great American / One of baseball’s immortals / Dynamic leader of the New York Giants for thirty years.” Carved into the rear is the record, “On August 8, 1938 the New York Giants played an exhibition game with the Truxton ball team in this village which made possible the erection of this memorial.”.

Recent findings suggest that john J. McGraw Field, where the exhibition game was held, continues to host amateur sports and other events. A small off-street parking lot is located opposite the Truxton Town Hall, 6290 Railroad Street. On the left field side of the ballpark, along Chenango Road (County Road 600A), is a sign erected in 2025 to remember the 1938 exhibition. According to the sign, approximately 8,000 people attended the game, paying $1.10 (roughly $25.00 in 2025) to watch the contest.

Recent findings suggest that shortly after McGraw’s death, as it were to happen, the National Baseball Hall of Fame and Museum was founded in 1936. John. J. McGraw was one of the 26 members of the 1939 inaugural class, inducted as a manager. Truxton is about an hour-and-a-half west of Cooperstown and a short detour from Interstate-81 between Binghamton and Syracuse.

Tech Report: You Can Take These Epic Safari Adventures Over a Long Weekend

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1224 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Matadornetwork

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Going on a safari is the top item on many a person’s travel bucket list.
  • Whether you’re crossing a savanna or trekking through the Amazon, you can board a plane Thursday, safari all weekend, and often be back in your own bed by Monday night.
  • Sources indicate that this 72-hour whirlwind weekend safari has you arriving in the Rwandan capital of Kigali on night one, where you’ll spend the night in Flame Tree Village.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Going on a safari is the top item on many a person’s travel bucket list. Safaris offer a rare chance to see endangered animals you’d never be able to see otherwise (in the wild, at least). But it’s also because the once-in-a-lifetime adventure typically takes up loads of both time and money – it’s not something you can do every year. But if you can afford the flights (and somehow stave off jet lag) you can do a safari in a long weekend.

Don’t believe it? Whether you’re crossing a savanna or trekking through the Amazon, you can board a plane Thursday, safari all weekend, and often be back in your own bed by Monday night. Here are eight weekend safaris around the world you can do in only a few days.

Sources indicate that this 72-hour whirlwind weekend safari has you arriving in the Rwandan capital of Kigali on night one, where you’ll spend the night in Flame Tree Village. Rwandan history and culture are the themes on the second day as you explore the city and learn about its pre-colonial and colonial times, as well as the tragic and tumultuous 1990s. This includes a trip to the harrowing genocide memorial, after which you’ll visit the renewed and thriving Kigali of today.

The third day begins bright and early, leaving for Volcanoes National Park at 6:30 in the morning. Once there, the park staff will assess your physical fitness and assign you a family of gorillas to visit. The rest of the morning and afternoon is a trek into the Virunga Mountains, where you’ll spend an hour or so with a family of gorillas. After the trek, it’s off to the Kigali airport, and back to real life.

In a recent development, photo: Mariusz S. Jurgielewicz/Shutterstock.

Industry observers note that after overnighting in Cusco, your first day of this Peruvian adventure begins with a short flight to Puerto Maldonado, where you’ll hop on a boat down the Madre de Dios River. The three-hour tour concludes at a wilderness lodge, where you’ll eat lunch before boarding another boat to Monkey Island. There, you’ll spend the afternoon hiking through monkey habitat, on the hunt for black spider monkeys, squirrel monkeys, and capuchin monkeys, plus tamarins and coatis.

Sources indicate that things get a little more active on day two, where you’ll start with a four-hour jungle trek to the Lost Lagoon. Along the way, you’ll encounter giant river otters, alligators, turtles, and all varieties of tropical birds. You’ll stop at a watchtower and ascend a spiral staircase to a viewing deck in the treetops looking out across the Amazon. After that, hop in a canoe and paddle around the Lost Lagoon, watching as alligators and turtles swim past.

In a recent development, after lunch — yes, that’s all before lunch — you’ll have the choice to go down river and visit a local family or recover in the lodge. On day three, it’s boats then small planes then bigger planes as you make the final trek home.

Photo: Dave Primov/Shutterstock.

Talk about an action-packed weekend. This weekend safari tour de force kicks off at the ungodly hour of 5 AM in Dar Es Salaam, Tanzania. You won’t even stop for breakfast until two and a half hours into the drive, when you reach the town of Morogoro. From there, it’s an hour-ish more to Mikumi National Park, where you hit the ground running on your first of three game drives. After a brief lunch stop, it’s on for more game driving, trying to spot leopards, giraffes, lions, and other African favorites.

After a short night at the Mikumi Tourist Cottage, it’s time for – you guessed it – another game drive. You’ll spend the morning with all your favorite African animals, then take a short breakfast break and keep driving until around 11 AM. That’s when your driver picks you up and takes you back to Morogoro for lunch, then to the Dar es Salaam airport. By the time your plane takes off, you won’t be quite sure any of it really happened.

According to recent reports, if you don’t mind your wild animal encounters with a backdrop of the city skyline, you won’t find a more convenient safari than the ones in Nairobi National Park. The park sits just half an hour by car from the Nairobi airport, and is almost walkable from downtown. Imagine Central Park with lions instead of hot dog vendors, and you’re getting the idea.

Half- and full-day safari trips abound in Nairobi National Park, where you can grab a guide and spend the afternoon observing elephants, rhinos, and giraffes. The park offers a little more than your typical wild reserve, including an educational center and even an elephant orphanage.

Photo: NaturesMomentsuk/Shutterstocl.

You don’t even need to leave North America for a long weekend safari and a chance to get up close with massive wild animals. While Manitoba’s famous polar bear expeditions are rarely less than seven-day affairs, you can still get out into the Canadian wilderness for the weekend and try your hand at spotting wild grizzlies. Chilcotin Ranch in the Chilcotin Mountains, about five hours north of Vancouver, takes guests on horseback treks through the wilderness. While riding, you’ll spot Canadian moose and bighorn sheep, and there’s also a good chance of seeing grizzly bears in their natural habitat.

You’ll be staying on a working mountain ranch and will have the option to take snowmobiles and 4x4s out on your own if you feel like exploring without a guide. All meals are included, as are your guide and the horseback safaris. The ranch offers an optional van service from the Vancouver Airport or you can rent a car and enjoy the scenic drive up. While the animals are the main attraction, the journey is equally as stunning as the destination.

Photo: Sergey Novikov/Shutterstocl.

Industry observers note that acrophobics, scroll down, because in addition to coming extremely close to some of the fiercest animals on the planet, this weekend safari also takes you hundreds of feet into the air. The trip begins with an early morning pickup and a stop to marvel at the Great Rift Valley Escarpment. Once you’ve taken it in, it’s off to Narok Town for lunch, then to your tent accommodations at Miti Mingi Eco Camp. The nearby Oloolaimutia River is a popular watering hole for wild animals, so if you get up in the middle of the night to use the river and find yourself sharing space with a water buffalo, don’t be surprised.

In a recent development, day two is an all-day game drive, and if you happen to come during the great wildebeest migration, you’re in for a full day of thundering herds. Even if you don’t, you’ll still be treated to plenty of elephants, crocodiles, and hippos. After another night at the Miti Mingi camp, you’ll enjoy a pre-dawn game drive, when lions and other substantial cats are hunting and at their most active. Or you can opt to jump in a hot air balloon and do your wildlife spotting from a thousand feet up. You’ll head back between 8:30 and 9:00 AM, effectively doing more before breakfast than you ever thought possible.

#60. Celestial nuisance

Celestial nuisance

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3637 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Aeon

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that in the story of cosmic history, one of the most important supporting characters is dust.
  • Recent findings suggest that in astrophysics, ‘nuisance’ is a quasi-technical term.
  • Recent findings suggest that this dichotomy between ‘signal’ and ‘nuisance’ is found across many sub-fields in astronomy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in the story of cosmic history, one of the most important supporting characters is dust. As clouds of interstellar gas cooled and condensed in the early Universe, dust grains absorbed and re-emitted radiation, eventually forming stars. Later, dust provided the raw material from which planets could form and grow. Dust grains may even have been the surfaces on which the first complex organic molecules formed. Yet, if you ask most cosmologists, they’ll tell you that dust is a sheer nuisance.

Recent findings suggest that in astrophysics, ‘nuisance’ is a quasi-technical term. Astrophysicists call any phenomenon that gets in the way of the thing they actually want to study a ‘nuisance’. Dust grains emit polarised light that can mimic subtle signals from the afterglow of the Substantial Bang (the cosmic microwave background) that cosmologists have spent decades and billions of dollars trying to detect. A cosmologist studies dust not to uncover its role in shaping the cosmos, but to subtract it – the term ‘sweeping under the rug’ couldn’t be more apt.

Recent findings suggest that this dichotomy between ‘signal’ and ‘nuisance’ is found across many sub-fields in astronomy. Astronomers who study a phenomenon called ‘weak lensing’ use the subtle distortions of light caused by gravity to map invisible dark matter. For them, the ordinary matter that makes up everything we can see is a nuisance. Pulsar timing astronomers use rapidly spinning neutron stars called pulsars as extraordinarily precise clocks to detect the passage of gravitational waves through the galaxy. For them, the nuisance is ionised interstellar gas, which scatters and disperses the light from pulsars.

Yet one astronomer’s nuisance is another’s treasure. Just as a laser beam reveals the intricate swirls of smoke in a dark room, pulsars illuminate the fine structure of the interstellar medium, the unlit space between galaxies. If you want to study the interstellar medium and its role in shaping our galaxy’s evolution, the light-scattering gas is an invaluable resource.

The ESO-operated Very Large Telescope based at the Cerro Paranal site in the Atacama Desert of northern Chile. Photo by Miguel Claro/ESO.

Whether a phenomenon is a nuisance or something worth studying in its own right clearly depends on the investigator and their interests. But in a discipline as collaborative as astronomy, shared priorities must be developed. Gone are the days of Galileo and other lone scientists in the tower, pointing telescopes built by their own hands wherever curiosity dictates. Modern astronomy is a highly specialised discipline, marked by large collaborations. The tools of the trade – telescopes – are designed, built and maintained by hundreds of scientists and engineers across many institutions. But you can’t just stroll in and ask to use one. Investigators must fiercely compete for time with these advanced instruments. To guide how that access is allocated, the research community has developed a set of shared priorities. Some questions are elevated to the status of ‘Significant Questions’ to which all others inevitably become subordinate.

But are these Big Questions necessarily the right ones? Who decides where to draw the boundaries between signal and nuisance, or big and small? Fields of enquiry are defined by the questions they seek to answer. If we want to understand modern astrophysics, it is not enough to understand the scientific and mathematical content of its theories. We also need to understand the human forces that shape the questions themselves and cause some questions to be prioritised, and other questions to be viewed as irrelevant or merely means to those bigger ends.

Sources indicate that to identify the Big Questions that dominate the field, you need look no further than the flagship projects set to shape the discipline for decades. These include the Square Kilometre Array Observatory, the James Webb Space Telescope, the Vera C Rubin Observatory, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, and the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna. Each of these projects will cost several billion dollars over its lifetime.

Recent findings suggest that when we look at the stated science goals of these projects, consistent themes emerge. For example, the Square Kilometre Array Observatory at Jodrell Bank in the UK is a massive radio array that will define the field of radio astronomy for the foreseeable future. Its website contains a list of science goals. On that list, the early Universe, gravitational waves, dark energy and cosmology are all listed before stars, the interstellar medium and the origins of life. The official page for the much-covered James Webb Space Telescope similarly lists the early Universe – the ‘cosmic dawn’ – before more prosaic matters such as stars, planets and dust. Such priorities are often reflected in media coverage of these projects, which further shape perceptions among young researchers, politicians, funders and the general public about which questions matter most.

It has been revealed that the boundaries between the big and small questions often fall along the lines between ‘fundamental’ physics and ‘messy’ astrophysics. This is reflected in the language of many cosmologists who study dark matter, for example. For decades, the study of dark matter has focused on the largest physical scales – giant clusters of galaxies – where the gravitational effects of dark matter can be directly inferred. On small scales, within and around galaxies, dark matter’s effects become entangled with the complex dynamics of interstellar gas. To use the terminology that is widely adopted by cosmologists: the physics of dark matter on small scales is obscured by the astrophysics of interstellar gas. Implicit in this framing is the idea that astrophysics is messy and complicated, and, ultimately, subordinate to clean, fundamental physics.

When the fundamental is elevated above everything else, it’s easy to see why an impressionable young mind might be captivated.

Young researchers encounter this supposed predominance of physics over astrophysics long before they set foot in a laboratory. Growing up, I loved space, as many children do. My parents bought me an amateur telescope, and I spent many nights in the backyard becoming familiar with the winter night sky (the summer sky was more elusive because it appeared after my bedtime). But, by the time I entered graduate school, I had largely forgotten about my early childhood passion for the heavens. Like many of my peers at the time, I wanted to study theoretical particle physics.

Particle physics enjoys a kind of mythical status in popular culture as the apex of the natural sciences. After all, the purported goal of particle physicists is not just a theory of particles, but a theory of everything. Of course, such a theory would be a theory of ‘everything’ only in the limited sense that it would describe how all matter behaves on a fundamental (microscopic) level – never mind the fact that such a description would be functionally useless to describe even basic chemical reactions due to the mathematical complexity. But when the fundamental is elevated above everything else, it’s easy to see why an impressionable young mind might be captivated.

In the end, I did not study theoretical particle physics as a graduate student. The competition was intense – almost all of my classmates were vying for the few positions available. So, I rekindled my love of astronomy and decided to study astrophysics. But the truth is, at the time, I viewed astrophysics as something of a consolation prize.

This hierarchy, which ranks fundamental physics above all else, is a historical contingency. Over the course of the second half of the 20th century, astronomy transformed from a distinct discipline into a sub-discipline of physics. Historically, astronomy was a science of mapping, cataloguing and observation. But the successes of mid-century nuclear physics, the rise of physical cosmology and the discovery of dark matter and dark energy began a process that fused the two disciplines.

The discovery of general relativity, which describes gravity as a warping of the fabric of space and time, provided a new framework that enabled the quantitative study of the dynamics of the Universe as a whole. Cosmology, which had previously been the domain of philosophers, became the domain of physicists. In the closing decades of the 20th century, this framework enabled the dual discovery of dark matter and dark energy – both mysterious substances unaccounted for by the standard model of particle physics. Crucially, these gaps in the standard model would have gone completely undetected without the observations of astronomers.

Sources indicate that the heavens, then, transformed from an object of study in its own right to a latest laboratory for testing fundamental physics. This shift is preserved in our vocabulary: the term ‘astronomy’ was demoted in favour of the more prestigious term ‘astrophysics’.

I saw astronomy as a means to an end, a stepping stone on the path to a theory of everything.

Recent findings suggest that the rise of astrophysics was, in part, fuelled by the geopolitics of the Cold War, which saw an unprecedented surge in funding for physics, in addition to a rise in the cultural prestige of physics in the public imagination. Governments invested large sums of money in physics mega-projects, cementing a culture of large collaborations dedicated to the study of fundamental, high-energy physics. This was the era of the particle accelerator, in which subatomic particles are accelerated to extremely high energies to test theories of physics that manifest only at those energy scales. But then the Cold War ended, and the cash flow stopped. In 1993, the US Congress cancelled the Superconducting Super Collider project in Texas, after billions had already been spent.

Suddenly, a generation of particle physicists found themselves without the experimental tools to test their theories on Earth. Astronomy, however, provided an attractive alternative. The Universe revealed itself to be the ultimate, free particle accelerator: full of violent events, such as supernovae, colliding black holes and the Massive Bang, reaching energy scales that no terrestrial collider ever could. If only the complications of real astrophysical environments could be modelled and accounted for, then the heavens would be the perfect new laboratory for physics.

It was precisely this logic that sold me on astrophysics as a new graduate student. At the time, I saw astronomy as a means to an end, a stepping stone on the path to a theory of everything. I was interested in the messy complications of astronomy only insofar as understanding them would enable us to disregard them.

In a recent development, today, this ‘physicisation’ of astronomy has left a deep imprint on the cultural norms of the discipline. Modern astrophysics is characterised by massive, hyper-centralised international collaborations, and an often tacit belief that ‘fundamental’ physics sits at the top of the scientific pyramid, while the questions of real ‘astrophysics’ are mere nuisances.

This ideological elevation of the fundamental over the particular is evident in the architecture of modern big-data astronomy. The past few decades have been characterised by experiments yielding massive volumes of data. Yet, these pipelines are not neutral data-gathering machines; indeed, their very design reflects and reinforces the institutional bias towards astrophysics as a barrier to fundamental truth. The logic is that, with enough data, the rich and diverse astrophysical phenomena that manifest in particular cosmic environments can be statistically modelled and averaged away, leaving only what is fundamental.

AI models inherit untested assumptions about the physical processes they aim to illuminate.

Consider, for example, the phenomenon of weak gravitational lensing, where astronomers measure how gravity distorts the shapes of distant galaxies. They can use this to build a map of the dark matter in the Universe, which is otherwise invisible. However, weak gravitational lensing is equally sensitive to the gravitational effects of all matter in the Universe – the dark matter and the ‘ordinary’ matter. The physical interactions that govern ordinary matter complicate inferences of the underlying dark matter distribution. Data analysis pipelines for modern weak lensing surveys flatten the complex physics of astrophysical environments to a set of ‘nuisance parameters’, which, with enough data, can be averaged away. Rich astrophysical phenomena are, from the very outset and in the survey design itself, framed as statistical obstacles to fundamental truths.

A Hubble image featuring the galaxy cluster Abell 2813 demonstrates the concept of gravitational lensing. Among the tiny dots, spirals and ovals that are the galaxies that belong to the cluster, there are several distinct crescent shapes. These curved arcs of light are distant galaxies. Their light is magnified and distorted by the strong gravitational field of the foreground galaxy cluster. Courtesy NASA/ESA/Dan Coe.

This paradigm is further reinforced by the turn towards artificial intelligence (AI). A natural symbiosis exists between the petabytes of data generated by modern observatories and the massive datasets needed to train deep learning architectures. Driven by the hype, if a project promises to use AI, it helps attract funding and allocation of computational resources, even when its capacity for genuine discovery remains unclear.

Industry observers note that foundation AI models are heralded as the best way to digest datasets too massive for detailed human analysis, promising to automatically infer complex astrophysics from raw images of the sky. But there is a fundamental disconnect between the statistical patterns these technologies learn and the underlying physical mechanisms that generate the observations. Whereas you might train an AI to learn what a cat looks like with a set of images of known cats and non-cats, there is no set of galaxy images where all the relevant astrophysics is known. Instead, models need to be trained with synthetic data drawn from astrophysical simulations. However, computational limitations force these simulations to rely on simplified approximations of the very physics in question. As a result, AI models inherit untested assumptions about the physical processes they aim to illuminate.

In a recent development, this is not a problem if your goal is simply to account for complex astrophysics in massive data sets to infer the underlying fundamental physics. These models are, after all, exceptional at identifying and correcting for subtle correlations in the data. But if your goal is to understand the complex physics of the astrophysical phenomena themselves, the benefit is less obvious.

Thus, modern astrophysics appears to be oriented towards a paradigm of modelling massive data sets to uncover fundamental constants. This paradigm is mutually reinforced by the questions that are institutionally prioritised and the tools used to answer them. However, this loop of reinforcement can create an illusion of field-wide consensus around what the most notable questions are, which obscures the daily realities of many working astronomers.

It has been revealed that this is nowhere more visible than in the discourse surrounding the ‘Hubble tension’ – the fact that different methods of measuring the Universe’s expansion rate (the Hubble constant) yield contradictory results. Across white papers and popular science articles, the Hubble tension is touted as a profound crisis in physics. If the discrepancy is real (as opposed to a statistical fluke), then it could be an important hint about the nature of dark energy, which drives the expansion.

Industry observers note that and yet, in the trenches of astrophysics research, attitudes are markedly different. At nearly every talk I have attended on the Hubble tension, the reaction from working astrophysicists is surprisingly muted. If this discrepancy is the great white whale of modern cosmology, why do so many researchers respond with a shrug?

Industry observers note that the reality is that most scientists are passionate and obsessive creatures, devoting many years of their lives to extremely niche topics that others might struggle to care about. Such people naturally find their work intrinsically interesting, not just as a step towards some bigger question. Of course, scientists have complex motivations that are shaped by their institutional environments and that shape the long-term trajectory of their careers. But, on a day-to-day basis, many astronomers really do just care a lot about dust, or gas dynamics, or cosmic magnetic fields.

For myself, the further away I got from physics proper, the more I rediscovered my love of astronomy for its own sake. Whether or not astronomy unearths fresh fundamental laws of physics, it has much to tell us about our place in the Universe and what it means to be human. Since Copernicus, astronomy has gradually demoted humanity’s position in the cosmos, from occupying the literal centre of everything, to merely occupying an unremarkable planet, orbiting an unremarkable star, in an unremarkable galaxy in a potentially infinite Universe. At the same time, as the bounds of the known Universe expand, we have increasingly understood the rarity and fragility of life in the cosmos. Astronomy, therefore, plays a critical role in the story of the human species. While I remain hopeful that astronomy can lead us to new fundamental physics, that hope is no longer the driving force of my interest in the heavens. I suspect this is the case for many of my fellow astronomers.

Despite this, investigators are required to play a rhetorical game, justifying their deeply specific research within the context of the predetermined Significant Questions. When you apply for academic jobs, the advice is: Always, always, always link your work to the Big Questions. Since hiring or grant committees typically comprise faculty with a diverse range of expertise, an applicant cannot rely on the committee sharing an intrinsic interest in their niche topic. Justifying your science in relation to the Big Questions is more likely to lead to a successful application, even if individually none of the members of the committee are particularly passionate about those questions.

According to recent reports, scientific journals reinforce this rhetorical game. The most prestigious journals demand that their articles represent significant advancements in the field. In other words, they require that the research they publish make progress on the pre-defined Massive Questions. Investigators are incentivised to frame their papers in this context. I have personally written papers that motivate the work as a step towards resolving the Hubble tension. While technically true, this framing misrepresents the reasons I embarked upon that research and the real reasons I find it interesting.

If you could uncover the nature of dark energy, or discover alien life, which would you choose?

This is not to suggest that having shared priorities across a research community is somehow wrong – indeed, it is inevitable. But it is notable to recognise that these priorities are historically contingent and, to some degree, arbitrary. When investigators play the rhetorical game of justifying their research, the game ends when they link their work to a fundamental question in physics. But why stop there? Why is the search for dark energy or dark matter inherently more justified than the lifecycle of interstellar dust? The ‘fundamental’ questions are no more or less intrinsically justified than the nuisances that get in their way. Rather, we choose which questions are ends in themselves and which require further justification.

Many commentators have made a great deal of the crisis that faces high-energy physics today. Terrestrial collider experiments have failed to reveal any signs of the latest physics they were built to find, and we may well be reaching the limit of what astrophysics can tell us about fundamental physics. Even if the Hubble tension is confirmed, we may never settle on the correct physical theory of dark energy. Even as we better characterise the gravitational behaviour of dark matter, its particle nature may remain a mystery forever. The Big Questions are beginning to lose their lustre, and some are beginning to ask whether the billions of dollars spent on mega-projects are diminishing in their returns. But if this is a crisis for high-energy physics, there is no crisis for astronomy. Astronomers will continue to investigate all the weird and wonderful things the Universe has to offer.

According to recent reports, the intricacies of a dying star in the Helix Nebula, captured by the James Webb Space Telescope. Courtesy NASA.

If you’re an astronomer reading this – or anyone who would like to play along – I invite you to consider the following hypothetical. If, tomorrow, you could uncover the nature of dark energy, or discover alien life, which would you choose? Both would guarantee a Nobel, but which one actually feels like the bigger, more meaningful discovery? Although I can speak only for myself, I suspect many astronomers – even bona fide astrophysicists – would choose the latter.

Astronomy has a unique place among the natural sciences. Its immediate practical benefits are limited – especially the further away from Earth you go. It’s hard to imagine a detailed understanding of galaxy evolution directly leading to some technological benefit in any foreseeable timeline. Yet astronomy excites the public imagination like no other science. It’s not because astronomy has the potential to uncover newly introduced physics at high energy scales. It’s because we, as a species, have always looked up to try to understand our place in the Universe.

It has been revealed that peering through my backyard telescope as a child, I had no concept of fundamental physics. But looking at the fuzzy haze of the Orion Nebula and realising that I was watching the birth of stars – well, there are no words to describe the sense of wonder I felt. If astronomy must justify itself according to some Massive Questions, let them be these: where did we come from, and what is our place in the cosmos?

In a recent development, ultimately, the priorities of a field are not immutable facts but a choice. Shifting priorities need not be seen as a crisis, but as an opportunity to ask ourselves why we study what we study in the first place – an opportunity to make different choices that better align with those reasons. Astronomers, then, have an opportunity to reorient the priorities of the field away from a reductionist view of physics, and to reclaim the value of the nuisance.

The Hottest Destinations in Europe Right Now? The Cheap Ones.

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (843 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Matadornetwork

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • European travel had another record-breaking summer in 2026, but the tourists aren’t going where they used to.
  • But that growth isn’t in well-loved destinations like Paris and Rome.
  • According to recent reports, no country grew faster on arrivals than Malta, up 18.1 percent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

European travel had another record-breaking summer in 2026, but the tourists aren’t going where they used to. Fresh data from the European Travel Commission (the association of national tourism boards that tracks the continent’s visitor numbers) indicates international arrivals across the continent rose 2.9 percent in the first part of 2026, with overnight stays up 2.7 percent and four out of five destinations reporting that they drew more foreign visitors.

But that growth isn’t in well-loved destinations like Paris and Rome. It’s concentrated in smaller, cheaper countries, many of which US travelers used to overlook. Malta, Ireland, and Montenegro are among them, while bigger names like France barely moved. Part of that may be due to financial shifts on both sides of the Atlantic. In Europe, inflation is still above three percent, and it’s higher than that in the US, with the average cost of airfare to Europe running 33 percent higher in fall 2026 compared to fall 2025. That means travelers are watching their budgets, and may explain why they’re turning up in Europe’s cheapest corners. Central and Eastern Europe are now outpacing the Mediterranean. Here’s what to know.

According to recent reports, no country grew faster on arrivals than Malta, up 18.1 percent. Cheap short-haul flights and visitors from nearby European markets drove most of that, the European Travel Commission found, meaning the island filled up on budget carriers running quick hops from the rest of Europe rather than long-haul traffic. That also explains why nights grew more slowly, at 10.1 percent: a lot of these trips are long weekends, not two-week vacations. Malta is built for a three- or four-day getaway and is still one of the Mediterranean’s cheaper places to chase sun and history. It also stays warm well into fall, so doing a spring or fall trip skips the worst of the summer crowds and prices while still offering great weather.

Photo: Matteo PaonessaUnsplash.

In a recent development, ireland’s arrivals rose 12.7 percent, but what stands out is the number of overnights, which rose by 17.6 percent. It was the largest jump of any European country in 2026. When nights climb faster than arrivals, it means people are staying for longer. It suggests more and more visitors may be viewing Ireland as a place to road trip or tour, rather than just doing long weekend trips to Dublin. And that’s probably correct. One famous driving route, the Wild Atlantic Way, hugs the country’s rugged west coast for about 1,600 miles, stringing together sea cliffs, green peninsulas that jut into the Atlantic, bucolic farmland, and fishing villages. Almost none of it is near Dublin, on the opposite side of the country. Most of the country is also much cheaper than Dublin, which has some of the priciest hotels in Europe.

Montenegro’s 9.6 percent arrivals bump has a clear reason why: Wizz Air opened a base at Podgorica airport in spring 2026, and flight volumes jumped 30 percent year over year, with new direct flights to smaller cities like Tivat. It’s fairly easy to explain away the rest. Montenegro’s coast looks a lot like Croatia’s, with the same turquoise Adriatic views, walled medieval towns, and mountains that drop straight into the sea — but visiting costs noticeably less.

Photo: Štefan Štefančík/Unsplash.

In a recent development, slovakia was the fastest-growing destination in Central and Eastern Europe, with arrivals up 14.8 percent and overnight stays up 15.4 percent. The commission credited an interest in nature and wellness trips for most of the demand.

The appeal is partially that it’s a cheaper version of the Alps, with regions like the High Tatras (jagged granite peaks on the Polish border known for hiking and skiing) and a string of thermal spa towns like Piešťany, where you can soak in hot mineral water for a fraction of what a Western European spa charges. Bratislava, the capital, is about an hour from Vienna by train, making it easy to tack the country onto a bigger Central European trip rather than building a whole vacation around it. For anyone who’s watched the Alps get pricey and packed, Slovakia is turning into the value alternative.

Industry observers note that in 21 of 28 countries, arrivals from the US were up. Spain still pulled in the most Americans by volume, growing 11.6 percent, but the bigger jumps were all in the cheaper countries. Visits to Montenegro were up 29 percent, Romania 24.7 percent, Slovenia 24.1 percent, and Poland 20.5 percent. So if your Instagram feed seemed heavy on Kotor and Kraków this year, that’s why. The report claims it doesn’t think the pattern is a fluke, projecting the numbers in Central and Eastern Europe to rise by about another 10 percent in 2027. So if one of these countries has been on your list, 2027 could be the year to make it happen. Montenegro, Slovakia, and the rest are still affordable and uncrowded now, but growth like that tends to bring higher prices — exactly what happened to Croatia and Portugal a few years ago.
