💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you ever find yourself wandering the quiet, postcard-perfect alleyways of The Hague, keep your eyes peeled around streetlamp height.
  • This isn't a modern street performer or an overly ambitious late-night reveler—it’s De Lantaarnopsteker (The Lamplighter), a delightful bronze creation brought to life by Dutch sculptor Loek Bos in 2008.
  • Before automated electricity ruined all the fun, keeping a city lit required a dedicated fleet of lamplighters who spent their evenings dashing through the chill with long torches and ladders, lighting every gas lamp by hand—only to march back out at dawn to turn them all off.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you ever find yourself wandering the quiet, postcard-perfect alleyways of The Hague, keep your eyes peeled around streetlamp height. Tucked into the charming cobbled sanctuary of Mallemolen, you’ll spot a gentleman mid-climb on a lamp post, his coat tails flying out behind him as if caught in a sudden gust of wind.

This isn't a modern street performer or an overly ambitious late-night reveler—it’s De Lantaarnopsteker (The Lamplighter), a delightful bronze creation brought to life by Dutch sculptor Loek Bos in 2008.

Before automated electricity ruined all the fun, keeping a city lit required a dedicated fleet of lamplighters who spent their evenings dashing through the chill with long torches and ladders, lighting every gas lamp by hand—only to march back out at dawn to turn them all off. It was cold, repetitive, and exhausting work.

According to recent reports, yet, rather than depicting a weary worker slaving away in the dark, the artist gave us a moment of pure joy and acrobatics. The sculpture captures a sense of effortless agility, turning a mundane 19th-century chore into a graceful ballet on a light post. If you look closely at the glass lantern above his head, you’ll even spot a couple of bronze birds perched on top, quietly judging his technique.

It’s a wonderful, witty tribute to the invisible hands that kept the night at bay, tucked into one of the city's best-kept secret corners.

Paul McCartney is the writer behind classic songs including âYesterdayâ and âHey Jude,â so itâs no surprise that this wordsmith has a love for well-told stories.

Clearly, though, there was something about Dickensâ The Life and Adventures of Nicholas Nickleby that stood out. To support his mother and sister, he acquires a teaching position at a squalid boarding school, and is later exposed to a variety of characters and cruelties in London. The book is considered a satire that takes aim at societyâs treatment of children, corruption in the education system, and other social injustices.

McCartneyâs love of literature was heavily influenced by Alan Durband, a passionate, Cambridge-educated teacher who taught at the Liverpool Institute for High School Boys when McCartney was a student.Â Â.

âHe inspired my love of reading and opened things up for me so much that I came to live for a while in a fantasy world drawn from books,â McCartney wrote in his book The Lyrics: 1956 to the Present. Durband often emphasized the importance of small details in literature, an approach that can be seen reflected in McCartneyâs highly specific style of songwriting. He also exposed McCartney to Dickens and William Shakespeare, among other greats.

McCartney went on to incorporate literary references into much of his work. The lyric âand in the end the love you take / Is equal to the love you makeâ from the Beatles track âThe Endâ was inspired by the way Shakespeare often closes his scenes with couplets. In The Lyrics: 1956 to the Present, McCartney also cited Lewis Carroll and Edward Lear, both pioneers of the ânonsense writingâ tradition whose influence can be seen in Beatles tracks like âYellow Submarine.â He and Lennon bonded early on over their mutual love for the genre. âI like surrealist art, I also like surrealist words,â McCartney shared. âA great example of this is Lewis Carroll writing Alice in Wonderlandâitâs a crazy thing, youâve got a cat sitting in a tree that grins and talks, and youâve got Alice falling down a hole and meeting the red queen, and so on. That whole tradition was something that I loved, and when I met John, I learned that he loved it too. So, it was something that became a bond between us.â.

Recent findings suggest that over the years, McCartney has written a number of books himself. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that dedicating some counter space to a soda maker comes with several benefits. For one thing, these appliances are a great way to cut down on single-use plastic and other waste by eliminating the recycling bags full of bottles, cans, and cardboard boxes you inevitably accumulate with a regular La Croix habit. But they will also save you some money in the long run, as carbonating your own water costs less than buying premade fizz from the store. One standard-size CO2 canister, which should cost roughly $15, can carbonate around 60 liters of water. Considering the $3 cost of a 2-L bottle of Canada Dry, that comes out to around three times as much soda water per dollar.

Industry observers note that after years of testing soda makers, I’ve found models that make it quick and easy to make zingy, fizzy drinks (including juice, wine, and cocktails) with the push of a button. Find our top picks below and scroll further down to see what I thought of the machines that didn’t earn a top spot.

Newly introduced in this revision: For this update, I tested two sparkling water makers by Drinkmate: the previously discontinued (and now recontinued) Drinkmate Spritzer and the Drinkmate Lux, which in between testing and publishing was subsequently discontinued and replaced with the new Sparkleup, welp!

Drinkmate Omnifizz Sparkling Water and Soda Maker.

Amazon (With 60-L CO2 Tank and Extra Bottle).

Home Depot (With 60-L CO2 Tank).

Height: 16.14"Machine material(s): PlasticBottle material: PlasticComes with starter CO2 tank: Yes (size varies by retailer)Requires proprietary CO2 tank: NoWarranty: 2 years.

According to recent reports, over years of testing, nothing has surpassed the Drinkmate Omnifizz’s mix of versatility and affordability. It is, full stop, the most affordable sparkling water maker that can also do other “fun” carbonating, like wine, cocktails, tea, and (pulp-free) fruit juice.

In a recent development, what I love: The Omnifizz has a well-designed detachable siphon with fast and slow pressure release tabs. It carbonates fast, delivering maximum sharp fizz in around two seconds. This gives you more control when carbonating anything with a syrup or other sugars (wine or cocktails, for example), which fizz up a lot more than plain water. The siphon design also offers a much more secure connection than the machines that require you to pop and/or twist the bottle into the base, which diminishes the likelihood of an accidental soda explosion to the face (which happens to the best of us!).

Sources indicate that what I’d leave: In addition to being kind of meh in the looks department (especially in a world where so many brands have placed a focus on the aesthetics of their soda makers), this carbonator is made of all plastic parts, so it doesn’t feel as durable as some others I’ve tested. It also screams like a banshee when its done. Depending on the retailer you order from, it may or may not ship with a CO2 cylinder, so be sure to read the product descriptions carefully.

Height: 16.9"Machine material(s): Stainless steelBottle material: PlasticComes with starter CO2 tank: Only if you buy the bundleRequires proprietary CO2 tank: NoWarranty: 2 years.

Breville has cornered the market on high-end small kitchen appliances with its top-performing countertop oven, induction burner, toaster, and immersion blender. In 2024, the brand added a sparkling water maker to that list.

What I love: The Breville Infizz Fusion is a sleek, versatile carbonator, and like the Drinkmate Ominifizz, it will carbonate more than just water. The default setting on the carbonator cap is a slow pressure release that allows carbonation of fruit juice, wine, cocktails, and even creamy drinks if you’re feeling weird. You can manually release the pressure faster if you just need a bottle of fizzy water in a hurry. Unlike the soda makers I liked in the $100 to $150 range, which usually have all plastic parts, parts of the InFizz Fusion are made of durable, high-quality stainless steel, which is available in a variety of finishes, though options vary by retailer. It also comes with a handful of accessories (including a juice filter and silicone bottle brush) to enhance the experience of using and cleaning the machine and bottle.

What I’d leave: Compared to the Drinkmate, this machine is slightly more fussy to operate. Not by much, but I prefer the Drinkmate’s quick click to Breville’s twist-and-lock design. Countertop soda makers are simple gadgets, and this is one of the priciest ones you can buy. If it’s worth it to you to pay for quality materials, aesthetics, and the ability to wow your dinner guests by transforming a bottle of bad rosé into something bubbly and palatable, you’ll likely be very happy with this (FWIW the Drinkmate can also sparkle bad rosé, it just wont look as nice doing it). But do keep in mind that the base model, which is $249 at the time of publishing, doesn’t ship with a CO2 tank, so you’ll either need to buy one or spend $30 more on one that comes with the tank.

Drinkmate Spritzer Portable Sparkling Water.

Height: 7"Machine material(s): PlasticBottle material: PlasticComes with starter CO2 tank: Only if you buy the bundleRequires proprietary CO2 tank: NoWarranty: 2 years.

Recent findings suggest that what I love: When I first tested the Spritzer several years ago, it was my top pick. But then Drinkmate discontinued it, which was sad, but now, it’s back. At this point I can’t give it the absolute top spot (I’ll get into that down below), but in a more niche position of portable carbonator, I still recommend it.

Beyond that, the Spritzer takes up less space and is easy to stow away, and it is also cheaper than the countertop version.

Recent findings suggest that what I’d leave: The Spritzer is designed to use smaller 10-L gas canisters rather than the standard 60-L size. Unless you source them directly from Drinkmate, the 10-L canisters are difficult to find, so you end up being reliant on its exchange program. The Spritzer will still work with a full size canister, but I wouldn’t recommend doing that because it doesn’t fit well in the carbonator and gets a bit unwieldy. Drinkmate also originally had a docking station for it the Spritzer, but unfortunately the brand got rid of it. Ultimately, the reason I don’t give this the top spot is that its design is such a departure from what most people expect in a soda maker it has a much narrower appeal.

According to recent reports, with every update I look at the most popular and highly rated countertop sparkling water makers, taking into consideration availability, price, and customer ratings. Then, I judge them on the following:.

I first assess how easy it is to use and assemble each machine. Looks matter too, but they aren’t everything. And if a machine can carbonate more than just water (what's up Drinkmate and Breville), that’s a huge plus as well.

Sources indicate that I used each machine several times to get a general sense of how long the machine takes to carbonate and the fizz level of each batch. For the first few rounds I follow the manufacturer’s instructions. After that I try pushing the machine to its maximum capability (usually until I hear the hissing of excess gas escaping). If the machine can carbonate more than just water, I’ll do a few rounds with juice and wine.

Mysoda Woody Sparkling Water Maker.

Sources indicate that this simple, stylish carbonator from Finnish brand Mysoda is made from renewable wood composite. It’s beautiful, sturdy, and, when it comes to the level of carbonation, performs as well as any SodaStream. And if you want an aesthetically pleasing, sustainably made, budget-friendly soda maker, you’ll be very happy with this purchase. But there’s a catch to that: Most soda makers ship with a starter CO2 tank, and this one doesn’t. New tanks, not tank trade-ins, cost $30 to $40. So when you factor that into the cost, the initial investment is more than the cost of our top pick, which did perform a little better anyway. If you want to stay under $100 all in, check out the Philips Sparkling Water Maker below.

Mysoda Glassy Sparkling Water Maker.

It has been revealed that this Mysoda distinguishes itself from the others with a glass carafe. Anytime I encounter a soda maker that carbonates in glass, I'm suspicious, because I haven’t seen them work well in the past. This might be because soda makers that carbonate in glass tend to be designed with additional safeguards to minimize the possibility of the bottle exploding, and those safeguards are usually fussy. Often they take the form of some sort of cover that goes over the entire bottle during the carbonation process. In the case of the Glassy, the bottle is covered by a curved sliding door that you shut by hand, reminiscent of a changing room curtain or a shower stall.

To use the machine, you place the bottle inside and twist it onto the gas nozzle to lock it in place. Then you shut the door and press the top of the machine toward the front to inject the gas (the top is mostly one large button). After a couple of pumps, you’ll hear a hissing sound, which signals that it’s ready. You then press the top toward the back of the machine, which causes the door to fly open, presenting your carbonated water like a magician’s assistant doing a quick change magic trick. It’s all very dramatic, which is kind of fun.

In a recent development, as far as soda makers that carbonate in glass, this is the best I’ve tried. That said, I'm not sure how notable it is to be able to carbonate in glass, especially with the risk (however small) that it will explode into shards with you close by. You can always just carbonate in a plastic bottle and pour it into a glass vessel for serving.

Check out our full review of the Glassy here.

The Philips Sparkling Water Maker is a handsome machine with a comparatively accessible price tag, and it’s easy to set up and operate with one button. More importantly, during testing, it made pleasantly sharp carbonated water. Like the Mysoda Woody above, it doesn’t ship with CO2, so you’ll still need to shell out for a standard screw-in 60-L CO2 tank. However, at the current retail price, even with the addition of a tank, it still comes in at just under $100.

Industry observers note that the Aerflo is even easier to tae on the go than the Drinkmate Spritzer. There is a carbonator mechanism inside the lid, which you activate by pressing a button on the top. Instead of full-size CO2 canisters used for most sparkling water makers, it utilizes smaller capsules typically used for airsoft or BB guns. Because of the capsules small size, you will need to swap them much more frequently; one capsule has enough CO2 for about one day’s worth of sparkling water. It’s cool and convenient if you really prefer carbonated water over still. But this is a product for a smaller subset of people than a countertop soda maker. If it appeals to you though, go for it.

Check out my full review of the Aerflo here.

Industry observers note that this is the model that came after the now-discontinued Aarke Carbonator II, and the main upgrades are materials. The Aarke Carbonator III has more stainless steel and fewer plastic parts than the II. Both models are highly aesthetic machines that are easy enough to use and make perfectly fine sparkling water. If you like the look of it, you’ll probably be very happy with it, but the Breville is in the same general price range and is more versatile. Plus, there are lower-priced machines that perform just as well.

It has been revealed that awa appears to be selling itself entirely based on aesthetics. Once you move beyond the body design though, this is a standard sparkling water maker with a single button for injecting CO2. It lacks a tilting nozzle or a slide-in lock, which makes it more annoying to use than the winning models. The build is also almost entirely plastic, save for a few metal details, which doesn’t really justify the premium price point. If you like how it looks, it will get the job done, but it’s not innovating on the form.

Fizzit Sparkli Carbonated Soda Maker.

A frequent complaint people have about sparkling water makers is their reliance on plastic bottles, as many consumers are looking to avoid plastic entirely. The Fizzit is one of the few soda makers that uses metal bottles instead. Apart from that, its design and performance are similar to the other soda makers sharing the same standard design on the market. Were this the only machine on the market to carbonate directly into stainless steel, maybe that would be something, but Sodastream also offers stainless-steel carbonator bottles, and I imagine more brands will follow suit. Also sorry to Spärklï, but the branding on this machine is a bit of an eyesore. If you’re looking for a machine that comes with metal bottles and aren’t a fan of Sodastream though, this might be for you.

The Fritaire carbonator flipped the conventional soda maker design on its head. It’s the only soda maker I’ve tested so far that carbonates from the bottom up, with a fold-up gas nozzle that makes for a slightly more compact machine. The bottle is also different, with mechanical components built in at the bottom, and a wide curved carafe-style lip. Unfortunately I could not get this to produce a satisfyingly sharp bottle of seltzer, no matter how much gas I pumped into the bottle. Where other machines make a clear sound when the pressure has been maxed out, the Fritaire’s was not obvious. The instructions recommend pressing the button for three seconds until you “hear the sound of pressure building.” Each time I tried, the water came out under-carbonated. On top of that, the lid for the bottle dribbled water even when tightly screwed on. I really tried to give this machine the benefit of the doubt, testing and retesting to try and get it not to leak on me and to get a proper fizz, but each time I encountered the same problems no matter what I did.

Smeg is known for its retro-futurist luxury kitchen products that really sell for their looks. This machine worked fine. You twist the metal dial clockwise to carbonate, a clever hidden feature that sets it apart from other carbonators, but it lacks the ability to tilt the nozzle, which makes screwing on the bottle more tedious. For a soda maker made almost entirely out of plastic, the price point is well beyond what it’s worth, but if you’re a Smeg collector, this is another piece to add to your collection.

According to recent reports, one of the few new electric sparkling water systems, the Carbon8 is quite different from other machines on the market. Instead of directly carbonating into the bottle, the Carbon8 has a refillable reservoir (much like a drip coffee maker) that instead, dispenses carbonated water straight into your glass. It has added flourishes, like a sanitizing UV light and a filter that remineralizes water while removing chlorine.

The brand implies superior eco-friendliness in their website copy because they don’t carbonate directly into a reusable PET plastic bottle; however, the reservoir and other parts of the machine are made of plastic, so I’m not sure they have much plastic-free ground to stand on. You could argue that since the plastic bottles of typical soda makers have to be replaced every couple of years, this system produces less plastic waste, but it’s a marginal difference in my opinion.

Industry observers note that as a premium machine this Carbon8 worked fine, but had one shortcoming: There seems to be no way to control the carbonation level of the machine, and when I tasted the finished product, I found the level of carbonation to be far less than what you’d expect from store-bought seltzer, or what you can produce with the winning machines. If the Carbon8 gave you control over how fizzy you wanted your water, it would make this a much better machine.

Industry observers note that ninja is among the most prolific small appliance manufacturers with coffee makers, countertop ovens, blenders, ice cream makers, juicers, toasters, air fryers—the list goes on and on and on. So it should come as no surprise that the brand is now in the soda maker business too. Like many of Ninja’s other offerings, the Ninja Thirsti is a bit gimmicky while still being kind of cool. Out of the box, this electric soda maker (yes, you have to plug it in) reminded us of a Nespresso machine. The water tank sits off to the side and the carbonation happens inside the machine before coming out of a little spout. There’s an opening on the front to add up to two proprietary flavoring cartridges, which you can put in your bubbly water individually or combine them both. Right now there are 30 flavors available and the machine shipped with four of them. The control panel on the front of the machine allows you to choose between still water or three levels of carbonation, and four drink sizes (6, 12, 18, or 24 oz.). After testing, I have mixed feelings about this machine. Overall, it seems like a bit much for something to have at home. It could maybe be a great addition to a teachers’ lounge or a small office. But keep in mind that the water tank does require chilled, cold water so you’d also need a fridge or ice nearby whenever you want to use it.

Glacier Fresh Sparkin Cold Soda Maker.

According to recent reports, if you’ve ever dreamed of having a club soda tap in your kitchen, this is probably as close as you’re going to get without cutting into your countertops. Like the Ninja above, the Glacier Fresh Sparkin Cold Soda Maker carbonates water in the machine, not in a bottle. Unlike the Ninja, the machine chills the water for you (though the manual still recommends filling the reservoir on the back of the machine with cold water). Once it’s filled, getting your bubbly water from the “tap” is a three-step process. First, you push a button to send water from the reservoir to the bubbling (and presumably chilling) chamber, then you push down on a lever to carbonate it. Once it’s sufficiently bubbly, you press another little lever on the front to dispense the water into a glass. It’s less complicated than it sounds, but with an 88-square-inch footprint, most people will be better off with a bottle-style carbonator. I will also note that when moved from the counter to a nearby table with the CO2 canister in place and some water still in the chamber (ill-advised, perhaps), it began to make a weird squealing noise.

Industry observers note that the SodaStream Art is marketed as the manufacturer’s premium carbonator, because of its retro-inspired body. Though it produces the exact same carbonated water as other SodaStream models, it operates a little differently: Instead of pushing a button to carbonate, you pull the lever and you can pull it up to six times for the bubbliest water. But it’s made of lightweight plastic that feels cheap. If you want something that looks good on the countertop, there are prettier options that are also sturdier.

Industry observers note that aarke carbonators are really easy on the eyes, and this “pro” version doesn’t skimp on materials. Instead of the typical plastic bottles, this one uses glass, and the top of the machine (which is available in a matte black, matte sand, or shiny stainless-steel finish) covers the top of the bottle in case you were to over-carbonate and cause the glass to explode. Unfortunately, it’s not very user-friendly. I had challenges getting everything to lock into place and ended up with an explosion—though, luckily, it was only water and not glass. I eventually got it to work, but for the price, it should be easier to operate.

Recent findings suggest that I loved the sleek design of this soda maker in pictures, but in person, the materials felt cheap and flimsy. Also, because it’s so sleek and slim, the water bottles are really tall and didn’t fit into any shelves in a standard sized fridge.

Instead of using a CO2 tank to produce carbon dioxide, this machine uses citric acid and baking soda. The mechanism is just way more high maintenance compared to the machines that utilize a gas canister, and I struggle to see why this method is in any way better than the industry standard.

Currently, the Terra is SodaStream’s most basic offering, and functionally, it’s a lot like the original SodaStream, the Fizzi. However, instead of a screw-in CO2 cartridge, this machine uses the brand’s Quick Connect cartridges, which click in. Because the Quick Connect feature is proprietary, using this machine means being married to Soda Stream’s cylinder exchange program. With products like the Mysoda Woody or the Philips Sparkling Water Maker, you can and should get something with a universal connection.

This style of carbonator is a relic of the 19th century, and while it has an abundance of charm, it’s more tedious, fussy, and impractical than its modern counterparts. It relies on small, single-use CO2 cartridges—which negates the whole eco-friendly argument for carbonating at home rather buying seltzer from the store— and you have to use two cartridges per liter if you like your seltzer extra sharp. Frankly, the only people I’d recommend this to would be that husband and wife on TLC who pretend they’re living in the 1950s.

There is nothing inherently wrong with the E-Duo. Of the carbonators that use glass bottles, it is the easiest to use. It does require a few additional steps to lock the bottle safely into place (just in case that glass bottle explodes!), but I didn’t find the safety mechanisms to be overly fussy. However, as with the Ninja, this soda maker requires electricity. With so many excellent soda makers that function effectively without electricity, I don’t really see the need to use one that does.

Latest Update: Cozy Up and Count Stars in the Canadian Rockies This Winter

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when the sun sets behind the Canadian Rockies in Jasper National Park, Alberta, the soaring peaks and deep valleys plunge into a peaceful stillness defined by crisp air, inky skies, and the shimmer of thousands of stars. Your evening in this small mountain town is just beginning.

Industry observers note that you’ve spent the day chasing powder turns at Marmot Basin ski area, and the indigo glow in the western sky signals it’s time for aprés-ski bevvies at a downtown lounge. Later, you’ll join a stargazing tour to search for celestial landmarks before sliding between Egyptian cotton sheets at your lakeside resort, the Fairmont Jasper Park Lodge.

According to recent reports, night-sky tourism is trending, and Jasper is the ideal destination to explore after dark, thanks to its designation as Canada’s largest accessible Dark Sky Preserve. Beyond the chance to see other galaxies or the rings of Saturn through a telescope, Jasper has perfected the hours between dusk and dawn with fireside moments and wood-fired saunas, craft cocktails and mountain cuisine. Here’s how to stay warm, nourished, and inspired after night falls.

Photo: Fairmont Jasper Park Lodge.

Sources indicate that few spots in Jasper are as welcoming as the town’s original resort, where wood smoke curls into the night sky from the chimneys of cabins and suites clustered around Lac Beauvert. In winter, the Fairmont Jasper Park Lodge embraces the Nordic concept of hygge — unplugging and being snug — with simple pleasures found around the resort.

After time outdoors, whether ice skating or snowshoeing, let the lakeside barrel sauna melt away the day’s exertions, then dunk in frigid Lac Beauvert for a Canadian twist on a cold plunge. Indoors at the spa, cocoon beneath heated stones during a massage, or simply exhale into the eucalyptus steam room’s enveloping air.

The lodge’s true hygge havens, though, are its newly renovated rooms, suites, and cabins. With warming amenities and decor touches like plush robes and slippers, comfy sofas facing the fireplace, and soft throw blankets to cuddle up in, you won’t want the night to end.

Industry observers note that lume. Photos: Fairmont Jasper Park Lodge.

In a recent development, A big day on the slopes calls for a round of Mountain Caesars — Canada’s answer to the Bloody Mary — at Lume, the mountain-view bar at Fairmont Jasper Park Lodge. Swap stories about the day’s adventures at the sleek wraparound bar with unimpeded views of mountain silhouettes, and share canapés on a cozy sofa.

Pair your Caesar with a charcuterie board layered with local artisan meats and cheeses, or indulge in some elevated appetizers like elk meatballs with tzatziki and smoked mint chimichurri. For family bonding time before dinner, pick up a deck of cards or a board game from the health club and let the fun begin.

According to recent reports, the Barbicon. Photos: Fairmont Jasper Park Lodge.

Dining at the Fairmont Jasper Park Lodge is an elegant affair, with roaring fireplaces and wood accents for ambiance. The food is equally elevated. Executive chef François Lecouvez marries local ingredients with his culinary roots to create mountain cuisine with a French flair that brings people together around the table.

It has been revealed that this fusion of Alberta beef with French sides and sauces is on full display at The Barbicon, the lodge’s fresh steakhouse, where the dining room centers on the lodge’s original 1922 Tyndall stone fireplace. Order your striploin or beef tenderloin as the chef recommends, and pair it with béarnaise sauce and a side of velvety French-style mashed potatoes.

Find family favorites like burgers and flatbread pizzas at Elderwood, a nature-inspired restaurant with earth-toned banquettes and vaulted ceilings that evoke a timber-framed lodge. Even the craft cocktails seem to toast the fading light with names like Afterglow and The Lantern.

In a recent development, the Maligne Range. Photo: Tourism Jasper.

Recent findings suggest that for a night on the town, Jasper packs in welcoming pubs and restaurants along Connaught Drive, the main drag that parallels the train tracks. At the townsite’s north end, Evil Dave’s Grill serves comfort food with Western influences — think bison and wild boar meatloaf, and cowboy sushi with grilled meat instead of raw fish.

In a recent development, newcomer The Maligne Range is a distillery and restaurant in one. Whisky tastings feature house-made barrel-aged products, plus whiskies, ryes, and bourbon-inspired spirits from across Canada. Pair the Maple Smoked Old Fashioned with the restaurant’s signature Alberta beef brisket that’s smoked on site.

Just down the road, the Jasper Brewing Company pours sessionable après-ski beers including hazy IPAs, refreshing pilsners, and malty ales. If you find yourself lingering a while, they’ve got you covered with late-night classics like chicken wings, poutine, and nachos.

Photo: Jeff Bartlett/Tourism Jasper.

In a recent development, as the night winds down, don’t forget to look up — there are numerous ways to stargaze in Jasper National Park. With limited artificial light, you can see thousands of stars and the arm of the Milky Way on clear moonless nights.

Sources indicate that on site at the Fairmont Jasper Park Lodge, the Jasper Planetarium provides a fun introduction to the night sky. The immersive show teaches why darkness matters to plants and animals and shares Indigenous star stories. Planetarium manager Tyler Burgardt recommends that northern lights chasers drive to nearby Pyramid Lake or Medicine Lake, or as far as Maligne Lake, where the wide open sky above the water gives you a dazzling view of the heavens.

In a recent development, for a deeper dive into the world of astronomy, dress for the weather and join a guided stargazing tour with Jasper Star Trails. On the shore of Lake Annette, you’ll learn to recognize iconic star patterns such as Orion’s Belt and the Massive Dipper, see guiding stars like Polaris (the North Star), and spot planets through a telescope.

Industry observers note that with an average of 15 hours of daily darkness in Jasper between November and March, it’s no wonder there are so many ways to welcome the day’s end with family and friends. Start planning your visit to cozy up and count stars in Canada’s best dark-sky destination.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that will Ferguson: If you drive east from Calgary, instead of going towards Banff and the mountains, if you go the other way, the landscape will suddenly fall away and you’ll find yourself in the Badlands. But before you hit that valley, before you make that descent, if you turn off the main road, you will come to a small hidden valley full of wild roses.

Industry observers note that in that little valley, you will find a small and improbable town—a town that should not exist. It’s at the very edge of these rolling canola fields, roses, a little valley. And it certainly should not be a major theater hub by any stretch of the imagination, but it is. And Rosebud is a town that kind of defies logic.

Industry observers note that kelly McEvers: I’m Kelly McEvers, and this is Atlas Obscura, a celebration of the world’s strange, incredible, and wondrous places. This episode was produced in partnership with Travel Alberta. Explore Canada’s Wild Side.

Recent findings suggest that this month, we’re talking to writers and artists who find inspiration in their home province of Alberta. Today, we’re talking to travel writer and novelist Will Ferguson. He’s lived in South America and Japan, where he taught English for five years. But his work is inspired by his home country.

It has been revealed that will has published over 20 books. Many of them cover Canadian identity and history. And today, he is taking us on a tour of the province of Alberta to tell us about the places that have inspired his work. from that improbable town he was just describing, to a Japanese garden, to a town that tells the story behind a 12 foot statue of a fur trader. Will Ferguson, welcome to the show!

According to recent reports, this is an edited transcript of the Atlas Obscura Podcast: a celebration of the world’s strange, incredible, and wondrous places. Find the show on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and all major podcast apps.

It has been revealed that kelly: For this conversation, of course, we asked you to tell us about three defining places for you in Alberta, places that have influenced your work. And before we get to those, I just want to talk a little bit about your upbringing there, if you don’t mind. Let’s just talk about growing up in Alberta. Where’s your family from? What was it like there?

Will: Well, I grew up in northern Alberta in a town, the teeming metropolis of Fort Vermilion, population 749, I believe.

Will: So I grew up there. That town is closer to the Arctic Circle than the American border, just by a nutshell. And I don’t know why we were proud of that. That was like a real point of pride that we were like just past the halfway point. So I always feel growing up there that I kind of emigrated to Canada. The weirdest thing is Canada, as we knew it from the radio signals and the television signals, was a southern country.

Industry observers note that so for me, Canada was to the south. That’s how I thought of it, as a southern country with shopping malls and paved roads and traffic lights.

Kelly: Wow. That is so interesting. What an interesting way to grow up, to think of yourself from this northern land that was somehow separate from the country that you were actually in.

Visitors sometimes think that he’s like a Paul Bunyan statue, character, that type of character. But no, he was real. He wasn’t 12 feet tall, of course.

Sources indicate that his name was Henry Davis. And the name, how he got the name was during the Caribou Gold Rush in the 1860s up in northern Canada and BC. And he arrived too late. All the good land had been staked. But he noticed that in the rush to stake these gold claims, people were a little bit sloppy.

You’re only allowed so much space, like so many feet for a claim. And he walked through it and measured and measured, and he realized that two miners had overstaked their claim by six feet each. They’d done the math wrong, but they’d each over-claimed by six feet. So he staked a claim on 12 feet on this narrow strip of land, and he reaped a fortune in gold on those 12 feet. He made what in today would be over $200,000. So from that’s where the name 12-foot Davis, he made his fortune on this thin strip of land because he thought to check.

And he used that money and he came to the Peace River to become a fur trader. He set up his own very successful fur trading, independent fur trading fort. And he was, you know, he’s very popular in the area and friendly by all accounts.

In a recent development, it’s always mentioned that he always left the door of his cabin open, which I think explains why he was robbed so often. But I’m kidding. No, he wasn’t robbed. But he did leave his cabin door open. So the idea is that if it’s windy or cold, you could always go in.

Recent findings suggest that he was what’s called a free trader. So he wasn’t aligned with the major companies, the Northwest Company or the Hudson’s Bay Company. So for almost 40 years, he clashed and rankled and fought with the Hudson’s Bay Company, which wanted and claimed a monopoly on the fur trade.

According to recent reports, so when he died, he asked to be buried. The statue is in the town, but his grave is up the hill. And he asked, and it’s a beautiful view. You get this kind of epic panorama of the Peace River and the Smoky River. It’s a very striking area. And he asked to be buried on the hill, looking down on the valley. Now, in the north, where we grew up, it was known that the reason he asked to be buried there was so that he could piss on the Hudson’s Bay Firm below.

Sources indicate that but the official reason, the official story was that you read in the tourist books is that he wanted to be buried there so that he could gaze out one last time upon the landscape that inspired and moved his heart. So again, whichever story you decide to take, it’s still 12-foot Davis country. Like it belongs to the short, stocky, very astute fur trader.

Equality talk

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4712 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Aeon

⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s no accident that equality comes first among the ‘self-evident’ truths articulated in the United States Declaration of Independence.
  • According to recent reports, yet today, it’s evident that the word ‘equality’ means very different things to different people.
  • Industry observers note that let’s begin by examining a group of people that generally prides itself on thinking (and speaking) more clearly than most: professional philosophers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s no accident that equality comes first among the ‘self-evident’ truths articulated in the United States Declaration of Independence. The claim that ‘all men are created equal’ serves there not simply as an abstract premise from which revolutionary consequences ought to follow, but as a concrete practical foundation on which the American colonists could claim to stand as equals with the greatest king and hold him to account. Still impressed by his own handiwork 50 years later, Thomas Jefferson even prophesied that the ‘palpable truth’ of equality enshrined in the Declaration would one day unite all of humankind.

According to recent reports, yet today, it’s evident that the word ‘equality’ means very different things to different people. What once seemed capable of providing common ground is now just another source of controversy. What explains this shift? I suspect that the deceptively simple, conceptual language of ‘equality’ has itself played a substantial role. A better understanding of ‘equality talk’ – as the application of this language to human beings and their relations – might therefore shed some light on our predicament.

Industry observers note that let’s begin by examining a group of people that generally prides itself on thinking (and speaking) more clearly than most: professional philosophers. What are they doing when they talk about equality?

It has been revealed that often, they’re saying something about human beings: about what we’re fundamentally like, and how we should be treated morally, politically and socially. When an academic philosopher claims that ‘all people are equal’, she’s generally saying that, despite differences of race and gender, economic class or individual merit, every person is somehow the same in some fundamental respect(s). While some philosophers will stress the human capacity for reason and moral agency, others emphasise our mutual vulnerability to suffering and violent death. Still, all generally agree that this sameness – whatever its underlying basis – ought to matter for our social and political arrangements, such that any persistent inequalities between human beings must require some justification or redress.

But here, a non-philosopher might wonder why the professionals insist on using the technical language of ‘equality’ as opposed to something more straightforward like ‘sameness’? One reason, I think, is that they are trading on the former concept’s mathematical resonances of quantitative precision and transcendent truth. Those resonances, in turn, make the problem of inequality seem relatively tractable – as something the existence of which can be measured, hence agreed upon. While other political values, like liberty, resist reduction to a common measure, the quantitative logic of equality thus promises an objective standard against which social progress can be judged.

In a recent development, the distinctly mathematical aspect of modern ‘equality talk’ isn’t upcoming. Consider the Declaration’s language of ‘self-evidence’. This was an allusion to Euclid’s Elements (c300 BCE), in which the transitive property of equality – ‘things that are equal to the same thing are also equal to one another’ – comes first among the so-called axiomata, or ‘worthy notions’. The truth of these geometric propositions could, in turn, be accepted without proof, and so serve as a shared starting point from which to reason to less-obvious conclusions.

If like cases are to be treated alike as a matter of logic, then ‘equals’ ought to be treated ‘equally’ as a matter of politics.

Two hundred years after the Declaration, we likewise find the philosopher Ronald Dworkin in Taking Rights Seriously (1977) describing the right of all persons to equality as ‘axiomatic’, and thereby taking the basic equality of human beings off the table as a topic of political controversy. Let metaphysicians and theologians quarrel about its basis, then, or whether nonhuman animals or artificial intelligence ought to count equally as moral persons. Political philosophers could get on with the altogether more vital business of determining what this equality implied for our social, political and economic relations. Much like Jefferson, Dworkin would also later lend his axiom world-historical significance, as providing ‘a kind of plateau in political argument’ characteristic of modernity. By this, Dworkin meant that most contemporary political ideologies – from liberalism to utilitarianism, and libertarianism to communism – must begin from a shared premise, that all ‘members of the community matter, and matter equally’. And so, whatever their differences, political opponents ought to recognise themselves as building upon a common foundation.

According to recent reports, today, Dworkin’s historical optimism about equality as a universal premise seems harder to sustain. Nevertheless, his ‘egalitarian plateau’ image remains popular among academic philosophers, for whom basic equality has come to mark an indelible ‘divide in moral thinking between (1) a premodern world in which nobles [were] regarded as having greater worth than peasants … and (2) a modern world that repudiates these crude prejudices.’ Moreover, if like cases are to be treated alike as a matter of logic, then surely ‘equals’ ought to be treated ‘equally’ as a matter of politics, too – for instance, by distributing to each the same amount of welfare, rights or resources. Dworkin’s Oxford colleague, the analytic Marxist G A Cohen, could thus simply ‘take for granted that there is something which justice requires people to have equal amounts of.’ The only question remaining was that posed by Amartya Sen: ‘Equality of what?’ (My emphasis.).

And yet, the idea that unequal treatment might sometimes be required to respect a person’s basic equality was also intuitive to many late-20th-century liberals, who supported policies like affirmative action. Dworkin himself framed this intuition influentially in terms of a distinction between treating people ‘equally’ – by applying the same standards or distributing the same amount to everyone – and treating them ‘as equals’, in a way responsive to their differences. This insight may, at first, sound similar to the much older, Marxist principle, ‘From each according to his ability, to each according to his needs.’ But as the historian Darrin McMahon observed in Equality (2023), Marx and Engels were themselves consistently critical of equality, dismissing it as a just another ‘popular prejudice’ to be dispelled by the coming communist revolution.

It has been revealed that in any case, it is Dworkin’s distinction, not Marx’s, that has since become central to contemporary theories of social or ‘relational’ egalitarianism, especially those associated with the philosopher Elizabeth Anderson. On this view, the point of equality is not to ensure a quantitatively identical distribution of stuff, whether of rights or resources, but rather the realisation of a just society in which every person can stand as an equal, without any hierarchical relations of inferiority or superiority. But the devil, as ever, is in the details, with relational egalitarians saying surprisingly little in positive terms about what relating as ‘equals’ actually looks like – and, specifically, when and what forms of unequal treatment might be involved.

Courtesy the Interaction Institute for Social Change/Angus Maguire.

One encounters a similar difficulty in recent debates pitting ‘equity’ against ‘equality’ as an approach to social justice. Proponents of the former insist that, unlike the latter, equity rejects a one-size-fits-all approach by taking certain differences – for instance, of race, disability or socioeconomic circumstances – into account. When pressed, however, equity’s defenders also tend to define ‘equitable’ treatment in strikingly Dworkinian terms, for instance as placing the disadvantaged on an ‘equal footing’ with the privileged. The result has been an odd convergence between equity’s progressive proponents and their conservative critics, with each presenting their preferred approach as the truly egalitarian one, with one side insisting that equal standing requires unequal treatment, and the other that, in a society of equals, the same rules ought to apply equally to everyone.

No wonder, then, that equality talk can feel so disorienting! Even among philosophers, it consistently promises more than it delivers. For some, equality means that we are the same in all the ways that matter, hence the same standards must apply; for others, it means that we are all different in ways deserving of respect. Even Dworkin’s supposedly clarifying formula of treating people ‘as equals’ reduces, under scrutiny, to the suggestion that we ought to treat people unequally when it is appropriate to their particular circumstances. If this is all equality demands, a hereditary aristocrat would find little to disagree with.

It has been revealed that here, however, a historian like McMahon might reassure us that the meaning of equality has always been ‘elusive’. In French, for instance, to say ça m’est égal can mean ‘it’s all the same to me’, yes, but it can also mean that our differences don’t matter, they’re matters of indifference. The varieties of English ‘equality talk’ can be more confusing still. When it was first published more than 250 years ago, Samuel Johnson’s A Dictionary of the English Language (1755) offered no fewer than eight definitions for the adjective ‘equal’, including ‘indifferent’, ‘like another in bulk, [or] excellence’, and ‘adequate to any purpose’.

It has been revealed that still, amid this multiplicity, one finds equality talk doing something distinctive in early modern English. Specifically, the adjective ‘equal’ – deriving originally from the Latin aequalis – consistently presented English speakers with a learned and socially elevated alternative to a more common Anglo-Saxon term, ‘alike’ (cognate with the German gleich). Whereas we today understand equality primarily in mathematical terms, however, to early modern English ears it meant something more like evenness, in the sense of being on a level or balanced, with neither side higher nor lower than the other.

Unlike sameness, equality was the absence of difference where one would normally expect to find it.

Consider the 14th-century Wycliffe Bible, which presented St Paul’s counsels of charity to the Corinthians as follows: ‘but of evenness [aequalitas] in the present time your abundance fulfil the need of them, that also the abundance of them be a fulfilling of your need, that evenness be made.’ Rich and poor were thus to be made ‘equal’ in this passage not by possessing identical amounts of wealth at any given moment, but by counter-balancing their holdings over time through reciprocal giving. One person’s abundance must meet another’s need in expectation of a future reversal. Here, the historical sense of equality-as-evenness clearly recalls the process of ‘levelling’ the scales or balances used by ancient merchants to weigh precious metals and trade goods in the marketplace. (Indeed, the English word ‘level’ derives originally from the Latin libra, meaning scale.).

Recent findings suggest that if we turn directly to the ancient Hellenic world, we find the same practical association between the concept of equality and the activity of balancing. This association may explain, in turn, why Greek mathematicians like Euclid took so much trouble to distinguish the idea of ‘equality’ (isotes) from other conceptual relations like ‘sameness’ and ‘similarity’ in their works. In the Metaphysics, Aristotle also distinguished equality by defining it in exclusively negative terms: ‘The equal, then, is that which is neither great nor small, but would naturally be either great or small.’ In other words, there was something exceptional about equality. Unlike sameness, it was the absence of difference where one would normally expect to find it.

This definition can, I think, help us make better sense of Aristotle’s celebrated observation in the Politics, that ‘justice is a kind of equality’, as well as his assertion that there were at least two competing definitions of equality in play in contemporary politics. Elsewhere, he would define these as ‘arithmetic’ and ‘geometric’ equality, respectively: the former distributing numerically identical shares to the parties despite their differences, for instance of wealth or virtue, and the latter assigning different amounts to each in direct proportion with their differences. In the Politics, then, these two kinds of equality re-appear as competing strategies for balancing political power between citizens, specifically between the poor many and the rich few. While democrats favoured the former principle – claiming that every adult male citizen should be assigned strictly equal political weight, like coins of equal value – oligarchs insisted that citizens should be weighed instead, like metals in the marketplace, with political power then distributed to each in proportion with his unequal wealth or virtue. In ancient Greece, the election of political officeholders by their fellow citizens was thus regarded as an oligarchic procedure, in contrast with the properly democratic alternative of sortition, or selection by lot, which afforded each a strictly equal (random) chance of exercising power.

In a recent development, notice, however, that, despite their differences, ancient democrats and oligarchs could alike embrace ‘equality’ as a political ideal without also committing to the view that every citizen, let alone every human being, must be somehow ‘equal’ as well. Even in the most economically inclusive and participatory polity in the ancient world, namely democratic Athens, Athenian democrats regarded certain people – namely native-born adult male citizens – as worthier and weightier than other ones – be they women, children, slaves or ‘barbarians’, or even other Greeks, including resident aliens like Aristotle. The point of equality then, even in Athens, was to ensure that no unequal part or person could over-balance the polity by outweighing or dominating the rest.

In a recent development, so far, my historical survey would appear to vindicate Dworkin’s ‘egalitarian plateau’ idea. While the ancient Greeks undoubtedly possessed sophisticated ideas about political equality, they also clearly believed in the basic inequality of human beings. Surely, then, modern egalitarianism must mark a radical break with this irredeemably hierarchical past?

Industry observers note that not so fast. Because elsewhere in the ancient world one finds statements remarkably similar to Dworkin’s ‘axiom’ of basic human equality – namely, in the Roman Empire. Consider the following extract from Ulpian, an imperial jurist of the early 3rd century CE, preserved in Justinian’s Digest: ‘As far as concerns the civil law, slaves are regarded as nothing; but as far as concerns the natural law, all humans are equal (aequales).’.

Recent findings suggest that here, we find what many philosophers today regard as a characteristically modern claim: that all humans (even slaves) are naturally equal. But, in context, Ulpian clearly meant something different. He was not saying that all people ought to be treated as equals, legally or politically, let alone that they must be afforded the same rights or resources. Ulpian’s point, rather, was that even enslaved people were equally subject to something he called ‘natural’ law, which applied to every human being without exception.

In the Hebrew Bible, the conceptual language of equality is conspicuously absent.

Sources indicate that for Ulpian, then, it seems that the ‘equality’ of human beings meant something more like indifference. Indeed, much like a modern French speaker declaring ça m’est égal, the law of nature took no notice of the extreme differences of power, wealth or status otherwise governing life within the Roman Empire. In other words, and much like the sun or rain or death, it fell indifferently on everyone, male or female, free or slave. But this ‘natural’ did not therefore deny or otherwise erase the many hierarchies characteristic of Roman life (or law). It simply identified a (necessarily limited) perspective of natural justice from which those hierarchies could be regarded as irrelevant.

Sources indicate that this observation of the Roman origins of the idea of natural equality challenges another, more familiar story about the sources of modern egalitarianism. To many modern readers, the biblical language of ‘creation’ found in the Declaration of Independence suggests that the equality of human beings was originally a religious idea, whether a Jewish or a Christian one. Yet if one consults the Hebrew Bible, the conceptual language of equality is conspicuously absent. In Genesis, the biblical God creates human beings, male and female, ‘in his own image’. But this divine likeness, in turn, does nothing to preclude the many forms of divinely sanctioned or permitted hierarchy, including slavery and patriarchy, found elsewhere in the Bible.

It is only later, in the 3rd and 4th centuries CE, that we find Roman Christian apologists like St Cyprian and Lactantius resisting persecution by deliberately combining the biblical account of human creation in ‘God’s image or likeness’, on the one hand, with the Roman legal language of ‘equality’ as a universal standard of legal justice, on the other. The result was an entirely fresh – and highly influential – way of talking about divine justice in Latin Christendom. Unlike the Roman civil law, the Christian God had been revealed to be truly ‘no respecter of persons’. Thus in his eyes, the worldly distinctions of slave and free, rich and poor, male and female, would one day count for nothing. All would instead be judged ‘equally’ – that is, by the same divine standard – and then rewarded or punished in proportion with their spiritual merit.

We can now see why, for most of its history, ‘equality talk’ proved not only consistent with hierarchy, but fundamentally supportive of it. It’s not because Greek democrats, Roman jurists and Christian theologians were paying lip service to an ideal they didn’t believe in, or that they were incapable of following through on the egalitarian logic of their own commitments. It’s because people in the past moved much less easily than we do from the premise that all (or some) people are equal towards the conclusion that they should, therefore, be treated as equals in a social or evaluative sense. To be ‘equal’ in the eyes of God, or of the law, or of a democratic lottery, simply meant that certain of our differences shouldn’t matter for that particular purpose. It did not follow that those differences must therefore be deemed irrelevant for every purpose, or that all humans were thus sufficiently alike in virtue or value to be treated socially or politically as peers. Indeed, emphasising the former equality was often a way of bringing the manifest disparities between certain individuals or social groups into sharper relief, thus fitting them for hierarchical relations.

It has been revealed that and yet, the same proliferation of historical meanings – as evenness and absence, balance and proportion, indifference and parity – that accounts for this disconnect, can in turn explain how ‘equality talk’ finally gained a newly introduced and uniquely powerful political force in early modern England. And, with that force, ordinary Englishmen and women began to exploit its many ambiguities in order to demand not only equal justice, but equal standing with the privileged.

In a recent development, john Lilburne, reading from Coke’s Institutes of the Lawes of England (1628-44) at his trial for high treason in 1649. Photo courtesy The British Library/Public Domain.

Recent findings suggest that to locate the precise moment of transformation, we must look beyond the summer of 1776, back to the summer of 1646, when a man called John Lilburne found himself on trial for libel before the House of Lords. Today, Lilburne is remembered chiefly as a leader of the Leveller movement active during the English Civil War. And the Levellers are remembered for demanding universal manhood suffrage at the Putney Debates of 1647, several centuries before it became a reality in modern Britain. Summoned before the Peers the previous June, however, Lilburne had done something comparatively trivial. He simply refused to kneel or to remove his hat before his aristocratic judges. His reason? That God had created ‘every particular and individual man and woman that ever breathed in the world … all equal and alike in power, dignity, authority and majesty.’ Hence no one could claim any ‘authority, dominion or magisterial power’ over another without their ‘mutual agreement or consent’.

The Leveller movement pushed this conceptual ambiguity to the hilt across pamphlets, protests and petitions.

So much for balance! So much for indifference! In that moment, Lilburne somehow managed to turn the equality of human beings before God into a demand that even commoners like himself could stand on the same level, as peers, with their supposed betters here on earth. In this way, Lilburne’s proposition offered an early – and indeed more radical – version of the levelling logic found later in the US Declaration of Independence. For starters, it explicitly included women among those created equal and entitled to an equal voice in how they were to be governed. (In the US, this addendum would have to wait more than 70 years, until the Seneca Falls Declaration of 1848.).

How did Lilburne do it? Well, he started by collapsing a conceptual distinction that earlier English equality talk had generally preserved, that between being ‘equal’ – in the sense being subject to or judged by the same standard – and being ‘an equal’ in the social and evaluative sense of being someone’s peer. In hindsight, we can see that Lilburne was assisted in this effort by a broader conceptual looseness in early modern English, by which many of the classical distinctions inherited from Greek and Latin had started to dissolve. For instance, in the earliest English translation of Aristotle’s Politics, published in 1598, the translator simply erased the philosophical distinction between being ‘equal’ (isos) and being ‘similar’ (homoios) by translating both terms as ‘equal’.

Recent findings suggest that such slippages undoubtedly offend against philosophical precision. Politically speaking, however, they created opportunities. Lilburne noticed one such opportunity in Magna Carta, specifically in its guarantee to every free man in the realm the right to a trial per pares, or by his peers. In early modern English, ‘peer’ could of course mean a social equal of whatever degree, high or low. But increasingly in political usage, it could also mean a member of the English aristocracy. If every ‘freeborn’ Englishman and woman had the right to be tried by ‘the lawful judgment of [their] peers (or equals)’, as Lilburne put it, then surely he or she must also be ‘entitled unto an equal privilege’ with the greatest Peer in the Commonwealth, as in Creation.

The Leveller movement subsequently pushed this conceptual ambiguity to the hilt across countless pamphlets, protests and petitions, in which they demanded not only that English commoners be treated ‘equally’ with aristocrats before the law, but also that they enjoy all of the political benefits of peerage. Thomas Rainborough’s celebrated demand for ‘equal voice’ at Putney, through a radical expansion of the franchise, followed the same levelling logic: ‘For really I think that the poorest he that is in England has a life to live as the greatest he.’ So did a remarkable 1649 Leveller women’s petition presented to the House of Commons, in which the female petitioners declared:.

In this way, even as the Leveller movement failed, its newly introduced way of talking about equality lived on. We find versions of its levelling logic in Thomas Hobbes’s Leviathan (1651), or in the writings of the so-called ‘first English feminist’ (and staunch Tory) Mary Astell, as well as in the US Declaration of Independence. Across these very different texts, with their different political conclusions, the language of equality continued to perform its distinctive function, cutting the great ones down to size while raising up the marginal and excluded to meet them. To claim equality was thus no longer merely to demand that the same law, or the same God, apply the same standards indifferently. It was to demand recognition as an equal in society: that is, someone entitled to speak, judge and be heard as a peer.

For centuries, it seems, this was the primary political function of equality talk. But, today, this language has lost much of its levelling power. At the same time, talk of equality no longer unifies, it disillusions and divides. Why?

Perhaps the problem ultimately lies with what made this conceptual language so appealing in the first place. Far from being simple, let alone self-evident, its history reveals that equality has accumulated a remarkable number of meanings over time. And when it comes to how human beings ought to relate to one another, those different meanings – as absence or balance, indifference or parity – are often in tension, if not outright contradiction.

According to recent reports, is it any wonder, then, that we talk past each other! Even as the word ‘equality’ suggests that better measurement or reasoning ought to resolve our disagreements. Now, one might conclude from this – as many contemporary progressives have done – that we would be better off rejecting equality altogether, in favour of some other, less historically ambiguous ideal. But that would, I think, be a mistake. Because historically, the problem with equality talk – namely, its conceptual ambiguity – has also been the source of its uncommon power.

English women could be tried by juries, but they did not ordinarily sit on them.

Again, consider Lilburne. His better-educated critics could (and did) object that his ‘general Proposition’ to the Lords was a non sequitur. It simply didn’t follow from the premise that God created men and women as equally subject to his divine justice, that they should therefore be recognised politically as peers. But this criticism did not stop Lilburne and his fellow Levellers from trading on the many different meanings of equality and drawing their own political conclusions. And their success was not simply a matter of ingenious wordplay or conceptual sleight of hand. The plausibility of their insistence that English commoners were just as capable of thinking and speaking for themselves as Peers rested on a familiar institution: the jury. When ‘12 men of the neighbourhood’ sat in judgment over a fellow commoner, their differences of wealth, occupation, education and ability didn’t disappear. They simply ceased to matter for the purposes of reaching a verdict. Hence the jurors came to see one another as ‘peers and equals’ because the institution required them to act as peers, as they listened, deliberated and judged together.

Recent findings suggest that in this way, the ‘doing’ of equality proceeded the idea of it. But if Leveller ‘equality talk’ rested on a particular social practice, the limits of that practice mattered, too. English women could be tried by juries, but they did not ordinarily sit on them; enslaved Africans in the English Atlantic, although admittedly ‘created Men’, were regarded as too ‘brutish’ to enjoy that privilege. For centuries, accordingly, these groups would struggle to leverage the same arguments in the absence of social practices and institutions within which they, too, could act – and be seen to act – as peers and equals.

Industry observers note that so much for the past. What about the future? Well, in the first place, the above analysis suggests that the work of making ‘equality talk’ meaningful is not primarily philosophical, it’s practical. Nonetheless, philosophers often proceed as though any difficulties with equality must be logical or definitional. If only we could identify the respect in which every person is ‘equal’ with enough precision, then our disagreements about justice would dissolve. But history suggests that the more crucial task is that of sustaining the social practices and institutions that make equality meaningful in the first place. (Hence, the reticence of contemporary relational egalitarians to spell out what equality demands of us in positive terms, beyond a general resistance to hierarchical relations, is a serious defect.).

So what would an historically informed approach to equality look like? For one thing, it would require attending to (or even just attending) things like jury service, among the other increasingly uncommon offline sites in which we encounter other people who are not like us – in bulk, excellence or ideology – as peers. Today, these sites are threatened not only by frictionless technologies like large language models or social media, but also by the growing price-stratification of so many consumer experiences – what Michael Sandel in 2012 dubbed the ‘skyboxification of American life’. But taking part in such activities on more even terms doesn’t make us identical, nor does it mean that we agree. It just means that we commit ourselves, for a limited time and purpose, to not letting our differences determine which of us matters – or whose voice ought to count.

Because, if history tells us anything, it’s that equality is not primarily an idea to be believed in, nor a partisan commitment to affirm. It’s something people did, and something we must do. Only then are we created equal – not by ‘the Laws of Nature and of Nature’s God’, but by each other, every day.

In 1737, Benjamin Franklin published a âDrinkers Dictionaryâ in the Pennsylvania Gazette. Although precisely who wrote the article is unclear, the dictionary listed a grand total of 229 quirky synonyms and other expressionsâfrom âaddledâ to âwater-soakenââfor describing someone who is drunk.Â.

As exhaustive as Franklinâs list was, it by no means tells the entire story. In fact, when it comes to words for drunkenness, the English language has several thousand words and phrases to fall back on, dating from the days of Old English to the present day. Not all of them remain in common use, unfortunately, but next time you want to drop something a little more obscure into the conversation down at your local bar, any one of these old-fashioned expressions will do.

In a recent development, in Victorian maritime slang, being bang-up meant to be drunk. As a more general intensifier, bang-up was also used in a bunch of longer phrasesâlike âbang-up to the markââto mean absolutely, fully, or first-rate.Â.

In olden times, you could be barrel-sick and pot-sick if you were drunk, while crop-sickness is a recorded Tudor-period phrase for the queasy aftereffects of a night of hard drinking.Â.

In 17th-century English, a bottlenose or bottlenozzle was someone with a noticeably large, swollen, or bruised nose, while the older term bottlenosed has meant large-nosed since the 1500s. But perhaps partly in reference to someone with a drunkardâs swollen noseâor perhaps in a more straightforward reference to a drunkard holding a bottle to their faceâbottlenosed has also meant drunk since the early 1700s.Â.

If youâre corky-headed, then youâre flighty or empty-mindedâbut if youâre just straightforwardly corky, then youâre half-drunk.Â.

One of the earliest recorded synonyms for being drunk in the Oxford English Dictionary, cup-shotten is recorded as far back as the 14th century; a simpler and more modern-sounding form, cup-shot, is recorded from the late 16th century.Â.

In a recent development, in the 1500s, the English writer Thomas Nash published a satirical pamphlet in which he jokingly identified eight types or levels of drunkenness, each one named after an animal. The first is ape-drunk, in which a man âleaps and singsâ and âdanceth for the heavens.â A man who is lion-drunk becomes courageous or rageful with drink, and âis apt to quarrel with any many that speaks to him.â Someone who is swine-drunk is âheavy, lumpish and sleepy.â A man who is sheep-drunk is âwise in his own concept,â and struggles to remain clear-headed. Someone who is maudlin-drunk will âweep for kindness.â A Martin-drunk person will keep drinking until theyâre sober again. Someone who is goat-drunk becomes uncontrollably lecherous when drunk. And, lastly, a fox-drunk person becomes characteristically wily and cunning when drunk, and âwill never bargain but when they are drunk.âÂ.

Grog has been an old word for liquor since the 1700s, in particular among sailors. Grogged is just an adjectival extension of that, dating from the mid-19th century.Â Â.

Another dialect term from the 19th century at least, havey-cavey is a fanciful extension of âhalfâ that emerged in the dialects of northern and central England. In literal terms it describes something that is in a trembling or precariously balanced positionâlike something teetering over the edge of a table, in the sense that something could go either way. In the late 19th century, it also came to be used to mean drunk.Â.

According to recent reports, probably in reference to the metal hoops that encase a barrel, hooped came to mean drunk in 18th-century English. (In later years, it was nonsensically expanded to the even better expression hoopsy-coopsy.)Â.

In 19th-century American slang, âbitten by the snakeâ was apparently a means of saying that someone was drunkâand this specific extension of that relates particularly to the aftereffects of a moccasin snakeâs bite.Â.

A jokey mishmash of âmortalâ and âcontagiousâ (or else perhaps based on an earlier dialect word, mortacious, used as a general intensifier), mortagious is recorded in Scots in the late 1800s.Â.

A lot of old-timey words and phrases referring to drunkenness allude to some sense of going too far or too long, and overflown is another example of that dating from the 1500s. You can also be overseen, overcome, overshot, or oversparred if youâve had one too many.Â.

Being owl-eyed meant intoxicated in the 1600s, whereas before then, you could also be âas drunk as a boiled owl.âÂ  Phrases like these perhaps allude to the wild staring eyes of a drunkard, or else to the notion of a blustering drinker who feigns intelligence and talks long-windedly about subjects he actually knows little about.Â.

It has been revealed that in 19th-century U.S. slang, you could be ramsquaddled. Exactly where that word comes from is a mystery, but âramââ is an old Scots prefix used as an intensifier, so perhaps thereâs a link to Scotland hidden somewhere in the mix here.Â.

The dialect word rozzle means to warm oneself by the fire, but if youâre rozzled, or rozzelt, then youâve warmed yourself by imbibing liquor (and are now suffering from doing so to excess).Â.

Sopped here means thoroughly soaked, while sack isnât the fabric bag but a general name for a kind of Spanish white wine popular in England in the 1500s (which is when this phrase dates back to).Â.

âShooting the catâ meant vomiting from drinking too much in 18th-century slang, and may have evolved into âshot in the neck,â another slang term with the same meaning that emerged in America in the 1800s.Â.

SNUG UNDER THE TABLE WITH THE DOGSÂ.

The American writer Parson Weems, also known as ML Weems, wrote in 1818 that at first a drunkard only has âa drop in his eye,â then is noted to be âhalf shaved,â then âa little on the staggers,â and then progressively âquite capsized,â then âsnug under the table with the dogs,â and lastly is able to âstick to the floor without holding on.âÂ.

Inspired by a line from Shakespeareâs Henry V, saying that someoneâs âbloody flag is outâ meant that they had become either red-faced with drunkenness, or else (more figuratively) that they were wild with a drunken rage.Â.

According to recent reports, most of our year wasn’t spent at a desk. Matador’s editors spent 2026 hauling potatoes and shellfish alongside islanders on Chiloé, hopping between trains and cable cars across the Dolomites without ever renting a car, and driving Nevada’s ghost-town highways in search of a good spook. We even slept in an all-electric hotel that offers a glimpse of hospitality’s greener future.

All that time on the move doubles as a field test. Every jacket, carry-on, charger, and packing cube we bring along gets put through its paces. That includes the snacks and screen-free distractions that keep our kids happy on long travel days. Some of it gets left behind. The pieces worth gifting are the ones that earned a permanent spot in our bags.

That’s what this guide is: the gear we actually reach for, trip after trip. Maybe you need a stocking stuffer, a crowd-pleaser for the white elephant swap, or something memorable for the traveler in your life. Either way, every pick here has already proven itself on the road, so you can shop with confidence.

These are the best travel gifts for 2026 to inspire 2027’s adventures.
