Paired with a foldable and portable keyboard, it holds my phone in whatever angle I need to use it for writing even in the tightest middle seat on a budget airline. — Nickolaus Hines, Managing Editor.

Recent findings suggest that finding good coffee just about anywhere is a lot easier today than it was in the past. But even the most ubiquitous fourth-wave coffee shop can’t be everywhere. With good grinds and hot water, good coffee itself can be everywhere an AeroPress Go is, though. It’s the most travel-friendly option from the already travel-friendly AeroPress brand. The whole setup fits into the included 16-ounce travel mug with a silicone top. Espresso-style coffee made quick and easy — something even the casual coffee drinker can enjoy (especially anyone who has sipped a lackluster hotel brew or whatever is made by the friend who swears they can brew “the best cowboy coffee” over the campfire). — Nickolaus Hines, Managing Editor.

Sources indicate that I love a good hands free sling bag (and find normal purses pretty annoying),but there’s one dub thing that stops me from using them more: there’s never anywhere to put a water bottle and I don’t really want to lug one around all day, ‘cause the defeats the whole “hands-free” thing. But hooray: The Vessel has an actual dedicated bottle compartment on the outside, so you can carry it and still have plenty of space left inside. At 4 liters, it holds a day’s worth of essentials without turning into a backpack, it’s weather-resistant, and the strap actually extends long enough to wear over a puffy jacket.

To be straightforward, I don’t eat much meat. I’m the guy who, when asked about dietary preferences, says, “I’m mostly plant-based.” Not because I don’t like meat, but because I don’t like the lack of ethics behind factory farming and at-scale cattle production, nor the horrendous climate impact these practices wreak on our planet. If I’m going to get down, I want the meal to be as responsibly sourced as the venison my best friend cooks after his annual fall hunting trip. Force of Nature is the closest I’ve found to that, and I recently put in an order for camping trips with my daughter. The hot dogs cook great over a fire, and the organization supports regenerative agricultural practices that focus on soil health and ecological restoration, as well as animal welfare.

Recent findings suggest that it’s a subscription service, but unlike most that want you to take a box every week or two and have a strict minimum price threshold, Force of Nature’s website allows you to pick only what you want and set your preferred timing for deliveries, up to every eight weeks. Given the high standards, the price points aren’t bad, either – a 14oz selection of ground elk runs $14.99, a 160oz package of beef runs just under that. Other options like meatballs, poultry, and ancestrals are available.

It has been revealed that in my neverending quest to dress better, I pounced on the Quince website as soon as the firm’s Instagram ads first hit my feed. The Cotton Pique Knit Overshirt was exactly what I was after. The first day I wore it to my coworking space, I received my first-ever “I like your fit” comment, and I haven’t looked back. This is now my go-to overshirt for dinners and evenings out, key “video-on” work calls, and any other time I’m genuinely trying to impress. It’s cozy and I can wear it either buttoned or unbuttoned (and I frequentlymove between the two throughout the day – oh, hello casual happy hour).

It has been revealed that by releasing the Cabin Mule slippers, SmartWool solved a problem that has eluded outdoor clothing companies for years: What to put on your feet in the car or at the lodge after a day on the mountains. Foot funk prevents one from wanting to put on a nice pair of shoes, of course, and you can’t wear socks into happy hour. The slippers are durable and very warm, great for after snowboarding and equally effective around the house.

Sources indicate that even though nice cameras can cost thousands, the strap that comes in the box with them is almost always garbage: a thin, unpadded nylon band that digs into your neck and is a genuine project to take on and off. WANDRD’s latest magnetic strap fixes the part that actually drives photographers nuts. It has magnetic quick-connectors that let you pop the strap off to mount the camera on a tripod or drop it in a bag, then snap it back in a second without having to double thread tiny straps through even tinier buckles. It comes in a version for heavier bodies and one for smaller setups, and since the brand’s camera bags are beloved by photographers, there’s no reason to think the strap won’t be, too. Sure, you can buy cheaper generic ones on Amazon, but those probably don’t have a lifetime guarantee, or the years of research from pro photogs that went into designing this strap.

I love a button down that looks good at the office and feels good on the trail. No garment has met this criteria better than Kuhl’s Relentr Shirt Jacket, which I’m wearing even as I type this. From afar, it hits like a sport coat, but it’s flexible and comfy and ideal for being on the go. It’s a great airport and plane shirt for these same reasons – I feel and look good but don’t have to worry about stuffy dress clothes.

According to recent reports, the Raidr Pant are more trail-centric, and are also great for travel days because they relieve you of the dreaded “denim crunch.” Kuhl built its reputation on trail pants, and this pair is the current master. I have no issue wearing them throughout a weeklong trip or for multi-night camping outings – they’re built for heavy use.

Industry observers note that I write a lot of stories about wilderness and backcountry rescues, and if there’s one thing I hear over and over from talking to search-and-rescue professionals, it’s that a huge share of the people they go looking for simply didn’t know where they were. The thing I hear most frequently after that is that onX is the app they keep naming as the fix. You download the maps for an area before you go, and from then on the app tracks your location over detailed topo maps even with zero cell signal, so you can see exactly where you are, where the trail went, and how to get back.

It covers hiking, backcountry skiing, mountain biking, and climbing, which makes it an easy gift for basically anyone who leaves the pavement. A year of Elite runs $99.99, and this version ships as a physical card you can actually wrap and hand over, instead of a code buried in an email. It may not be the sexiest gift out there, but it’s a good one – and helps keep your friends and family safer (at least until the membership expires).

The fact that two insulated booties made a list written by frequent travelers reveals how essential they’ve become among outdoorsy types. I’ve had a pair of insulated camp booties for close to a decade, and they’re some of the most-worn shoes I own. In fact, I’ve gone through a few pairs because I wear them probably too much. I pull them on to take the dog out at night, slip them on when my feet are sore after a long hike, and use them as indoor slippers in a pinch. One of the best out there is the ThermoBall Traction Bootie, with insulation that stays warm when wet, a water repellent shell so wet grass at the campsite won’t reach your socks, and a tall front cuff so your ankles don’t get cold around the campfire. They pack flat, are useful for just about anyone, and (right now) are at a super-reasonable price point.

If you know, you know, and if you don’t, the person you’re shopping for almost certainly does, assuming they’re a hiker. The Melanzana Micro Grid Hoodie, a.k.a. “the Melly,” is a cult object among serious hikers and thru-hikers. It’s a simple Polartec grid-fleece hoodie that’s earned near-mythical status mostly because it’s so hard to get. It’s designed, cut, sewn, and sold in Leadville, Colorado, by a tiny operation that for years would only sell it in person. It still limits online restocks to a couple of drops per year that vanish in minutes. You genuinely have to set a calendar alarm: if you’re buying for a Christmas present, be ready to buy it at 9 AM MST on December 7. Snagging one is half the gift.

Scarcity aside, there’s a reason it’s so in-demand: it’s a light, breathable, fast-drying mid-layer that you’ll see everywhere on the AT and PCT. It’s the move for the person in your life who sleeps in their van and daydreams about getting paid to test hiking gear.

In a recent development, the best way to choose a pair of sunglasses is to compare multiple types and brands head to head. Thing is, this isn’t easy to do on the internet, where buying sunglasses generally means going to the website of a brand you know or shopping from a substantial-box retailer that sells a million different products but isn’t an authority on any one of them. This is made even more complicated for prescription lenses, which some brands don’t offer and even if they do, you may have to settle for a shade or style you don’t actually want. Enter SmartBuyGlasses — which offers hundreds of types of sunglasses across every style from all the top brands, and — here’s the kicker — allows you to browse and compare them all in one place, and swap in prescription lenses as needed. I got a pair of Spy sunglasses with prescription lenses from the brand this year after not owning a pair of Spy’s for at least a decade, and never having owned prescription sunglasses because I could never find a pair that I liked. What sold me on this pair was that because I could see how they looked compared to competing brands, and that the site let me enter my glasses prescription and swapped out the standard Spy lenses for ones that match what I need. Bada-bing, bada-boom. — Tim Wenger, Transactional Content Editor.

I can’t think of a reason why someone who travels even just once in a while wouldn’t love being gifted an AirFly Pro — unless they already have one. The gadget plugs into airplane seatback TVs, allowing listeners to use their personal Bluetooth headphones to watch in-flight entertainment. I use it on almost every flight since my noise-canceling personal earbuds are way better than the cheap plastic headphones airlines give you for free. It’s easy to use and pair with any type of Bluetooth headphones, and you can even pair it with two different listening devices. It’s made for use on planes, but it works with any 3.5 mm headphone jack. — Suzie Dundas, Editor.

Sources indicate that no one is ever going to convince me that using the TRTL Travel Pillow doesn’t look pretty darn dumb – but who cares? This is one of two pillows that actually works for sleeping upright on a plane (the other being the Cabeau Evolution Pillow), but the TRTL arguably is easier to pack in most carry-ons. Instead of having padding like most pillows, it has a flexible but firm neck panel that holds your head at a gentle angle, so it takes up less space than a traditional pillow. It’s one of the best tools available for sleeping on a plane, and comes in a host of patterns and colors, in case you want to try to camouflage it in your favorite travel sweatshirt. — Suzie Dundas, Editor.

Recent findings suggest that I drink my coffee black — not because I’m trying to be dramatic, but because I’m officially a coffee snob (I didn’t choose this life; it chose me). Hotel coffee usually tastes stale. Keurig pods? A tragedy in a cup. So I started traveling with single-serve pour-over filters, and honestly, they’ve changed the game. They pack flat, take seconds to set up, and all you need is hot water, which I’ve fetched from airport Starbucks counters, poured from a thermos mid-hike, and used in countless hotel rooms where “complimentary coffee” is a crime. The beans stay fresh, they’re roasted in Guatemala (so more revenue stays with local farmers), and the founder is a third-generation coffee grower who actually knows what makes a perfect cup. — Kelsey Wilking, Email Marketing Specialist.

If you’re shopping for someone who runs or hikes early in the morning or after dark, the Knog Bilby 400 Headlamp is a thoughtful and genuinely useful gift. Unlike most headlamps that bounce or pinch, this one uses a soft medical-grade silicone band that stays put. It’s waterproof, rechargeable via built-in USB, and bright enough (400 lumens) for everything from trail runs to setting up camp. I also love that it’s easy to wipe clean after sweaty runs, and that it comes in a range of fun colors (Fluro Organe is my favorite). — Katie Gavin, Editor.

I’ve come to trust Roark as my go-to brand for travel and adventure clothing. As such, I looked to the California-based outfitter for shirts and found the combo of the Made to Fade Longsleeve Button–Up and the Well-worn Thermal to be perfect for fall and winter in the Rockies. I tend to feel quite confident wearing these items, a feeling that isn’t always guaranteed for me when a collar comes into play. The shirt is available in both long and short sleeves, and I suggest picking up one of each. The jacket lends itself to evenings and more formal settings where you need to look professional but still want to feel natural. I’ve worn the Hwy 128 jeans for years, and come back each time I need a new color. — Tim Wenger, Transactional Content Editor.

If you’re buying for someone planning an outdoorsy vacation, I’d highly recommend a pair of Nocs binoculars. They’re lightweight and easy to hold in one hand, making them easy to use, and I’ve noticed very few issues around double vision or blurriness with my pair. Binoculars are a handier item than you might think, especially when they’re easy to carry like the Nocs models. I’ve used mine for safari trips, whale watching, national park trips (excellent for spotting wolves in Yellowstone National Park) and on daily hikes around my neighborhood. They’re especially fun for older travelers who may enjoy the outdoors but not be able to hike long distances, and they create a fun way to spend time out in nature. — Suzie Dundas, Editor.

Photo: Screenshot of Hungryroot page.

A grocery subscription for a frequent traveler sounds like an odd option, but I tried Hungryroot this year to feed my five-year-old daughter and I while moving about places with a kitchen, and it was perfect. It’s sort of like a cross between a grocery subscription and a packaged meal subscription – most meals require cooking but little prep work. I have my subscription set to be all vegetarian, and the options are great, including Beyond Burgers and tofu as well as less-processed plant-based hits like sous vide potatoes, plenty of good rice- and quinoa-based meals, and some indulgent treats. My subscription is $179 per delivery, to feed two people, and the order lasts for about two weeks if you mix in a few meals out.

I’m not a fan of all the plastic – so many things come wrapped in plastic. Fortunately, I have a x subscript in my TK recycle hard to recycle plastics and was able to send much of it in. However, the package is chilled with NutriIce instead of traditional dry ice, which can be used either as plant food or poured safely down the train without toxins entering the water stream. The box and its insulation are recyclable.

According to recent reports, because I’m cooking for myself and my five-year-old daughter, and the meals in my cart are typically designed for two, more than once I ended up with a bit of leftovers to take with me for lunch at work the next day. Much of my order was organic, and as promised the meals were both healthy and delicious. As a bonus, the recipes were easy to follow.

I like a comfy, bulky hoody for the autumn and winter, and this is the one for me this year. I’ve been wearing it each morning and out on evening walks, as well as for mountain forays and travel. It’s super warm, and is baggy enough that it can go over anything. Its a heavyweight, garment-washed cotton fleece with a crossover hood, a kangaroo pocket, and contrast stitching that nods to the brand’s 1990s alpine catalog. Both hands have a pocket, which makes it much more productive for actually carrying things than a traditional cross-body hoody pocket.

This is a splurge, full stop, but it’s the rare one where everyone I know who’s gotten it as a gift (and that’s a lot, seeing as I live somewhere very outdoorsy), is absolutely obsessed with it. The brand builds everything it makes to what seems like an obsessive standard not common in a culture that is becoming increasingly throw-away. It’s made with stainless steel, glass, and brass and looks so nice that I wouldn’t be surprised if these are the cool vintage item campers in the year 2070 can’t wait to bust out. It also has a lifetime warranty, so it’s a buy-for-life situation. It can do a drip brew or pourover and packs into its own storage bag for easy storage and travel.

This is one of the most fun gifts I think you can give to an outdoorsy person or frequent traveler. The Portal AFN7 is a screen-free, point-and-shoot adventure camera with a vintage, almost disposable-camera feel, 16MP photos, 4K video, and six film-inspired (and optional) presets filters built in.It’s way, way easier to use than a GoPro and is built to take a beating. It’s IP56 weather-sealed against dust, rain, and splashes, and light enough (under 5 ounces) that you can clip it to a pack strap and forget it’s there. The clever part, and the reason it’s a real gift for a wildlife person, is that it pairs with Nocs binoculars and monoculars to shoot straight through the magnified optics. That means someone can get a close-up frame of a distant elk or a bird without dropping a couple grand on a DSLR and a telephoto lens. It’s quirky, nearly indestructible, and a cool addition to any outdoorsy person’s kit. — Suzie Dundas, Commissioning Editor.

Recent findings suggest that PAKA celebrated 10 years of alpaca clothing this year with special-edition clothing and a video recap that was as inspiring as the brand’s sweaters are comfortable. The Matador team wears PAKA almost on the daily, with Suzie Dundas offering a fitting testament: I bought my husband one of these years ago, and my only real complaint is that he wears a men’s large so I can’t steal it back and wear it every day. At some point, I’m just going to break down and buy my own. The sweater is made from royal alpaca, which is softer than cashmere but far tougher and regulates temperature across a huge range, so it works from chilly mornings to actual winter. You can also wear it a bunch of times between washes. His has held up for years without pilling or sagging, which is the whole point. Basically, even though it looks dainty, it’s engineered for all kinds of activity, including distance hiking, backpacking (the through Europe in hostels kind), and outdoorsy pursuits.

It has been revealed that I also love it because I’m getting increasingly angry about fast fashion and cheap, greenwashed brands that are still making bad clothing. PAKA sweaters are knit in Peru by one of the brand’s 300-plus women artisans and hand-signed by whoever made it, the company is a certified B Corp with traceable alpaca sourcing, and the sweater is built to be worn for a decade, not a season. For the person who’d rather own one genuinely great thing than a drawer of disposable ones, here’s your gift. — Suzie Dundas, Commissioning Editor.

In a recent development, I added the Vika Tur pants from HH to my wardrobe when I was headed to the Arctic Circle and figured I needed the most durable, most waterproof hiking pants on the market. But they’re so comfortable and useful that I now wear them basically any time I’m going outside with a chance of rain in the forecast.

It has been revealed that there’s not much not to like, with large, zippered thigh pockets, Velcro adjustments at the ankles to accommodate all types of boots, and an articulated fit (meaning slightly pre-bent knees) so you can squat, lunge, and step as much as you like. I recently wore them on a wet waterfall scramble where I was scooting on my butt across fallen logs and rocks, and they still look brand newly introduced. I may even snag another pair while they’re still on sale. — Suzie Dundas, Editor.

Sources indicate that when I picture the average fishing boots, fashion does not come to mind. The Korker line of Neo Flex 100 percent waterproof boots, though, offers a steadfast grip performance while also sporting a modern look. Available in five different colors, including one sexily named “ganache,” these boots provide ultimate traction with a Non-Marking Kling-On Deck rubber outsole intended for dry and wet surfaces alike. While most boots are more functional than comfortable, these are built with Cush-Tech for a purposefully padded midsole to keep your feet supported and cozy. On top of that, they’re easy to slip on and off when you’ve got your hands filled with boating equipment or fishing supplies after a day on the water. — Keven Gungor, Matador Creators Manager.

Industry observers note that the Lowepro Flipside 200 has been an ideal backpack for my photography outings, offering flexibility and comfort in one sleek design. I particularly love how I can rearrange the main compartment to fit my gear perfectly. I have carried everything in this, from an assortment of lenses up to two cameras with mounted lenses. Everything stays tightly protected in its adjustable spaces, giving me peace of mind when moving from one shooting spot to the next. Despite its compact appearance, it feels surprisingly spacious compared to other photography backpacks I’ve tried, even accommodating my Manfrotto travel tripod. Beyond storage, the Flipside 200 stands out for its comfort. Whether I’m on a city walk or a full-day hike, it sits well on my shoulders, reduces strain, and gives me easy access to all my gear whenever inspiration strikes. This backpack is a must-have for any photography adventure, combining practicality with comfort and the reassurance that my equipment is safe and ready to go. — Rulo Luna, Photo Editor.

The Altra Women’s Lone Peak 9+ caught my eye because I wanted a single shoe that could seamlessly transition from a hike to a run (or vice versa). For my sins, I do a lot of hill running, so I need a sturdy trail shoe that can handle uphill slogs, support me on descents, and hold up during stretches of hiking. The Lone Peak is also ideal for anyone who runs on both trail and tarmac. I have broad feet, so I love the roomy FootShape toe box. It also means I can wear different socks depending on the weather or mileage — and even after hours on the move, my feet still feel fresh. The midsole cushioning hits the sweet spot between soft and stable, and the ripstop upper feels impressively durable. Comfortable, versatile, and tougher than they look, these shoes are now my go-to for a run, hike, or even just a fall afternoon stroll with my husband. — Katie Gavin, Editor.

I’ve lost count of how many duffel bags I own. In part, that’s because I always reach for the same one: the Patagonia Black Hole Duffel 40L. There’s a lot to love about Patagonia’s Black Hole series — the bags are endlessly spacious, hard to wear out, and able to be carried comfortably a few different ways — but where this particular duffel excels is its size. Weekend away? It’s small enough not to feel burdensome while being able to fit everything I need and then some. Two-week trip? There’s still plenty of space for a light to moderate packer like me to bring all of the clothes, toiletries, and accessories I need, plus multiple pairs of shoes. As a bonus, my duffel’s electric teal color is fun and easily identifiable should I ever need to check the bag — but then, why would I when it’s perfectly sized for a carry-on? — Alex Bresler, Editor and Branded Content Editor.

It has been revealed that malibu Sandals started as a California beach shoe firm making modern huaraches. The Latigo are indeed wonderful for trips to the shore, though the utility extends far beyond, and these are my go-to travel day shoes. The 100-percent natural Malaysian crepe gum rubber outing on the sole is grippy, and the vegan upper is no-sock soft and doesn’t even need a break-in period. I’ve walked miles on end in these shoes and finish the day with feet feeling like they just got done walking across a street of pillows. I’m not a big fan of laces on shoes in general, except for sports, and the slide on top makes slipping these on and cinching tight easy no matter how much of a TSA rush there is. I’ll be the first to admit that the product photos had me skeptical whether the Latigo would fit my style — or any style that I’d be associated with, for that matter. They fit in a much more sleek way than the photos suggest and are versatile enough for a variety of casual looks from the airport to the bar. — Nickolaus Hines, Managing Editor.

In a recent development, the Smartwool Second Cut Fleece is among the most impactful pushes toward circular design and sustainability on the outdoor market today. The fleece is constructed partly from pre-consumer Smartwool Merino wool scraps—reintegrating material waste from the firm’s own production cycle — and combines it with recycled polyester or plastic bottles to form a warm, durable, and technically capable fabric. Reviews highlight that it features a blend with roughly 79 percent upcycled materials (22 percent pre-consumer Merino wool plus 57 percent recycled polyester). I acquired the Second Cut Fleece and have been wearing it everywhere as the weather has cooled down — it’s an ideal overlayer for work days and a great mid-layer for cold-weather outdoor activities.

It has been revealed that beyond its sustainable credentials, the Second Cut Fleece is built for practical use in diverse conditions. It offers the natural advantages of Merino—such as moisture wicking, temperature regulation, and odor resistance — while maintaining a regular fit that allows layering without bulk. Smartwool The garment incorporates functional design touches too: secure zip pockets, a locker loop, and a warmth rating (CLO) of at least 1.15. Together, these features make the Second Cut Fleece a compelling choice for someone who cares about both environmental impact and outdoor-ready performance. — Tim Wenger, Transactional Content Editor.

Industry observers note that I resisted getting an Outerknown Blanket shirt for years but after giving in this fall I regret the delay. I acquired a classic in Pitch Black and I wear it almost daily — for work, for lounging, on travel days, you name it. It’s comfy, warm, and flexible, and has received multiple compliments from other parents at my kid’s soccer games and gymnastics classes. — Tim Wenger, Transactional Content Editor.

During my recent trip to Santiago, Chile, I fell victim to credit card fraud. My bank notified me about unauthorized transactions, including a hefty hotel bill and an attempted purchase at an Apple store. Panicking, I found my bank card in my wallet, so the most likely culprit was a skimming device. This probably occurred in a taxi, which is common in the city. Determined to avoid this happening again, I got this stylish and functional card protector from Carl Friedrik. Crafted from premium aluminum encased in supple vachetta leather, this sleek accessory offers protection and elegance. Its compact design effortlessly slips into my pocket or purse, while the soft interior lining safeguards my cards from scratches and damage. It’s the perfect travel companion with ample space for up to five cards and a discreet cash compartment. I opted for the cognac color, but the protector is also available in sophisticated chocolate and classic black. — Katie Gavin, Editor.

Industry observers note that I’ve been using my Secrid Mini Wallet for nearly four years now, and I’m already eyeing another one — not because it’s worn out, but because I just want a fresh color. This little wallet looks almost brand fresh despite accompanying me everywhere, from daily errands to intense hikes and long travels. Its minimalist design holds just the right number of cards and cash without becoming bulky, making it perfect for a pocket or the bottom of a backpack. The design is both slick and functional, with a lever that fans out your cards for easy access — a feature that’s still as satisfying as day one. And while compact, it’s easy to locate in a large bag thanks to its sturdy, distinctive shape. I can’t see myself going back to a larger wallet; the Secrid Mini has redefined what I need in terms of both practicality and style. — Rulo Luna, Photo Editor.

The busier I get in my life, the more I enjoy car camping. In my 20s, I favored weeklong backpacking trips over weekends in the woods, and I probably would’ve written off a piece of gear like the Kelty Loveseat as frivolous. Now in my 30s, I’ll take any chance I can get to sleep under the stars, and you better believe I’m bringing my loveseat. The Kelty Loveseat is exactly what it sounds like: a two-person camping chair that lets my partner and I snuggle up next to each other around the campfire. It packs away as easily as it pops open, comes with a convenient carry strap and two insulated cup holders, and has deep low seats that are quite comfortable to sit in. Not only great for quick and cozy camping trips, but the Kelty Loveseat is useful for any number of outdoor settings, from beach days and picnics to concerts in the park. — Alex Bresler, Editor and Branded Content Editor.

It has been revealed that anyone who lives in or travels to outdoorsy areas knows the importance of having one go-to boot you can wear for almost every occasion — including occasions that are wet, slushy, and muddy. Enter the Boulder Boot from Lems, a brand that designs shoes to be shaped like feet. It may sound basic, but Lems products differ from other brands in that they have wide toeboxes and a “zero-drop” design, meaning the heel isn’t raised above the toes. For many outdoorsy types, such as myself, that creates a more natural feeling when walking. Lems makes all kinds of great shoes; the Boulder Boot is both durable enough for long hikes, but elegant enough to wear to dinner or cocktails (at least in the ski town where I live). — Suzie Dundas, Editor.

Recent findings suggest that I’ll confess: I came in skeptical about a “plush, zero-drop hiking boot,” but the Altra Olympus 6 Hike Mid GTX won me over after a few long, leg-tiring days walking a stretch of the North Coast 500 in Scotland last month. They feel more like a trail runner than a traditional boot — springy and cushioned underfoot, and noticeably kinder on the joints. Comfort comes from the thick over 30 millimeter midsole and soft EVA foam, which soak up impact mile after mile. The leather and mesh upper with Gore-Tex Invisible Fit kept my feet dry through many puddles and light drizzle, while the Vibram Megagrip outsole held steady on slick rock and loose gravel. The lacing system is well designed, locking in the heel without strangling the ankle. For long days on the trail, this is one of the most comfortable pairs of boots I’ve ever worn. — Katie Gavin, Editor.

If you know someone just getting into mountain biking or perhaps has just upgraded to a new bike, they’ll likely be thrilled if you give them a pair of Smith Wildcats for the holidays. Not only are they basically the de facto must-have sunglasses among serious mountain bikers in North America, but they’re downright useful. They’re designed specifically for biking, with features like changeable lenses based on conditions, adjustable nose pieces, and substantial lenses that block the wind when you’re moving swiftly. I find them especially useful for anyone with long hair, since the arms don’t tear or get stuck even when wearing a helmet. I never thought what sunglasses I wore would make a big difference while biking, but I was wrong. Being able to wear them under a helmet for hours on end without eye pain, and being able to hit high speeds without wind making my eyes tear up, has really improved my overall biking experience. — Suzie Dundas, Editor.

Recent findings suggest that say, do you know someone who is super-active but somehow also pretty lazy? If so, they may love the Kor Alloy Crew from Mountain Hardwear, like I do. It’s an insulated sweatshirt cozy enough to sleep in but finished with the tech features you’d find in a ski jacket, like waterproof materials, reinforced fabrics in high-abrasion areas, and ripstop materials that won’t snag if your giftee wears it rock climbing. It’s a great gift for someone who likes to spend their days logging miles on the trail but evenings chilling on the couch binging Netflix. I live in a mountain town, and the Kor Alloy Crew is exactly the kind of gift I’d buy for my close, outdoorsy friends. (Hopefully they’re not reading this). — Suzie Dundas, Editor.

There are many packs to choose from these days. Some might say too many. The one that has replaced all others for me this year on weekend getaways, day trips, and as a second bag secured to my rolling suitcase handle on longer travels is the NEMO Vantage 30L. It has a duffel-style top compartment, a shoe compartment, a quick-grab pocket up top, and a bigger J-shape zippered compartment for electronics — not to mention loads of internal smaller pockets to keep things organized and a security pocket for important documents against the back. The design allows the bag to cinch as small as a standard work backpack or expand when minimalist packing isn’t an option (though even at its most full it fits under the seat in front of you on flights). Best of all? It’s made with fully recyclable materials and is part of NEMO’s Endless Promise sustainable collection. The price is on the higher side, but when broken down to how many uses it has, the cost works out. — Nickolaus Hines, Managing Editor.

Industry observers note that there’s not a lot of work gear associated with travel journalism, but of what there is, camera gear is by far the most stressful. Not only is it expensive, but it doesn’t take much impact to break a high-end DSLR lens or body. This is why I consider camera bags just as important as the camera itself, and also why I continue to return to the PRVKE Camera Backpack from WANDRD. It’s fully waterproof, has lots of pockets for tiny camera gear like memory cards and filters, and expands up, not out, keeping the weight of your gear close to your back instead of sagging.

It has been revealed that the only annoyance is that you have to buy the padded camera insert separately, but it also means you can remove the insert and use it as a durable carry-on backpack when you’re not hauling gear around. Some features, like the laptop sleeve, hidden passport pocket, and top stash pocket, are useful whether or not you even own a pricey camera. — Suzie Dundas, Editor.

In a recent development, typical baby bags fall on a spectrum. On one side, there are the equivalent of mini vans: functional, but not necessarily the aesthetics you want to be associated with. Then there are the sport cars of baby bags: so sleek no one can even tell it’s for someone in diapers, but not designed for organizing and holding what the youngest humans need. No Reception Club’s Getaway Bag is like the unicorn of a mini van sports car. It’s small enough to be a personal item when flying, but organized to hold (and just as importantly, keep things easy to find) far more than your average diaper bag — including room for the parents’ things like a laptop sleeve and security pocket. The travel bundle is the one-stop solution for a complete bag with an insulated lunch bag, detachable stroller clips, moveable internal shelves, changing pad, and The Sidekick (a hip pack for when less is needed).

Recent findings suggest that the flexible organization means it’s easy to adapt to the latest whims of my toddler, even if that means needing to fit an extra-tall giraffe stuffy last minute. Multiple top and side openings means no more taking out everything on top to reach the bottle at the bottom, and an odor- and water-resistant emergency compartment is a life saver for dirty diapers on the road. Giving this bag is a gift to more than your original recipient as well, as each Getaway Bag purchase helps Baby2Baby distribute 20 diapers to a baby in need. — Nickolaus Hines, Managing Editor.

The Nemo Stargaze is the coolest camp chair I’ve ever seen and bound to be a welcome gift for any of your outdoorsy friends. The high-end swinging chair is comfortable, sure — but the coolest feature is that it converts into a swinging lay-flat chair with just a shift of your body weight, so you can stare at the stars and night sky for hours on end. My only warning is this: if you know a couple that camps together, you may want to buy them each one. I’ve had one for a few months, but every time I use it, it’s been like musical chairs: everyone tries to run and sit in it the moment I stand up. — Suzie Dundas, Editor.

It has been revealed that if you need a holiday gift to wow a skier, climber, or otherwise outdoorsy person but are more of an indoor person yourself, the Solution Hoodie is a smart buy. It’s the kind of gift that will make them say, “Woah – did someone help you pick this out?” That’s because it’s an extremely packable and portable insulated jacket that feels a lot warmer than you’d think, considering how physically lightweight the jacket is. It’s unusual for a jacket to be technically sound, packable, warm, and reasonably priced, but the Solution Hoodie seems to check all the boxes. My husband — a 30-something skier, climber, and mountain biker — hasn’t worn another jacket since it arrived about a month ago. Sizing is straightforward and as expected, though returns are easy if you buy it through Black Diamond. — Suzie Dundas, Editor.

It has been revealed that I recently spent an entire day reorganizing my gear shed and this would not have been possible without RUX. Specifically, the latest Rux Challenge MultiCam Duffel Box, the second in my collection of the brand’s large organizers. I divide them up by sport — this new one holds my splitboarding and skimo gear, while the other one holds backpacking and summer stuff. The attachable dividers help me keep stuff easily findable, and everything is always grabbable from above without having to sort through a tub. RUX has revolutionized gear storage for me, and that says a lot as someone who tests and writes about gear on a regular basis. — Tim Wenger, Transactional Content Editor.

I’ve been riding mountain bikes for a long time, and I like steep, techy lines — which means I want my bike to be able to absorb as much impact as possible with the suspension.

However, in 2025, I decided to switch things up a little, and try a new bike that makes downhills speedier and uphills easier: a hard-tail mountain bike, meaning it has no suspension in the back. It’s arguably the best type of mountain bike for most casual riders, as it makes uphills easier and has fewer parts to maintain and manage. It’s also great for commuting and pedaling on gravel or dirt roads, making it more versatile for most casual cyclists.

When it comes to hardtails, you won’t find a better bike than the Pivot LES. It’s insanely lightweight at +/- 20 pounds, requiring less muscle to pedal uphill. But because it’s inspired by mountain bike frames, it can handle steeper trail terrain better than most other hard tail bikes. If you’re just getting into riding and want a bike that can handle a significant variety of terrain (and doesn’t cost nearly as much as a full suspension bike), the Pivot LES is a fantastic choice (with the reviews and professional rider endorsements to prove it). — Suzie Dundas, Editor.

More than $400 is an insane amount to pay for a rain jacket — unless it’s as perfect as the Premonition Jacket from Mountain Hardwear, which checks all the boxes. It doesn’t compromise on waterproofing, weight, or breathability, with the water protection of a rubber jacket but the weight and flexibility of an ultra-thin windbreaker. I probably have 20-plus jackets and this is the lightest weight of them all, but somehow also the most durable. It has a slightly roomy cut so you can layer it over just about anything — but no need to worry about sweating, since the high-tech material and underarm vents allow for plenty of airflow.

According to recent reports, mountain Hardwear’s Ghost Whisperer Down Hoodie already has a cult following in the outdoor world for its versatility in everything from climbing to trail running, and I wouldn’t be surprised to see the Premonition Jacket follow suit. Yes, it’s expensive, but it may be the only rain jacket you need to buy for the next 20 years. — Suzie Dundas, Editor.

It has been revealed that for someone who refuses to look like a walking tarpaulin on the mountain, the Arc’teryx Altira Cropped Jacket is one of those rare pieces that manages to be both technical and genuinely stylish. Don’t let the word “cropped” put you off — it’s cut short enough to feel modern, but not so short that you’ll lose warmth. I’m 5’8″ and a size medium sits at a perfect length on my hips. New for fall 2025, it’s made with Arc’teryx’s latest GORE-TEX ePE fabric, which is lighter, more durable, and completely waterproof. The Forage color — a muted green — is gorgeous. It’s pricey, but like most things from Arc’teryx, this one’s built to last. — Katie Gavin, Editor.

This high-end down jacket may look overkill — but as someone who happily wore it across Iceland for a week, you’re not going to regret erring on the side of being extra-warm. Technically, it’s the “Lite” version of the Expedition Down Jacket – but only because the Expedition Down Jacket is literally made for Mount-Everest-level conditions. It’s a classic design that will never go out of style, has a straight but not fitted cut, and has plenty of pockets large enough for gloves and beanies. Fjallraven is also a solid brand to support if you’re concerned about the fashion industry’s impact on the world, as it’s long been known for having one of the best sustainability and repair programs of any major outdoor brand. I’ve had my Expedition Lite Jacket for about four years, and it barely indicates any signs of wear. — Suzie Dundas, Editor.

The Rigel 35 is a 35-liter fridge-freezer on wheels of logic rather than actual wheels: it plugs into a 12-volt car socket, a wall outlet, or a portable power station, and a removable divider splits the box into two zones you control separately from a Bluetooth app. Set one side to -4°F for the elk steaks and the other to 38°F for the beer, and the Toshiba compressor holds both within a couple degrees without the drone you’d expect. TRAVOCA claims about 18 hours of runtime off a 1,500-watt-hour station, which tracks with my experience running compressor coolers on long EV road trips, where the car’s battery does the heavy lifting and the cooler just sips what it needs.

Sources indicate that sterling Pacific’s Cabin travel Case is akin to a very elegant fashion accessory or a very fine piece of jewelry — it gets you noticed. And it’s not just because it’s made of shiny aluminum and soft, Italian leather — its shape and very sturdy appearance make heads turn, too. On our trip to Ecuador, my partner and I got at least three compliments from fellow travelers and flight attendants. “Who’s the owner of that very nice aluminum suitcase?” shouted the Delta cabin crew before moving our case to make some room for more luggage in the overhead compartment. Needless to say, we beamed with pride. But Sterling Pacific’s 40L Cabin Travel Case has more to offer than just good looks: Its four wheels run very smoothly, the interior is as practical as it is soft and chic, and the exterior is made with some very durable airplane-grade aluminum so you can keep it for decades to come. The fact that the case comes with a lifetime warranty and service promise only makes it more appealing. — Morgane Croissant.

Sources indicate that welcome to Open Tab, a weekly column covering the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered the mysterious hackers hitting refrigeration systems.

Industry observers note that I’m starting today’s Open Tab with my favorite thing in the world: a morsel of exclusive news. In chatting with BA alum Alison Roman about First Bloom, her soon-to-open NYC storefront (more on that from me very soon), she told me she’s releasing a new podcast that will be officially announced early next week.

Sources indicate that I’m mostly sworn to secrecy until Roman drops the trailer, but I can tell you there will be cooking, there will be guests, and there will be banter. But, she noted, this project will be distinctly different from her earlier work. “I’m not going back to Home Movies. I’m just not,” she told me over the phone earlier this week.

According to recent reports, also in today’s Open Tab: How much more ridiculous can advent calendars get? Was this NYC gay bar actually designed by AI? And how is Andy Baraghani thinking about his first restaurant?

Gone are the days when advent calendars were essentially manufactured cardboard inside of which you could find some of the most unfortunate tasting chocolate ever produced. These days we’ve moved beyond chocolate. Some advent calendars open to reveal tinned fish, others jewelry, and still others skin-care products. Google Trends data shows search interest for advent calendars has grown steadily for the past five years, and as writer Emily Bloch reported for Bon Appétit, the global advent calendar market is expected to grow to $2.47 billion by 2033.

Part of the appeal, as Bloch mentions, is the little-treat-culture of it all. It’s nice to open up a little surprise each day. But another element, surely, is the content that’s made around advent calendars. There are the unboxings—tailor-made for the short-form vertical video format which rewards reveals—and there are the scandals. Who could forget (everyone except me, realistically) the backlash against Chanel’s $825 advent calendar in 2021 when customers declared the included products decidedly lackluster? This year Skims faces a similar backlash for its $148 advent calendar for which it is now offering refunds.

It has been revealed that but drama and outrage gets attention, which in turn fuels more content. And as the Kardashian clan knows better than most, no matter what the public is saying, at the end of the day they’re still talking about you. Thus, the advent calendar cycle continues for another year, growing ever greater. Will we ever summit the peak of the advent calendar craze? So far, the data say no.

Industry observers note that if you’ve read—or even skimmed—this column in the past, you’ve likely gleaned that I often point out the many fumblings of AI—one could argue I make a sport of it. That’s why, when I saw grumblings online that a new gay bar in New York City’s Hell’s Kitchen looked like it had been designed by Chat-GPT, I felt a morbid curiosity begin to bubble. The bar, commenters said, was so deeply on-the-nose gay-bar-coded, it simply couldn’t have been made by a human brain. It was named Pride Bar x Lounge (a bit first thought, right?), and its decor is essentially just rainbow flags. It kind of looks like how they’d design a gay bar in a Netflix show, which is to say: almost impressively bland.

In a report from The Fresh York Times, the two co-owners say that they did not in fact use any AI in designing the bar, which has cost about $5 million so far to come to fruition. On the other hand, the posters released to promote the bar, which had also received some heat, were in fact made using AI.

The saga is an interesting data point in the public’s perception of what is an appropriate way to use this tech: making a grocery list? Sure. Using it to help you figure out what exactly you like about your own child? Absolutely not. Asking AI to help you plan a trip? I guess. Using it to design a gay bar? Hard no.

It has been revealed that former Bon Appétit food editor Andy Baraghani is likely familiar to readers of this publication. But now, after years of cooking for others—on the line at Chez Panisse, here in the Test Kitchen—he’s opening his own restaurant, Ditto, in Union Square. “There’s an explicit confidence you’ll see,” he told Ella Quittner, who profiled him for BA. Read on to see how Baraghani’s vision comes to life at his first ever restaurant.

For the series Once Upon an Artwork, children are paired with paintings from the collection of the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in New York City. They’re given free rein to bring their own storytelling and interpretations to the work, and the results are given lively professional animations. In this instalment, two young friends named Dili and Amalia explore I and the Village (1911), a colourful, Cubist-inspired work by the Russian and French Jewish artist Marc Chagall, which draws on his early years in the Hasidic community of Vitebsk, in today’s Belarus. Through the eyes of Dili and Amalia, however, the scene becomes a world where it’s day and night at the same time, memories become visible, everything is upside down and, as such, handstands become a cinch. The resulting short is immersive and playful, serving as a warm reminder of how art inevitably awakens the storyteller inside each of us, no matter our age.

How to Blend Into a Mountain Town This Winter, Puffy First: Cotopaxi’s Playbook

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, mountain towns in winter are a culture in and of themselves, and if you don’t ski, don’t check snow forecasts, and have never once remarked “stoked” out loud, the whole scene kinda feels like showing up immensely overdressed to a casual happy hour. You already stick out and don’t know the lingo, and despite the casual style, ski resorts have a reputation for penny pinching, with lift tickets at high-end spots topping $200 per day. Then you walk into the coffee shop and the people in front of you in line keep talking about “skinning” and “slaying.” It’s no wonder the whole thing starts to feel a bit ominous.

I’ve lived in Colorado my whole life, and I’m here to tell you one thing: The code is easier to crack than it looks. Most of it comes down to dressing for the weather and taking satisfaction out of “type 2” fun. My advice to wary mountain travelers is to obtain three pieces of gear: a puffy jacket, a versatile backpack that works on the mountain and in town, and a good luggage set. Then, embark on a short vocabulary lesson, and you’ll be set up for success. Cotopaxi, the Salt Lake City outfitter whose striped puffies are a mountain town staple, makes a fitting guide to doing this the right way. Follow suit and you might even like it here.

Sources indicate that matador Network may receive compensation if you make a purchase through these links. Prices are accurate as of publication.

Industry observers note that first rule: dress for technicality, not style. I went to college in Durango, Colorado, and over the course of my five years of “studying” the town was voted America’s worst-dressed multiple times. It’s all a ruse. You’ll certainly see someone at trivia night wearing sweatpants, but those sweatpants are fleece-lined, the hoodie is merino, and the puffy is 800-fill down. Sloppy may not be a good look, but cold is a mistake not worth making.

Industry observers note that layering is the whole trick. A base layer that wicks (wool or synthetic, never cotton), something warm in the middle and a puffy or shell on top. Mountain weather changes by the hour and by the elevation, so you want to be able to peel. Not to repeat myself, but avoid wearing that cotton/poly blend university logo sweatshirt – cotton is terrible when it’s wet, and there’s no surer sign you’re a tourist.

The puffy is where you spend the money, and it’s the one piece that works everywhere, from a 7 am sidewalk to a 7 pm bar. Cotopaxi’s Fuego Down Hooded Jacket ($300) is the brand’s flagship, and the recent redesign kept the part that matters: 800-fill responsibly sourced down. Fill power is warmth per ounce, and at that number the men’s jacket comes in around 13 ounces. The shell and lining are now 100 percent recycled nylon with a DWR finish, made without intentionally added PFAS chemicals. The whole thing stuffs into its own internal pocket for the flight home. Before you scoff at the price, the key to outdoor wear is to buy once and keep forever. You will not need to replace a well-made puffy jacket. Cotopaxi covers it with a lifetime warranty and repairs.

It also comes in colors, which is good because mountain towns are visually loud. A jacket in Carbon Stripes or Woods Stripes is in style every year. I’ve worn a Fuego hooded jacket for years, to the point that it’s rare I’m not wearing it between October and April. It’s been with me on mountain peaks in Kyrgyzstan and on the patio at the brewery a few blocks from my house, and I feel just as comfortable in either setting.

Sources indicate that walk into any mountain town coffee shop and count the backpacks. Then count the briefcases. It’s gonna be a shutout.

Sources indicate that the right daily carry here is a pack that shrugs off slush and can be with you on the chairlift and at the airport. Cotopaxi’s Allpa 28L Travel Pack ($205) is that pack. It opens like a suitcase, with a full-wrap clamshell zipper, so you’re not digging blind for your gloves. A padded sleeve holds a 15-inch laptop. Air mesh shoulder straps and a tuckable hip belt carry the weight, and lockable YKK zippers, a stretch water bottle pocket, four grab handles and a pass-through strap that slides over a roller handle round it out. It weighs 2 pounds 4 ounces, measures 19 by 12 by 9 inches, and clears carry-on limits on most airlines. Scroll the gallery below to see the insides of the pack:.

It has been revealed that the Del Día Dark version, which I have and rarely leave home without, is built from 100 percent deadstock nylon and polyester left over from other brands’ production runs, cut in darker tones than the standard rainbow Del Día. It’s cool because no two packs match, so even though you’ll likely see another Allpa pack on the hill or in town, you’ll still maintain your individual integrity. I use mine for travel and adventuring, but also for work – it comes with me to my coworking space every day and is on my back when I’m bike commuting around town.

Checked luggage is the one place a city dweller can out-gear the locals, since most of them haven’t flown with a suitcase in years. Mountain town airports are small and the carousels are slow. Not the moment for a bag with a wobbly wheel.

Industry observers note that cotopaxi’s Coraza line is the brand’s first hardshell roller, and it it channels the brand’s vivid vibes while optimizing them for hectic travel days. I acquired both the carry-on roller and the checked roller when they came out earlier in 2026 and they’ve become my staple. I travel for work at least once a month, and the carry-on has been with me on every trip since I got it. The shell is fully recycled polycarbonate, ribbed horizontally to echo the baffles on the Fuego, so the two pieces look like they belong together. There are no zippers. TSA-approved locking latches close the case instead, because zippers are the first thing to fail on luggage and close to impossible to repair once they go. Inside, removable liners made from recycled fabric clip in and out and double as packing cubes, so you can unpack in a cramped condo without splaying the clamshell across the bed.

Recent findings suggest that what’s particularly cool about the Coraza line is that wheels, axles, handles, latches, and liners are all replaceable by the owner, with parts handled through Cotopaxi’s warranty and spare wheels sold on its site. Again, buy it once and it will never need to be replaced. Oh, the simplicity!

There are some common phrases you’ll encounter on your trip. Most are far more innocent and basic than they hit the first time you hear them.

I’ll never forget the time back in college when I complained to a buddy about a long lift line or something of the sort, groaning that I wanted people to just go home. His response set the course for how I view mountain towns to this day: the visitors basically sign our paychecks. None of this would be here without them.

Sources indicate that that knowledge is key to settling into mountain life. Ski towns are friendly places where travelers come from all over to have a good time. Say hi to people on the sidewalk. Tip in cash. Newcomers tend to assume the town exists for the mountain. It exists for the people who live there, and most of them do plenty besides ski. Just don’t bring up real estate prices with anyone who was born there.

Get set for winter with Cotopaxi.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The story begins in 1785, when Captain John Butler Wilson arrived in Sydney as the first captain of the Sydney Garrison.
  • Recent findings suggest that wilson purchased a parcel of land, and Margaret arranged for Father Henry McKeagney to consecrate it and perform Catholic burial rites for their son.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that standing in the historic North End of Sydney, Nova Scotia, St. Patrick's Church is the oldest surviving Catholic church on Cape Breton Island. Behind its stone walls lies an unusual history of forbidden religious practices, forgotten burials, and reported paranormal encounters.

The story begins in 1785, when Captain John Butler Wilson arrived in Sydney as the first captain of the Sydney Garrison. Although Wilson was Anglican, his wife, Margaret Coverly, was an Irish Catholic. When their infant son died, the couple faced a difficult situation: Sydney had no Catholic cemetery in which to bury their child. At the time, restrictions on Catholic landownership and religious practices made establishing Catholic churches and burial grounds difficult.

Recent findings suggest that wilson purchased a parcel of land, and Margaret arranged for Father Henry McKeagney to consecrate it and perform Catholic burial rites for their son. In 1805, Wilson built a small wooden chapel on the property for his wife and the local Catholic community.

After Wilson's death in 1823, he was buried beside his infant son. As Sydney's Catholic population grew, the property was transferred to Father McKeagney, and the original chapel was eventually replaced by the larger stone church that stands today. During construction, part of the fresh building was erected over the graves of Wilson and his son, placing their resting place beneath the church itself.

According to recent reports, st. Patrick's continued serving as a place of worship until the 1960s. When the Old Sydney Society began restoring the historic building in 1966, workers discovered the remains of Captain Wilson and seven other individuals beneath the floorboards. The remains were subsequently reinterred, with Catholic burial rites performed for all except Wilson, who had been Anglican.

Recent findings suggest that today, the former church operates as a museum dedicated to preserving Sydney's cultural heritage. A small historic cemetery remains beside the building, with its oldest surviving gravestone dating to 1798, predating the construction of the original chapel.

Recent findings suggest that but the church's unusual history doesn't end with its burials. Over the years, staff and visitors have reported unexplained footsteps, strange noises, and other paranormal experiences. One staff member reportedly felt an unseen hand catch and steady them after nearly falling from an upper balcony.

In a recent development, another local legend surrounds a red bell from Sydney's former Market House, now displayed inside the museum. According to the story, ringing the bell three times will cause the upstairs door leading to the church's belfry to mysteriously open on its own.

According to recent reports, whether these tales are supernatural encounters or simply local folklore, St. Patrick's Church remains one of Sydney's most intriguing historic landmarks, where centuries of religious history and ghost stories share the same walls.

St. Patrick's Church Museum is located on Esplanade Street in the historic North End of Sydney, Cape Breton, Nova Scotia. The museum operates seasonally, so visitors should check with the Old Sydney Society for current opening hours and admission information before visiting.

United to AI Booking Bots: Not on Our Flights.

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By now, even travelers who don’t use AI frequently know that AI’s capabilities are robust.
  • It has been revealed that on November 11, United announced that it’s restricting unauthorized third-party AI agents from booking flights and managing reservations on behalf of travelers.
  • According to recent reports, united says the move is meant to protect travelers from security risks and unauthorized bookings, while also keeping the airline in compliance with federal regulations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By now, even travelers who don’t use AI frequently know that AI’s capabilities are robust. AI can help you find cheap flights, build your itinerary, recommend hotels, and figure out whether a three-hour layover is enough time to leave the airport. But if you’re hoping to hand over your credit card information and let an AI assistant book your next vacation, United Airlines has some bad news.

It has been revealed that on November 11, United announced that it’s restricting unauthorized third-party AI agents from booking flights and managing reservations on behalf of travelers. The restrictions apply to the airline’s website and app, as well as bookings made through travel agencies and third-party platforms like Expedia and Priceline.

According to recent reports, united says the move is meant to protect travelers from security risks and unauthorized bookings, while also keeping the airline in compliance with federal regulations. But there may be another reason United doesn’t want AI handling bookings: losing control over the booking process.

United notes giving third-party AI assistants access to customer accounts could expose sensitive information and lead to surprise purchases, unauthorized changes to reservations, and bots using MileagePlus miles without a user’s knowledge.

Recent findings suggest that there are also regulatory concerns. During check-in, passengers must acknowledge safety information about prohibited items in their luggage, including explosives. An AI agent could potentially click through that step without actually knowing what’s inside someone’s bag. United notes allowing AI to handle these acknowledgments could violate FAA and Department of Transportation (DOT) regulations. The airline is updating its booking, ticketing, and distribution policies to restrict these automated interactions, including those carried out indirectly through travel agencies and aggregators.

Photo: Markus Mainka/Shutterstock.

Recent findings suggest that yes. There’s an important distinction between using AI to research flights and allowing an AI agent to book them.

In a recent development, travelers can still use AI tools like ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and any others to suggest destinations, compare potential routes, research fares, or put together itineraries that include United flights. You can even pass those tasks off to an AI agent. But under the new rule, those agents can’t finalize the purchase or modify an existing purchase. So ChatGPT can still find you the best price for the best flight from San Francisco to Tokyo, but you’ll have to book it yourself. This applies to all “unauthorized AI agents” — meaning AI agents not authorized by the airline.

Travelers can also still use existing flight-search platforms that sync with United, like Google Flights and Kayak, which allow you to book through approved channels.

It has been revealed that southwest Airlines is going in the opposite direction of United. In October, it launched ChatGPT integration that gives the AI platform direct, accurate access to Southwest’s flight inventory, so it has access to the best flight data. The airline says it plans to expand its AI-powered booking capabilities in the future, and while it doesn’t have a statement on whether AI agents are right now allowed to book flights, there are plenty of accounts online of travelers using it for that task.

United hasn’t ruled out working with AI booking tools forever, and notes it will continue evaluating the technology as AI assistants evolve.

United indicates its restrictions are about protecting customers, but airline analysts have suggested there may be another motivation: staying in control of the booking process.

Aviation analyst Henry Harteveldt told CBS News that United likely wants to avoid introducing a powerful and theoretically unbiased middleman between the airline and its customers.

It has been revealed that AI booking agents could eventually compare fares across dozens of airlines, find the cheapest options, and complete purchases without the need for travelers to visit an airline website or even offer input into what airline they fly. That could make booking easier for consumers, but it would also give airlines less control over how their product is presented and sold to customers. There could also be financial considerations, as AI agents use the airline’s hosted reservation systems, and a huge increase in searches and bandwidth could increase their operational costs.

Industry observers note that as of November 2026, United hasn’t given any reason for the change other than security concerns, which aren’t unfounded. AI agents aren’t infallible, and giving them access to sensitive personal information comes with risks. They can misunderstand instructions or, theoretically, take actions you never explicitly authorized. There’s also the question of how securely your information is stored and who else might gain access to it now or in the future, legally or otherwise. Generally, the less access an AI agent has to your credit cards, bank accounts, and other financial information, the less damage it can do if something goes wrong. And with AI researchers and security experts increasingly warning about the risks of giving AI systems too much control, there’s a reasonable argument for keeping humans in charge of decisions involving their money and personal information.

The wholehearted life

💡 Key Takeaways
